days.title: First commands & files
days.objective: The very first commands: check the system, make files and folders, and move around.

questions.q: Which command shows which Red Hat version your machine is running?
questions.explain: `/etc/redhat-release` is a small text file holding the OS version; `cat` prints it.

questions.q: What does `whoami` print?
options: The username you are currently logged in as
questions.explain: It answers "who am I right now" — useful when you switch users later.

questions.q: What does `touch linux{1..50}.txt` create?
options: 50 files named linux1.txt through linux50.txt in one command
questions.explain: `{1..50}` is brace expansion — bash expands it to 1 2 3 … 50 before touch runs.

questions.q: What is wrong with `mkdir mydata1 mydata 2 mydata3`?
options: mkdir cannot make more than one folder
The space in "mydata 2" makes mkdir create two folders: "mydata" and "2"
questions.explain: Spaces separate arguments, so `mydata 2` is read as two names. Write `mydata2` with no space.

questions.q: What does `cd ..` do?
options: Moves up one level to the parent directory
questions.explain: `..` means "parent". `cd ~` (or just `cd`) goes home; `cd /` goes to the root.

questions.q: Linux is case-sensitive. Why did `cd desktop` fail but `cd Desktop` work?
options: The folder is named "Desktop" with a capital D, and Linux treats names case-sensitively
questions.explain: `Desktop` and `desktop` are different names on Linux.

questions.q: Create an empty file called myfile.txt.
questions.explain: `touch` makes a new empty file (or updates the time on an existing one).

questions.q: Create three files at once named myfile.doc, myfile.pdf and myfile.html.
questions.explain: `touch` accepts several names separated by spaces.

questions.q: Make 50 folders named linux51 through linux100 in one command.
questions.explain: Brace expansion works for mkdir too.

questions.q: Print the full path of the directory you are standing in.
questions.explain: "print working directory".

questions.q: Go back to your home directory from anywhere.
questions.explain: `cd` with no argument, or `cd ~`, returns home.

labs.title: Your first files and folders
labs.scenario: Check your Red Hat version and who you are, make a folder "mydata", create files linux1.txt to linux50.txt, then make folders linux51 to linux100.

labs.title: Navigation practice
labs.scenario: From your home directory, go into Desktop, list it, come back up, go into Downloads, then return home. Watch the prompt and pwd at each step.

theory.h: Talking to Linux through the terminal

blocks.x: When you open the terminal you are typing to the **shell** (bash), which runs your commands. A command usually has three parts: the **command** itself, **options** (flags like `-l`), and **arguments** (what it acts on). Linux is **case-sensitive**, so `Desktop` and `desktop` are different names — this is why `cd desktop` failed but `cd Desktop` worked in class.
`cat /etc/redhat-release` prints which Red Hat version the machine runs.
`whoami` prints the username you are logged in as.
`pwd` ("print working directory") shows the full path of where you are.
`touch name` creates an empty file (or updates its time). You can make several at once: `touch a.txt b.txt`.
`mkdir name` makes a folder; `mkdir a b c` makes several.

**Brace expansion** is a shortcut bash expands before the command runs: `touch linux{1..50}.txt` creates linux1.txt … linux50.txt, and `mkdir linux{51..100}` makes 50 folders. Watch out for **spaces**: `mkdir mydata 2` makes two folders ("mydata" and "2"), because spaces separate arguments.
`cd` changes directory. Remember the shortcuts:
`cd Desktop` go into a folder, `cd ..` go up one level (note the **space** — `cd..` fails), `cd` or `cd ~` go home, `cd /` go to the very top.
After moving, `pwd` confirms where you are, and `ls` lists what's there.

days.title: cat and echo: creating and filling files
days.objective: Use cat and echo to create files, write into them, and append.

questions.q: What does `cat linux10.txt` do?
options: Prints the contents of linux10.txt on the screen
questions.explain: `cat` shows a file's contents.

questions.q: What does `cat > linux10.txt` do?
options: Creates (or overwrites) the file and lets you type its contents; press Ctrl+D to finish
questions.explain: `>` redirects what you type into the file, replacing anything already there.

questions.q: What is the difference between `cat > file` and `cat >> file`?
options: `>` overwrites the file; `>>` adds to the end (appends)
questions.explain: One arrow replaces, two arrows append — the same rule applies to `echo`.

questions.q: What does `echo welcome to jspm > linux1.txt` do?
options: Writes the text "welcome to jspm" into linux1.txt, overwriting it
Prints the text on screen only
questions.explain: `echo` prints text; `>` sends that text into the file instead of the screen.

questions.q:
`echo -e "i
am
root"` — what does `-e` and `
` do?
options: -e enables escape sequences, and \n inserts a new line
questions.explain: With `-e`, `\n` = newline, `\t` = tab, `\b` = backspace, `\v` = vertical tab.

questions.q: Why does `echo"hello"` fail but `echo "hello"` work?
options: A space is needed between the command "echo" and its argument
questions.explain: The shell needs a space to separate the command from what you give it.

questions.q: Print the file linux1.txt to the screen.
questions.explain: `cat` dumps the whole file.

questions.q: Create the file linux10.txt and type its contents from the keyboard (overwriting it).
questions.explain: Finish typing with Ctrl+D.

questions.q: Add more lines to the end of linux10.txt from the keyboard.
questions.explain: `>>` keeps the existing contents and appends.

questions.q: Write "welcome to rscoe" to the end of linux1.txt without erasing it.
questions.explain: `>>` appends; `>` would overwrite.

questions.q: Print three words on three separate lines using echo with escapes.
questions.explain: `-e` turns on `\n` as a newline.

labs.title: Overwrite vs append
labs.scenario: Create linux1.txt with "hii i am pranjal", view it, then append "welcome to rscoe", view it again, then overwrite it with "hii i am linux user".
steps: echo hii i am pranjal > linux1.txt
echo hii i am linux user > linux1.txt

labs.title: Escape sequences
labs.scenario: Use echo -e to write text with newlines into a file called linuxg.txt, then view it.
steps:
echo -e "i
am
root for this
linux class only" > linuxg.txt

blocks.x: `cat file` prints a file's whole contents to the screen. Its name comes from "concatenate" because it can also join files. But in class you also used `cat` to **create and fill** files.
The arrows `>` and `>>` send output into a file instead of the screen — this is **redirection**:
`cat > linux10.txt` creates (or **overwrites**) the file and lets you type its contents; press **Ctrl+D** on an empty line to finish.
`cat >> linux10.txt` **appends** — it keeps what's there and adds your new lines at the end.
The single rule to remember: **one arrow `>` overwrites, two arrows `>>` append.**
`echo` prints text. Combined with redirection it's a quick way to write files:
`echo "welcome to jspm" > linux1.txt` writes that line into the file (overwriting).
`echo "welcome to rscoe" >> linux1.txt` adds a line to the end.
Note the **space** after echo: `echo"hello"` fails, `echo "hello"` works.
Normally `echo` prints text as-is. With the **`-e`** option it understands **escape sequences**:
`\n` = new line, `\t` = tab, `\b` = backspace, `\v` = vertical tab.

So `echo -e "i
am
root"` prints the three words on three separate lines. You can send it into a file too: `echo -e "i
am
root" > linuxg.txt`.

days.title: date and cal
days.objective: Read and format the date, and print calendars.

questions.q: What does `date` with no options print?
questions.explain: Add a `+format` to show only the parts you want.

questions.q: What does `date +%B` show?
questions.explain: `%b` is the short month name (Oct), `%B` the full one (October).

questions.q: Which format code gives the 4-digit year?
questions.explain: `%Y` = 2026, `%y` = 26 (two digits), `%m` = month number, `%d` = day of month.

questions.q: What does `cal 2026` display?
options: The full calendar for the whole year 2026
questions.explain: `cal` alone shows this month; a year number shows all 12 months.

questions.q: What does `cal -j` show?
options: A calendar with Julian day numbers (day-of-year, 1–365)
questions.explain: `-j` numbers each day by its position in the year.

questions.q: How do you read the manual for the date command?
questions.explain: `man date` opens the manual; `cal --help` gives a quick option summary.

questions.q: Show today's day-of-month number only.
questions.explain: `%d` is the numeric day (01–31).

questions.q: Show the full month name of today.
questions.explain: `%B` = full month name.

questions.q: Show the 4-digit year.
questions.explain: `%Y` is the four-digit year.

questions.q: Print this month's calendar.
questions.explain: `cal` alone shows the current month.

questions.q: Print the calendar for the whole year 2026.
questions.explain: A year argument prints all 12 months.

labs.title: Date formatting drill
labs.scenario: Print, each on its own line: the day number, the month number, the short month name, the full month name, and the four-digit year.

labs.title: Calendars
labs.scenario: Show this month, then the whole of 2026, then a calendar with Julian (day-of-year) numbers. Read the manual for cal.

blocks.x: `date` on its own prints the current date and time. To show just the part you want, add a **`+format`** with percent codes:
`%d` day of month (01–31), `%m` month number (01–12), `%y` two-digit year, `%Y` four-digit year.
`%b` short month name (Oct), `%B` full month name (October), `%D` the short date (mm/dd/yy).
So `date +%B` prints the full month name, and `date +%Y` prints the four-digit year.
`cal` prints a calendar:
`cal` alone shows the current month.
`cal 2026` shows the whole year 2026.
`cal -n 3` shows several months around now; `cal -j` numbers each day by its day-of-year (Julian, 1–365); `cal -m` starts the week on Monday.
Every command has documentation:
`man date` and `man cal` open the full manual (press `q` to quit, `/word` to search).
`cal --help` prints a quick summary of options.
These built-in help sources matter because the RHCSA exam has no internet.

days.title: Exploring the filesystem
days.objective: Move through the Linux directory tree and read system files.

questions.q: On Linux, everything lives under which single top directory?
questions.explain: There are no drive letters; `/` is the root of the whole tree.

questions.q: Which directory holds system configuration files like /etc/passwd?
questions.explain: `/etc` = configuration. `/bin` and `/usr/bin` hold programs, `/var/log` holds logs.

questions.q: What does /etc/passwd contain?
options: One line per user account with fields separated by colons
questions.explain: The password itself is not here (it shows as `x`); it's the account list.

questions.q: What is the difference between `ls -l` and `ls -ld` on a folder?
options: `ls -l` lists what's inside the folder; `ls -ld` shows the folder's own details
questions.explain: `-ld` is how you check a directory's own permissions and owner.

questions.q: Why does `cd..` (no space) fail while `cd ..` works?
options: A space is required between the command and its argument
questions.explain: `cd` is the command, `..` is the argument — they must be separated by a space.

questions.q: Which command recalls the commands you have typed before?
questions.explain: `history` lists them; you can also search with Ctrl+R.

questions.q: Go to the root of the filesystem.
questions.explain: A single `/` is the top of the tree.

questions.q: Print the account list file.
questions.explain: Each line is one account.

questions.q: Show the details (permissions, owner) of the folder mydata itself, not its contents.
questions.explain: `-d` means "the directory itself".

questions.q: Show your command history.
questions.explain: Numbers let you rerun with `!number`.

labs.title: A tour of the tree
labs.scenario: Starting from /, visit and list these directories, noticing what each holds: /etc, /bin, /var/log, /usr/bin, /tmp. Return home afterward.

labs.title: Read system files
labs.scenario: Look at the Red Hat version, the account list, and the long listing of /etc.

blocks.x: Linux has no drive letters. Everything hangs off a single **root** directory written as `/`. Other disks and devices appear as folders inside this one tree. Learning where things live saves time later.
`/etc` — system **configuration** files (like `/etc/passwd`).
`/bin` and `/usr/bin` — programs (commands) you run.
`/usr/sbin` and `/sbin` — administrator programs.
`/var/log` — log files that record what the system is doing.
`/tmp` — temporary files.
`/dev` — device files; `/proc` — live information about running processes; `/mnt` and `/media` — places to attach other disks.

`cat /etc/passwd` shows one line per user account, with fields separated by colons: `name:x:UID:GID:comment:home:shell`. The real password is **not** here (the `x` is a placeholder) — this file is just the list of accounts. You'll come back to it when creating users.
`ls -l` gives a **long listing** — permissions, owner, size and date for each item.
`ls -ld folder` shows the **folder's own** details instead of listing its contents (the `-d` means "the directory itself").
`history` recalls commands you've typed; rerun one with `!number`.

days.title: Searching text with grep
days.objective: Find lines that match a pattern, and change what grep reports.

questions.q: What does `grep root /etc/passwd` do?
options: Prints every line of /etc/passwd that contains "root"
questions.explain: `grep PATTERN FILE` prints matching lines.

questions.q: What does `grep -n` add to the output?
options: The line number of each match
questions.explain: `-n` prefixes each matching line with its number.

questions.q: What does `grep -v pranjal passwd` show?
options: Every line that does NOT contain "pranjal"
questions.explain: `-v` inverts the match.

questions.q: What does `grep -o pranjal passwd` print?
options: Only the matched word "pranjal" from each match, not the whole line
questions.explain: `-o` shows only the matching part.

questions.q: What does `grep -e prasanna -e pranjal passwd` do?
questions.explain: Each `-e` adds another pattern to search for.

questions.q: How do you see all the options grep supports quickly?
questions.explain: `grep --help` prints a summary; `man grep` is the full manual.

questions.q: Show the lines of /etc/passwd that contain "root".
questions.explain: Classic way to find the root account's line.

questions.q: Show matching lines with their line numbers for the word "passwd" in the file tmp.
questions.explain: `-n` adds line numbers.

questions.q: Show the lines of tmp that do NOT contain "pranjal".
questions.explain: `-v` inverts the match.

questions.q: Print only the matched word (with line numbers) for "pranjal" in tmp.
questions.explain: `-o` only the match, `-n` line numbers — options can be combined.

labs.title: grep on the account file
labs.scenario: Copy /etc/passwd to a file called tmp, then: find lines with "root", find lines with numbers, show lines without "nologin", and print only the word "bash" where it appears.

labs.title: Two patterns at once
labs.scenario: In tmp, find any line containing either "root" or "bash", with line numbers.

blocks.x: `grep` searches text for lines that match a **pattern** and prints those lines. The basic form is `grep PATTERN FILE`, for example `grep root /etc/passwd` prints every line containing "root". It also reads from a pipe: `command | grep word`.
Small options change the behaviour a lot:
`-n` adds the **line number** to each match.
`-v` **inverts** the search — lines that do NOT match (e.g. `grep -v nologin tmp`).
`-o` prints **only the matched word**, not the whole line.
`-e pattern` lets you give more than one pattern: `grep -e prasanna -e pranjal tmp` matches either word.
Options combine: `grep -on word tmp` shows only the match with its line number.

`grep` is how you pull useful lines out of big files — log files, the account list, config files. On the exam you'll often filter `/etc/passwd` or a log with grep. Use `grep --help` for a quick option list, or `man grep` for the full manual.

days.title: sed, cut, sort and counting
days.objective: Transform and summarise text: substitute, extract columns, sort, and count.

questions.q: What does `sed "s/pranjal/pranju/" tmp` do?
options: Prints tmp with the first "pranjal" on each line replaced by "pranju" (file unchanged)
questions.explain: `s/old/new/` substitutes; add `g` to replace every match on a line.

questions.q: What makes sed change the file itself?
options: Nothing; sed always edits the file
questions.explain: Without `-i`, sed only prints the result and leaves the file as it was.

questions.q: What does `sed '5,7s/purva/pranjal/g' file` do?
options: On lines 5 to 7 only, replaces every "purva" with "pranjal"
questions.explain: `5,7` is a line range; `$` means the last line (e.g. `7,$`).

questions.q: What does `cut -d: -f1 tmp` print?
options: The first field of each line, using ":" as the separator
questions.explain: `-d` sets the delimiter, `-f` picks the field number. `/etc/passwd` uses `:`.

questions.q: What does `sort -n` do that plain `sort` does not?
questions.explain: `-r` reverses, `-t:` sets a field separator, `-k4` sorts by the 4th field.

questions.q: Which counts the number of LINES in a file?
questions.explain: `-l` lines, `-w` words, `-c` characters/bytes.

questions.q: Replace "bin" with "bbin" throughout the file tmp, changing the file itself.
questions.explain: `-i` edits in place; add `g` to catch more than one per line.

questions.q: Print only the first colon-separated field of tmp.
questions.explain: The username field in /etc/passwd.

questions.q: Sort the file tmp in reverse order.
questions.explain: `-r` = reverse.

questions.q: Count how many lines are in tmp.
questions.explain: One line per account, so this also counts accounts.

questions.q: Show the first 2 lines of tmp.
questions.explain: `head` shows the top; `tail` shows the bottom (`tail -6` = last 6).

labs.title: Transform the account file
labs.scenario: Using your tmp copy of /etc/passwd: substitute "nologin" with "lllog" (preview only), then pull out the username column, then sort it, and finally count the lines.

labs.title: Sorting by a field
labs.scenario: Sort tmp by the 3rd field (the UID) numerically, using ":" as the separator.

labs.title: head, tail and wc
labs.scenario: Show the first 7 lines, the last 6 lines, and the line, word and character counts of tmp.

blocks.x: `sed` is a stream editor that transforms text. Its most common job is **substitution**: `sed "s/old/new/" file` prints the file with the first "old" on each line replaced by "new".
Add `g` at the end to replace **every** match on a line: `s/old/new/g`.
By default sed only **prints** the result and leaves the file unchanged. The **`-i`** option edits the file **in place**: `sed -i "s/bin/bbin/" tmp`.
You can limit it to **line ranges**: `sed '5,7s/purva/pranjal/g' file` only touches lines 5–7, and `$` means the last line (`7,$`).
`cut` pulls out **fields** (columns):
`-d` sets the **delimiter** (separator) and `-f` picks the field number. Since `/etc/passwd` uses colons, `cut -d: -f1 tmp` prints the username column, and `-f3` the UID.
`sort tmp` sorts lines alphabetically; `-r` reverses, `-n` sorts **numerically**, `-t:` sets a field separator and `-k3` sorts by the 3rd field (so `sort -t: -k3 -n` sorts by UID).
`head -n N` shows the first N lines, `tail -n N` (or `tail -6`) the last.
`wc` counts: `-l` lines, `-w` words, `-c` characters. `wc -l tmp` counts accounts.
These small tools chain together with pipes to analyse any text.

days.title: Users and groups
days.objective: Create and modify user accounts and groups.

questions.q: Which command creates a new group called linux?
questions.explain: `groupadd` makes a group; `useradd` makes a user.

questions.q: After `useradd myuser1`, how do you set its password?
questions.explain: `passwd NAME` (as root) sets another user's password.

questions.q: What does `id user2` show?
options: The user's UID, primary group (GID) and supplementary groups
questions.explain: `id` is how you check an account's identity and group memberships.

questions.q: What is the key difference between `usermod -G` and `usermod -aG`?
options: -G replaces all supplementary groups; -aG appends without removing the others
questions.explain: Always use `-aG` to add a group safely — `-G` alone wipes the existing list.

questions.q: What does `usermod -g class user2` change?
questions.explain: Lowercase `-g` = primary group; uppercase `-G` = supplementary groups.

questions.q: What does a shell of /sbin/nologin do for an account?
options: Prevents that account from logging in interactively (used for service accounts)
questions.explain: Set it with `usermod -s /sbin/nologin name` or `useradd -s /sbin/nologin name`.

questions.q: Create a group named linux.
questions.explain: Verify with `cat /etc/group`.

questions.q: Create a user called ram with UID 1089.
questions.explain: `-u` sets the UID; check with `id ram`.

questions.q: Add the user ram to the group kkk WITHOUT removing his other groups.
questions.explain: `-aG` appends; forgetting `-a` would replace all his supplementary groups.

questions.q: Set ram's primary group to class.
questions.explain: Lowercase `-g` for the primary group.

questions.q: Create a user varsha with UID 1095, primary group 2076, and a no-login shell.
questions.explain: Combine options in one useradd command.

questions.q: Set a comment (full name) of "developer2" on the user john_toddler.
questions.explain: `-c` sets the comment/GECOS field; see it in /etc/passwd.

labs.title: Create users and groups
labs.scenario: Create group "linux". Create users prann and user1, both in group linux. Create user2, then change its primary group to a new group "class". Check each with id.

labs.title: Append vs replace groups (the -aG lesson)
labs.scenario: Create user ram. Add him to group kkk, then also to class, then also to linux — all without losing the earlier groups. Then check his groups.

labs.title: One-line account spec
labs.scenario: Create user varsha with UID 1095, primary group 2076 (create the group first), and shell /sbin/nologin. Confirm.

blocks.x: Every person or service is a **user account** with a numeric **UID**, and belongs to groups (a **primary** group plus any number of **supplementary** ones). Two files store this: `/etc/passwd` (the account list) and `/etc/group` (the groups). View them with `cat /etc/passwd` and `cat /etc/group`.
`groupadd linux` makes a group; `useradd myuser1` makes a user; `passwd myuser1` sets its password; `id myuser1` shows its UID and groups.

Useful `useradd` options: `-u 1095` sets the UID, `-g 2076` sets the primary group, `-G linux` adds a supplementary group, `-s /sbin/nologin` sets a non-login shell. You can combine them: `useradd -u 1095 -g 2076 -s /sbin/nologin varsha`.
`usermod` changes an existing user. The important distinction the class drilled:
**`-g group`** changes the **primary** group.
**`-G groups`** sets the **supplementary** group list — but used alone it **replaces** the whole list, wiping the others.
**`-aG group`** **appends** a supplementary group safely. Always use `-aG` to add a group.
`-c "comment"` sets the full-name/comment field; `-s /sbin/nologin` changes the shell; `-u` changes the UID.

A shell of `/sbin/nologin` creates an account that **cannot log in interactively** — used for service accounts that need to exist but should never be a login. Set it at creation (`useradd -s`) or later (`usermod -s`).

days.title: Permissions and ownership
days.objective: Change who owns files and what each class of user may do.

questions.q: In `ls -ld` output like `drwxr-x---`, what are the three groups of rwx for?
questions.explain: Each group is read(r) write(w) execute(x) for that class of user.

questions.q: What does `chmod o+w /mydata` do?
questions.explain: Symbolic mode: who (u/g/o/a), operator (+/-/=), permission (r/w/x).

questions.q: What is the difference between `chmod o=rwx` and `chmod o+rwx`?
options: `=` sets others to exactly rwx; `+` adds rwx to whatever others already have
questions.explain: `=` is absolute, `+`/`-` are relative.

questions.q: What does `chmod 771` mean in numbers?
options: rwx for owner (7), rwx for group (7), execute-only for others (1)

questions.q: What does `chmod g+s` on a directory do (the SGID bit)?
options: New files created inside inherit the directory's group — good for shared folders
questions.explain: You saw this on /data/impdata so a team shares the group automatically.

questions.q: `ls -l /usr/bin/passwd` shows an `s` where owner-execute should be. What is that?
options: The SUID bit: passwd runs with its owner's (root's) privileges so you can change your password
questions.explain: SUID lets a normal user update /etc/shadow safely through passwd.

questions.q: Make myuser the owner of the folder /unnati.
questions.explain: `chown USER path` changes the owner (root only).

questions.q: Change the group of /unnati to sales.
questions.explain: `chgrp` changes just the group (or `chown :sales /unnati`).

questions.q: Give others exactly read, write and execute on /unnati.
questions.explain: `=` sets exactly those permissions for "others".

questions.q: Set /test/impdata to rwx for owner and group, execute-only for others, using numbers.
Turn on the SGID bit on /data/impdata so new files inherit its group.
questions.explain: Or `chmod 2771` (the leading 2 is SGID).

labs.title: Owner, group and permissions
labs.scenario: Create /unnati. Make "myuser" the owner and "sales" the group. Give the owner read+execute, the group rwx, and others nothing. Check with ls -ld after each change.

labs.title: A shared team directory (SGID)
labs.scenario: Create /data/impdata. Make "amit" the owner and "redhat" the group, set mode 771, then add the SGID bit so files made inside belong to the redhat group.

labs.title: See SUID in action
labs.scenario: Look at the permissions of the passwd program and explain why a normal user can change their own password.
steps: # the 's' in the owner slot = SUID: it runs as root (its owner)

blocks.x: Run `ls -l` (files) or `ls -ld` (a folder itself) and look at the left column, e.g. `drwxr-x---`. After the first type character, the nine letters are **three groups of rwx** for three classes of user: **owner (u)**, **group (g)**, and **others (o)**. `r` = read, `w` = write, `x` = execute (and on a directory, `x` means "may enter it").
`chmod` sets permissions two ways:

**Symbolic**: `who operator permission`. Who = `u g o a`; operator = `+` (add), `-` (remove), `=` (set exactly); e.g. `chmod o+w /mydata` adds write for others, `chmod o=rwx /unnati` sets others to exactly rwx, `chmod o=--- /unnati` removes everything for others.
**Octal (numbers)**: r=4, w=2, x=1 added per class. `chmod 771` = rwx owner (7), rwx group (7), execute-only others (1).
`chown myuser /unnati` makes myuser the **owner** (root only).
`chgrp sales /unnati` changes the **group** (or `chown :sales /unnati`).
These decide which class — owner, group, or others — a given user falls into for a file.
Beyond rwx there are special bits shown as an `s`:

**SUID** on a program makes it run with its **owner's** privileges. `ls -l /usr/bin/passwd` shows an `s` in the owner slot — that's why a normal user can change their own password (passwd runs as root).
**SGID** on a **directory** (`chmod g+s /data/impdata`, or octal `2771`) makes new files inside inherit the **directory's group** — perfect for a shared team folder.

days.title: Switching users and sudo
days.objective: Become another user, and grant admin rights with wheel and sudo.

questions.q: What is the difference between `su user1` and `su - user1`?
options: `su -` does not ask for a password
`su -` loads user1's full environment and home directory (a login shell); `su` keeps your current environment
questions.explain: Prefer `su -` so the environment matches the target user.

questions.q: When you run `su user1` as a normal user, whose password is asked?
questions.explain: `su` asks for the target user's password; `sudo` asks for your own.

questions.q: On RHEL, members of which group get sudo (admin) rights by default?
questions.explain: Add a user with `usermod -aG wheel name`. The rule is in /etc/sudoers.

questions.q: What is the safe way to edit the sudoers file?
options: visudo (it checks the syntax before saving)
questions.explain: A syntax error in sudoers can lock everyone out of sudo; visudo prevents that.

questions.q: A sudoers rule `user1 ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD:ALL,!/usr/bin/passwd` means user1 can:
options: Run any command as root without a password, EXCEPT the passwd command (the ! excludes it)
questions.explain: The `!` negates a command, carving an exception out of "ALL".

questions.q: Switch to the user deep with a full login shell.
questions.explain: The dash gives deep's environment and home directory.

questions.q: Add the user deep to the wheel group so he can use sudo.
questions.explain: `-aG` appends wheel without removing deep's other groups.

questions.q: Safely open the sudoers file for editing.
questions.explain: Always use visudo, never edit /etc/sudoers directly.

labs.title: Become another user
labs.scenario: Create user vilas, give him a bash shell, then switch into his account with a full login shell and check who you are.

labs.title: Grant sudo via wheel
labs.scenario: Create user deep, add him to the wheel group, switch to him, and confirm he can run an admin command with sudo.

labs.title: A custom sudo rule
labs.scenario: Using visudo, let user1 run all commands as root without a password except changing passwords, then test it.

blocks.x: `su` lets you become another user:
`su user1` switches to user1 but keeps your current environment; it asks for **user1's** password.
`su - user1` starts a **login shell** — it loads user1's full environment and moves to their home directory. Prefer `su -`.
`su -` with no name becomes root. Type `exit` to return to your own account.

theory.h: Giving admin rights: the wheel group

blocks.x: Instead of sharing the root password, RHEL grants admin rights through **sudo**. Members of the **wheel** group can run commands as root using their **own** password:
`usermod -aG wheel deep` adds deep to wheel (note `-aG` so you don't wipe his other groups).
Then `deep` can run, for example, `sudo cat /etc/shadow` and type **his own** password.
The difference to remember: `su` asks for the **target** user's password; `sudo` asks for **your own**.

theory.h: Editing sudo rules safely with visudo

blocks.x: sudo's rules live in `/etc/sudoers`. **Never edit that file directly** — a typo can lock everyone out of sudo. Use **`visudo`**, which checks the syntax before saving. A rule has the form `user host=(runas) commands`:
`user1 ALL=(ALL) ALL` lets user1 run any command as root (with a password).
`user1 ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD:ALL,!/usr/bin/passwd` lets user1 run anything as root **without** a password, **except** the passwd command — the `!` carves out an exception.

days.title: Shell basics and getting help
days.objective: Access shell prompts, issue commands with correct syntax, and find answers in man, info and /usr/share/doc.

questions.q: In the prompt `[student@servera ~]$`, what does the final `$` tell you?
options: A command is still running in the background
You are logged in as root
You are logged in as a regular (non-root) user
questions.explain: A `$` prompt means a normal user; `#` means root. Always glance at it before running admin commands.

questions.q: Which command searches the short descriptions of all man pages for a keyword?
questions.explain: `man -k` is the same as `apropos`. If it returns "nothing appropriate", build the index as root with `mandb`.

questions.q: Which man section documents configuration file formats such as /etc/fstab?
questions.explain: Section 1 = user commands, 5 = file formats, 8 = admin commands. Use `man 5 fstab`.

questions.q: Open the manual page for the /etc/passwd file format (not the passwd command).
questions.explain: Without the section number, `man passwd` opens section 1, the command.

questions.q: Where do packages usually install extra documentation such as example config files?
questions.explain: Look in `/usr/share/doc/<package>` for READMEs and examples. It is available during the exam.

questions.q: Which keyboard shortcut searches backwards through your bash command history?
questions.explain: Press Ctrl+R, type part of an old command, press Ctrl+R again to go further back, Enter to run it.

questions.q: Show only the last 20 commands from your history.
questions.explain: `history` alone shows everything; `!N` reruns entry number N.

questions.q: What does `!!` do in bash?
options: Inverts the exit code of the last command
Repeats the last argument of the previous command
Opens the history file in an editor
questions.explain: `!!` is the whole last command (handy as `sudo !!`). `!$` is only the last argument.

questions.q: Find out whether `cd` is a shell builtin, an alias, or a program on disk.
questions.explain: `type` reports how bash resolves a name. Builtins have no separate man page; use `help cd`.

questions.q: Inside a man page, how do you search forward for the word "UID"?
options: Type /UID and press Enter, then n for the next match
questions.explain: man uses the `less` pager: `/pattern` searches forward, `n` next match, `N` previous, `q` quit.

labs.title: Find answers only with the built-in documentation
labs.scenario: Without using the internet, find out: (1) which man section documents /etc/shadow, (2) which useradd option sets a specific UID, and (3) which commands have "partition" in their description.
hints: `man -f name` lists every section that has a page with that name.
If `man -k` finds nothing, the index has not been built yet.
steps: man useradd        # then type /UID and press n
sudo mandb         # only if man -k printed "nothing appropriate"

labs.title: Practise history and shell shortcuts
labs.scenario: Run five different commands. Rerun the third one by its history number, reuse the last argument of a command with `!$`, find an old command with Ctrl+R, then save your whole history to ~/myhistory.txt.

blocks.x: When you open a terminal on Linux you are talking to a **shell** — a program that reads the commands you type, asks the kernel to run them, and shows you the result. The default shell on RHEL is **bash** (the Bourne-Again SHell). Everything you do on the RHCSA exam happens through this text interface, so being fast and confident here is the foundation for the whole exam. A command line usually has three parts: the **command** (the program to run), its **options** (flags that change how it behaves, like `-l`), and its **arguments** (what it acts on, like a filename). For example in `ls -l /etc`, `ls` is the command, `-l` is an option, and `/etc` is the argument.
Before every command the shell prints a **prompt**. On RHEL it looks like `[student@servera ~]$`. Read it carefully because it tells you a lot:
`student` is the user you are logged in as.
`servera` is the hostname of the machine.
`~` is your current directory (`~` means your home directory).
The final symbol is the most important: `$` means you are a **normal user**, while `#` means you are **root** (the all-powerful administrator). Always glance at this before running admin commands.
The exam has **no internet**, so knowing the built-in documentation is essential. Three sources cover almost everything:
**man pages** — `man command` opens the manual for a command. Inside, it uses the `less` pager: press Space to page down, `/word` to search, `n` for the next match, and `q` to quit.

**man sections** — the manual is split into numbered sections. Section 1 is user commands, section 5 is file formats (like `/etc/fstab`), and section 8 is admin commands. If a name exists in more than one section, pick the one you need: `man 5 passwd` shows the file format, `man 1 passwd` the command.
**`--help` and /usr/share/doc** — most commands accept `--help` for a quick summary, and installed packages drop examples and READMEs into `/usr/share/doc/<package>`.
If you do not know a command's name, search the descriptions with `man -k keyword` (also called `apropos`). If it says "nothing appropriate", build the index once as root with `mandb`.

theory.h: Working faster with history and shortcuts

blocks.x: Bash remembers the commands you type. This saves huge amounts of time:
`history` lists past commands; `!42` reruns command number 42; `!!` reruns the previous command (handy as `sudo !!`); `!$` reuses the last argument of the previous command.
**Ctrl+R** starts a reverse search — type part of an old command and bash finds it; press Enter to run it.
**Tab completion** finishes filenames and command names for you; press Tab twice to see all matches.
`type name` tells you whether a name is a shell builtin, an alias, or a program on disk.

days.title: Managing files and directories
days.objective: Create, delete, copy and move files and directories; understand the filesystem hierarchy.

questions.q: Where are system-wide configuration files kept on RHEL?
questions.explain: `/etc` holds configuration. `/usr` holds installed software, `/var` holds variable data such as logs.

questions.q: Which directory holds data that changes while the system runs, such as logs, spools and caches?
questions.explain: Logs live in `/var/log`, for example `/var/log/messages` and `/var/log/secure`.

questions.q: Which of these paths is absolute?
questions.explain: An absolute path starts with `/` and works from any current directory.

questions.q: Create the directory tree a/b/c in one command, creating missing parents.
questions.explain: Without `-p`, mkdir fails if `a` or `a/b` doesn't exist.

questions.q: Copy the directory /etc/skel and everything inside it to /tmp/skelcopy.
questions.explain: Directories need `-r`. `-a` (archive) also keeps permissions, ownership and timestamps.

questions.q: What is the difference between `rmdir dir` and `rm -r dir`?
options: rmdir only removes empty directories; rm -r removes the directory and its contents
rmdir asks for confirmation; rm -r never deletes hidden files
questions.explain: Use `rmdir` when you want a safety check that a directory is empty.

questions.q: Which files does the glob `file?.txt` match?
options: file1.txt and fileA.txt, but not file10.txt
Only a file literally named file?.txt
questions.explain: `?` matches exactly one character, `*` matches any number, `[abc]` matches one of a set.

questions.q: Create report1.txt through report5.txt with a single touch command.
questions.explain: Brace expansion `{1..5}` expands to 1 2 3 4 5 before the command runs.

questions.q: As a regular user with no aliases, what happens with `mv a.txt b.txt` when b.txt already exists?
options: mv refuses and prints an error
b.txt is overwritten without any prompt
questions.explain: Use `mv -i` to be asked first. On RHEL, root has aliases `rm -i`, `cp -i` and `mv -i` set in /root/.bashrc.

questions.q: Go back to the directory you were in just before the current one.
questions.explain: `cd -` toggles between your last two directories. `cd` alone goes home.

labs.title: File management workout
labs.scenario: As student, build ~/lab2 with subdirectories projects, archive and trash. Create notes1.txt to notes3.txt inside projects. Copy notes1.txt into archive, rename notes2.txt to draft.txt, move notes3.txt into trash, then delete the trash directory with everything in it.
hints: Brace expansion saves typing for both mkdir and touch.

labs.title: Tour the filesystem hierarchy
labs.scenario: Find where these live on your RHEL VM and note them down: the SSH server config file, the kernel image, the `ls` binary, the system log file, and the home directory of root.

blocks.x: Linux organises everything under a single root directory called `/`. There are no drive letters like on Windows — even other disks appear as folders inside this one tree. The layout follows the **Filesystem Hierarchy Standard (FHS)**, so the same directories mean the same thing on any RHEL system. Knowing where things live saves you from hunting during the exam:
`/etc` — system-wide **configuration** files.
`/home` — regular users' home directories; `/root` is root's home.
`/var` — **variable** data that changes as the system runs: logs in `/var/log`, spools, caches.
`/usr` — installed software (`/usr/bin`, `/usr/sbin`, libraries, `/usr/share/doc`).
`/boot` — the kernel and boot loader files.
`/tmp` — temporary files, wiped periodically.
`/dev` — device files; `/proc` and `/sys` — live kernel/hardware information.

A **path** is how you name a file's location. An **absolute path** starts from the root and always begins with `/`, for example `/home/student/notes.txt` — it works no matter where you currently are. A **relative path** is measured from your current directory, for example `notes.txt` or `../reports/q1.txt`. Two special names help you move around: `.` means "the current directory" and `..` means "the parent directory". `~` is a shortcut for your own home directory.
A few commands are your eyes and feet on the system:
`pwd` prints the directory you are standing in ("print working directory").
`cd` changes directory: `cd /etc` (absolute), `cd ..` (up one), `cd ~` or just `cd` (home), and `cd -` toggles back to the previous directory.

`ls` lists contents. The flags do the work: `-l` gives a detailed long listing, `-a` shows hidden dotfiles, `-h` shows human-readable sizes, `-t` sorts by time, `-R` recurses into subdirectories. You will use `ls -lah` constantly.
These verbs manage files and directories:
`mkdir` makes directories; `mkdir -p a/b/c` builds a whole nested path at once.
`touch file` creates an empty file (or updates a file's timestamp).
`cp source dest` copies; add `-r` to copy a whole directory tree, and `-a` (archive) to also preserve permissions, ownership and timestamps.
`mv` moves a file, or **renames** it if the target is in the same directory.

`rm` deletes files — there is **no recycle bin**, it is gone. `rm -r` removes a directory and everything in it, and `rm -f` forces with no prompt. `rm -rf` is powerful and dangerous, so double-check the path.

Two conveniences save typing: **brace expansion** like `touch file{1..5}.txt` creates file1 through file5, and **globbing** with wildcards where `*` matches any characters, `?` matches exactly one, and `[abc]` matches one character from a set.

days.title: Links and finding files
days.objective: Create hard and soft links, and locate files with find.

questions.q: What is true about a hard link?
options: It breaks when the original file is deleted
It points to the same inode as the original file
It can point to a directory
It stores the path of the original file
questions.explain: Hard links are extra names for the same inode. The data stays until the last name is removed.

questions.q: What happens to a symbolic link when its target file is deleted?
options: The link keeps a copy of the data
The link remains but is broken (dangling)
questions.explain: A soft link stores a path. If nothing exists at that path, the link is broken. `ls -l` shows it in red.

questions.q: Which of these can a hard link NOT do?
options: Share the same inode as the original
Point to a directory or to a file on another filesystem
Point to a file in the same directory
questions.explain: Soft links can cross filesystems and point to directories; hard links cannot.

questions.q: Create a symbolic link /root/hosts-link that points to /etc/hosts.
questions.explain: Order: `ln -s TARGET LINKNAME`. Leave out `-s` to make a hard link.

questions.q: Find every file on the system owned by user natasha, hiding "Permission denied" errors.
questions.explain: `2>/dev/null` discards error messages from directories you cannot read.

questions.q: Which find test matches files larger than 100 MiB?
questions.explain: `+` means more than, `-` means less than. Units: k, M, G.

questions.q: Find files under /etc that were modified in the last 2 days.
questions.explain: `-mtime -2` = less than 2 days ago. Use `-mmin` for minutes.

questions.q: In `find / -user harry -exec cp -a {} /root/harry/ \;` what does `{}` stand for?
questions.explain: `\;` ends the -exec command. find runs it once for every match, putting the path in place of `{}`.

questions.q: What does the second column of `ls -l` output show for a file?
options: The number of users who opened it
The number of hard links to it
questions.explain: `ls -i` shows the inode number. A link count of 2 on a file means one extra hard link exists.

questions.q: Find every file under /usr that has the SUID bit set.
questions.explain: `-perm -4000` means "at least these bits". `ls -l` shows SUID as an `s` in the owner execute slot.

labs.title: Hard links vs soft links

labs.title: Find a user's files and copy them (exam classic)
labs.scenario: Create user harry and give him a few files in /tmp and his home. Then, as root, find every regular file owned by harry and copy it into /root/harryfiles, keeping permissions.
hints: Create the destination directory before running find.

theory.h: Inodes: the real identity of a file

blocks.x: Every file on a Linux filesystem is really an **inode** — a numbered record holding the file's data location, permissions, owner, size and timestamps. The **name** you see in a directory is just a label that points to an inode. This idea explains how links work. See the inode number with `ls -i` or `stat`.

A **hard link** is an additional name pointing at the *same inode*. Both names are equal — neither is "the original" — and the file's data survives until the **last** name is removed. Because a hard link is just another directory entry for the same inode, it cannot cross to another filesystem and cannot point to a directory. The second column of `ls -l` shows the **link count**: how many names point to that inode. Create one with `ln target linkname` (no `-s`).

A **symbolic link** is different: it is a tiny special file that stores a *path* to another file, like a shortcut. Because it stores a path, it **can** cross filesystems and **can** point to directories — but if the target is deleted or moved, the link is left **dangling** (broken) and `ls -l` shows it in red. Create one with `ln -s target linkname`, and remember the order is always target first, then the link name.
`find` is the most powerful search tool because it walks the filesystem live and can test many properties and then act on the matches. The pattern is `find <where> <tests> <action>`:
Tests: `-name '*.conf'`, `-type f` (files) or `-type d` (directories), `-size +100M` (bigger than 100 MiB), `-mtime -1` (changed in the last day), `-user natasha`, `-perm -4000` (SUID bit set).
Action: by default it prints matches; `-ls` shows details; `-exec cmd {} \;` runs a command on each match, where `{}` becomes the matched path and `\;` ends the command.

A very common exam pattern is copying every file owned by a user: `find / -user harry -type f -exec cp -a {} /root/harry/ \; 2>/dev/null`. The `2>/dev/null` hides "Permission denied" errors from directories you cannot read. `locate name` is a faster name search using a prebuilt database, but the database can be stale — refresh it with `updatedb`.

days.title: Redirection and pipes
days.objective: Use input-output redirection (>, >>,

questions.q: What does `2>` redirect?
questions.explain: File descriptors: 0 = stdin, 1 = stdout, 2 = stderr.

questions.q: What does `command > out.txt 2>&1` do?
options: Sends both standard output and standard error to out.txt
Sends output to out.txt and errors to a file called 1
questions.explain: `2>&1` means "send stderr to wherever stdout goes now". The order matters.

questions.q: With `command 2>&1 > file`, where do the errors go?
options: Nowhere; bash reports a syntax error
questions.explain: Redirections are processed left to right. At the time of `2>&1`, stdout still pointed at the terminal.

questions.q: Append the line "hello" to notes.txt without overwriting it.
questions.explain: `>` truncates the file first. `>>` appends.

questions.q: Search the whole filesystem for files named passwd, throwing away all error messages.
questions.explain: /dev/null discards everything written to it.

questions.q: What does `tee` do?
options: Copies its input to a file and to standard output at the same time
Splits a file into two parts
Joins two files side by side
questions.explain: Example: `ls -l | tee list.txt | wc -l` saves the listing and still counts it.

questions.q: Save the output of `ls -l /etc` to /root/etc.txt and also show it on the screen.
questions.explain: Use `tee -a` to append instead of overwrite.

questions.q: In bash, what does `&> file` do?
options: Runs the command in the background and writes to file
Redirects both stdout and stderr to file
questions.explain: `&> file` is short for `> file 2>&1`. Use `&>> file` to append both.

questions.q: What does the pipe `|` connect?
options: The stdout of the left command to the stdin of the right command
The stderr of the left command to the right command
The exit code of the left command to the right command
questions.explain: Errors are not piped unless you add `2>&1` first (or use `|&`).

questions.q: Count the number of lines in /etc/passwd.
questions.explain: Each line in /etc/passwd is one account, so this also counts accounts.

labs.title: Redirection practice
labs.scenario: Run `ls /etc /nonexistent` four ways: output only to ok.txt, errors only to err.txt, both to all.txt, and append a second run to all.txt. Check each file after every step.

labs.title: Build a pipeline
labs.scenario: Show the 5 largest files in /usr/bin with their sizes in human-readable form and save that list to /root/biggest.txt while also printing it.

blocks.x: Every Linux program automatically has three data streams, each with a number (a "file descriptor"):
**stdin** (0) — standard input, where the program reads from (normally the keyboard).
**stdout** (1) — standard output, where normal results go (normally the screen).
**stderr** (2) — standard error, where error messages go (also the screen by default, but a *separate* stream).
Keeping output and errors separate is what makes redirection powerful.
**Redirection** sends a stream to a file instead of the screen (or reads it from a file):
`command > file` sends stdout to a file, **overwriting** it. `command >> file` **appends** instead.
`command 2> file` sends only stderr to a file. `command 2>> file` appends errors.
`command > out 2>&1` sends stdout to `out`, then sends stderr to "wherever stdout now points" — so both go to `out`. Order matters here. The shorthand `command &> file` does the same.
`command < file` feeds a file into the program's stdin.
`/dev/null` is the "black hole": anything sent there is discarded, so `2>/dev/null` throws away errors.

A **pipe** `|` connects the **stdout** of one command to the **stdin** of the next, letting you build a chain where each tool does one job. For example `ls -l /etc | grep conf | wc -l` lists `/etc`, keeps only lines containing "conf", and counts them. Errors are not sent through a normal pipe unless you first merge them with `2>&1`.

theory.h: tee: output to a file and the screen

blocks.x: Sometimes you want to *save* output and still *see* it. `tee` copies its input to a file **and** to stdout at the same time: `ls -l /etc | tee list.txt` shows the listing and writes it to `list.txt`. Use `tee -a` to append. A key exam habit: only produce exactly what a task asks for — do not add `sort` or other changes unless the task says so, because the grader checks the actual file.

:$ for the first line, :0 for the last

questions.q: In vim, which key enters insert mode before the cursor, and which opens a new line below?
options: Insert key only; there is no key for a new line
I inserts at the cursor; n opens a line below
a inserts before the cursor; O opens a line below
i inserts before the cursor; o opens a new line below
questions.explain: `a` appends after the cursor, `A` at the end of the line, `O` opens a line above.

labs.title: vim speed drill
labs.scenario: Copy /etc/services to ~/services.txt and open it in vim. Show line numbers, jump to line 100, delete 3 lines, go to the end of the file, add a line "# edited by me", replace every "tcp" with "TCP", then save and quit.

theory.h: Reading files without opening an editor

blocks.x: Often you just want to *look* at a file:
`cat file` dumps the whole file to the screen (and can join files: `cat a b > c`).
`less file` shows it one screen at a time — Space pages down, `b` pages back, `/word` searches, `q` quits. It is the same pager `man` uses.

`head file` shows the first 10 lines (`head -n 20` for 20); `tail` shows the last 10. **`tail -f file` follows a file live** as new lines are added — essential for watching logs such as `tail -f /var/log/secure`.

`echo` prints text or the value of a variable: `echo "Hello"`, `echo $PATH`. Combined with redirection it is a quick way to create or append to files: `echo "a line" >> notes.txt`. Variables in bash are written `$NAME`; double quotes `"$NAME"` expand the variable while keeping spaces intact, whereas single quotes `'$NAME'` treat it literally.
`nano` is a beginner-friendly terminal editor. The important shortcuts are shown at the bottom of the screen: **Ctrl+O** writes (saves) the file, **Ctrl+X** exits. It is fine for quick edits.
`vim` is the editor to know for the exam because it is always installed. It is **modal**, meaning keys do different things depending on the mode:

**Normal (command) mode** is where you start — keys move and edit. `dd` cuts a line, `yy` copies a line, `p` pastes, `u` undoes, `Ctrl+R` redoes, `gg` jumps to the top, `G` to the bottom, `:set nu` shows line numbers.
**Insert mode** is for typing text — press `i` to insert before the cursor, `a` to append after it, or `o` to open a new line below. Press **Esc** to return to normal mode.
**Command-line mode** starts with `:` — `:w` writes, `:q` quits, `:wq` (or `ZZ`) writes and quits, `:q!` quits without saving, and `:%s/old/new/g` replaces every "old" with "new" in the whole file.
If you only learn one thing: press **Esc**, then type `:wq` to save and quit, or `:q!` to bail out. Running `vimtutor` once (about 30 minutes) teaches everything you need.

days.title: grep and regular expressions
days.objective: Use grep and regular expressions to analyze text.

questions.q: Show the lines of /etc/passwd that start with "root".
questions.explain: `^` anchors the match to the start of the line.

questions.q: Which regular expression matches lines that end with "bash"?
questions.explain: `$` anchors to the end of the line. `^$` matches an empty line.

questions.q: In a basic regular expression, what does `.` match?
questions.explain: Escape it as `\.` to match a real dot, for example `grep '\.conf$'`.

questions.q: Show all lines in /etc/ssh/sshd_config that are neither comments nor empty lines.
questions.explain: This is the quickest way to see what a config file really sets.

questions.q: What does `grep -E 'cat|dog' file` print?
options: Lines containing cat followed by dog
Only the words cat and dog
questions.explain: `-E` turns on extended regex so `|`, `+`, `?` and `{n}` work without backslashes.

questions.q: Count how many lines in /etc/passwd contain "nologin".
questions.explain: `-c` prints a count instead of the lines.

questions.q: What does `grep -w root` do differently from `grep root`?
options: It only matches "root" as a whole word
questions.explain: With `-w`, "rootkit" and "chroot" no longer match.

questions.q: Search every file under /etc for "PermitRootLogin" and show file names with line numbers.
questions.explain: `-r` recursive, `-n` line numbers, `-i` ignore case, `-l` file names only.

questions.explain: Don't sort or change the output unless the task asks. Check with `cat /root/ssh.txt`.

questions.q: Which grep option makes the match case-insensitive?
questions.explain: `grep -i error` matches Error, ERROR and error.

labs.title: Text hunting with grep
labs.scenario: Using /etc/passwd: list users whose shell is /bin/bash, count them, list accounts with UID 0, and save the non-login (nologin) account names to /root/nologin-users.txt.
hints: Use `cut -d: -f1` to keep only the user name field.

labs.title: Regular expressions on a log
labs.scenario: As root, find in /var/log/secure every failed password line, count them, and print only unique source IP addresses. (Create failures first by trying a wrong password with `ssh wronguser@localhost`.)
steps: ssh wronguser@localhost      # type a wrong password a few times

blocks.x: `grep` searches text for lines matching a pattern and prints those lines. It is the workhorse of log analysis and config inspection. The basic form is `grep pattern file`, and it also reads from a pipe: `command | grep pattern`. Useful options:

`-i` ignores case, `-v` inverts the match (lines that do **not** match), `-c` counts matching lines, `-n` shows line numbers, `-w` matches whole words only, `-r` searches recursively through a directory, and `-l` prints only the names of matching files.
A **regular expression** (regex) is a pattern language that makes grep powerful. The core pieces:
`^` anchors to the **start** of a line, `$` anchors to the **end**. So `^root` matches lines starting with root, and `bash$` matches lines ending with bash. `^$` matches an empty line.
`.` matches any single character; escape it as `\.` to mean a literal dot.
`*` means "zero or more of the previous item".

With **extended** regex (`grep -E`), you also get `|` (or), `+` (one or more), `?` (optional), and `{n}` (repeat) without needing backslashes. For example `grep -E 'cat|dog'` matches lines containing cat or dog.
A few patterns come up again and again:
Show what a config file really sets, ignoring comments and blank lines: `grep -Ev '^#|^$' /etc/ssh/sshd_config`.
List the users who use the bash shell from `/etc/passwd`: `grep '/bin/bash$' /etc/passwd`.
Count failed SSH logins in the security log: `grep -c 'Failed password' /var/log/secure`.
Combine grep with `cut -d: -f1` to keep just the first colon-separated field (like the username in `/etc/passwd`).

days.title: Local users and groups
days.objective: Create, delete and modify local user accounts and groups.

questions.q: How many colon-separated fields does each line in /etc/passwd have?
questions.explain: name:password:UID:GID:comment:home:shell. The password field is `x` because the hash is in /etc/shadow.

questions.q: Where are the password hashes stored?
questions.explain: /etc/shadow is readable only by root. It also stores password-aging fields.

questions.q: On RHEL, which UID does the first regular user account get by default?
questions.explain: UID 0 is root, 1-999 are system accounts. The range comes from /etc/login.defs.

questions.q: Create a user named harry with UID 2000.
questions.explain: Check with `id harry`.

questions.q: Add the existing user natasha to the supplementary group sysmgrs without removing her other groups.
questions.explain: Always use `-a` with `-G`, or the other supplementary groups are removed.

questions.q: What happens if you run `usermod -G sysmgrs natasha` (without -a)?
options: sysmgrs is added to her existing groups
natasha's supplementary groups are replaced by only sysmgrs
questions.explain: `-g` changes the primary group; `-G` sets the full supplementary list.

questions.q: Create the user sarah with a shell that does not allow interactive login.
questions.explain: `/sbin/nologin` and `/usr/sbin/nologin` are the same file on RHEL.

questions.q: Create a group named sysmgrs with GID 3000.
questions.explain: Verify with `getent group sysmgrs`.

questions.q: Which command deletes the user harry together with his home directory and mail spool?
questions.explain: Without `-r`, the home directory stays on disk, owned by a now-unused UID.

questions.q: What does the "user private group" scheme mean on RHEL?
options: Users cannot belong to more than one group
Each new user gets a primary group with the same name as the user
Every user joins the users group
questions.explain: That's why `useradd harry` also creates a group called harry.

labs.title: Exam-style user setup
labs.scenario: Create group sysmgrs. Create users natasha and harry with sysmgrs as a supplementary group. Create user sarah with a non-interactive shell who is not a member of sysmgrs. Set the password of all three to "Rhcsa@2026".
steps: for u in natasha harry sarah; do echo 'Rhcsa@2026' | passwd --stdin $u; done
verify: id natasha; id harry; id sarah

labs.title: Modify accounts

steps: grep sarah /etc/shadow      # a ! appears before the hash

theory.h: Users, UIDs and the account files

blocks.x: Every person or service on the system is a **user account** identified by a number called a **UID**. Three files define accounts:
`/etc/passwd` holds one line per user with seven colon-separated fields: `name:x:UID:GID:comment:home:shell`. The password field is just `x` because the real hash lives elsewhere.
`/etc/shadow` holds the encrypted password hashes and password-aging information; it is readable only by root.
`/etc/group` defines groups.
On RHEL, **root** is UID 0, system accounts use UIDs 1–999, and the first regular user gets UID **1000** (the range comes from `/etc/login.defs`).

theory.h: Groups and the user private group scheme

blocks.x: A **group** lets you give a set of users the same access. Each user has one **primary group** (used for files they create) and any number of **supplementary groups**. RHEL uses the **user private group** scheme: creating user `harry` also creates a group called `harry` as his primary group. This keeps each user's files private by default while still allowing shared groups for teamwork.
The core commands:
`useradd harry` creates a user (with `-u` to set the UID, `-s` to set the login shell, `-G` to add supplementary groups, `-c` for a comment/full name).
`passwd harry` sets or changes a password; `echo 'secret' | passwd --stdin harry` sets it non-interactively (handy in scripts and the exam).

`usermod` changes an existing account. The most important rule: to **add** a supplementary group without wiping the others, always use `usermod -aG groupname user` — the `-a` means "append". Leaving out `-a` **replaces** the whole supplementary list.
`userdel -r harry` deletes the account **and** its home directory; without `-r` the home directory is left behind.
`groupadd`, `groupmod` and `groupdel` manage groups; `id harry` and `getent passwd harry` show what an account looks like.
A shell of `/sbin/nologin` gives an account that cannot log in interactively — used for service accounts.

days.title: Passwords, aging and sudo
days.objective: Change passwords and adjust password aging; configure privileged access.

questions.q: What does `chage -M 90 harry` set?
options: harry gets a warning 90 days before expiry
harry must wait 90 days before changing his password
harry must change his password at most every 90 days
questions.explain: -M max days, -m min days, -W warning days, -I inactive days, -E account expiry date.

questions.explain: Setting the last-change date to 0 means the password counts as already expired.

questions.q: Make natasha's account expire on 2026-12-31.
questions.explain: The account (not just the password) stops working after this date.
