questions.explain: Look for PASS_MAX_DAYS, PASS_MIN_DAYS and PASS_WARN_AGE.

questions.q: You edit PASS_MAX_DAYS in /etc/login.defs. Which accounts does it affect?
options: Only accounts created after the change
questions.explain: For existing users, run `chage` on each one.

questions.q: Show the password-aging information for harry.
questions.explain: It shows last change, expiry, min, max and warning days in readable form.

questions.q: Set sarah's password to Secret123 without an interactive prompt.
questions.explain: `--stdin` is a RHEL passwd option; it's handy in scripts and exam tasks.

questions.q: What is the safe way to edit sudo rules?
options: Use visudo, or put a file in /etc/sudoers.d/ and check it with visudo -c
questions.explain: visudo checks the syntax before saving. A broken sudoers file can lock everyone out of sudo.

questions.q: Which sudoers line lets members of sysmgrs run any command as root without a password?
questions.explain: `%` marks a group. Without the `%`, sudo treats the name as a user.

questions.q: On RHEL, members of which group get full sudo access by default?
questions.explain: /etc/sudoers contains `%wheel ALL=(ALL) ALL`. Add a user with `usermod -aG wheel user`.

questions.q: What is the difference between `su harry` and `su - harry`?
options: `su -` starts a login shell with harry's full environment and home directory
`su` without the dash only works for root
`su -` does not ask for a password
questions.explain: Prefer `su -` so PATH and variables match the target user.

labs.title: Password policy task
labs.scenario: Make passwords of all NEW users expire after 30 days. For the existing user harry, set maximum password age to 60 days with a 7-day warning, and force him to change his password at next login. Make natasha's account expire on 2026-12-31.
verify: useradd testuser && chage -l testuser | grep Maximum

labs.title: Configure privileged access
labs.scenario: Members of sysmgrs must run all commands as root without a password. User alex may only run `systemctl` as root (with a password). Use files in /etc/sudoers.d and check the syntax.
verify: su - natasha -c 'sudo -n id'      # should print uid=0 with no password prompt

theory.h: Why passwords live in two files

blocks.x: When you log in, Linux checks your password. But the account details and the secret password are kept apart for safety. `/etc/passwd` is readable by everyone and holds the account basics; the actual scrambled password (a **hash**) lives in `/etc/shadow`, which only root can read. This way an ordinary user can look up account info without ever seeing the hashes.
`passwd` changes a password.
As a normal user, typing `passwd` on its own changes **your own** password (it asks for the current one first).
As **root**, `passwd harry` sets another user's password without knowing the old one.
`echo 'Secret123' | passwd --stdin harry` (RHEL-only) sets a password without the interactive prompt — very useful in scripts and on the exam.

`passwd -l harry` **locks** an account (puts a `!` in front of the hash so no password works); `passwd -u harry` unlocks it; `passwd -e harry` **expires** the password so the user must change it at next login.
"Aging" means forcing passwords to change over time. `chage` (change age) controls this per user:
`chage -l harry` **lists** harry's current aging settings in plain language — always start here.
`chage -M 90 harry` sets the **maximum** days a password is valid (must change every 90 days).
`chage -m 7 harry` sets the **minimum** days before it can be changed again.
`chage -W 7 harry` sets the **warning** days before expiry.
`chage -E 2026-12-31 harry` sets an **account** expiry date (the whole account stops working after that day).
`chage -d 0 harry` sets the last-change date to zero, which counts as already expired — so harry must set a new password at next login.

System-wide defaults for **new** users live in `/etc/login.defs` (look for `PASS_MAX_DAYS`, `PASS_MIN_DAYS`, `PASS_WARN_AGE`). Changing that file only affects accounts created afterward; existing users need `chage`.

theory.h: Becoming another user: su and sudo

blocks.x: Sometimes you need more power than your own account has.

`su - harry` **switches** to harry (asks for harry's password). The dash is important: `su -` starts a full **login shell**, loading harry's environment and moving to his home directory. Without the dash you keep your own environment. `su -` with no name means "become root".

`sudo command` runs a single command **as root** (or another user), but you type **your own** password, and only if you have been granted permission. This is safer than sharing the root password and it logs who did what.
On RHEL, members of the **wheel** group get full sudo by default. Add a user with `usermod -aG wheel harry`.
sudo's rules live in `/etc/sudoers`, but you must **never** edit it directly with a plain editor — a typo can lock everyone out. Instead:
Run `visudo`, which checks the syntax before saving.
Better, drop a small file into `/etc/sudoers.d/` (e.g. `/etc/sudoers.d/admins`) and check it with `visudo -c`.

A rule looks like `harry ALL=(ALL) ALL` (harry may run any command as anyone). A group rule starts with `%`: `%sysmgrs ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL` lets the sysmgrs group run anything as root **without** a password. `%wheel ALL=(ALL) ALL` is the default wheel rule.

days.title: Standard permissions
days.objective: List, set and change ugo/rwx permissions and ownership.

questions.q: What is `rwxr-x---` in octal?
questions.explain: r=4, w=2, x=1 per group of three: 7 (rwx), 5 (r-x), 0 (---).

questions.q: What does the x (execute) permission mean on a directory?
options: You can enter the directory and reach files inside it
You can run every script inside it
questions.explain: r on a directory lets you list names; x lets you enter or traverse; w lets you create and delete entries (it needs x too).

questions.q: What permission do you need to delete a file?
options: Read and write on the file
Write and execute on the directory that contains it
questions.explain: Deleting changes the directory, not the file. The sticky bit changes this rule.

questions.q: Add write permission for the group on report.txt using symbolic mode.
questions.explain: Symbolic mode: who (u g o a), operator (+ - =), permissions (r w x).

questions.q: Set script.sh to rwxr-xr-x using octal mode.
questions.explain: 7 = rwx, 5 = r-x.

questions.q: Make harry the owner and sysmgrs the group of /data in one command.
questions.explain: `chown :group file` changes only the group, same as `chgrp`.

questions.q: Change the group of /shared and everything inside it to sysmgrs.
questions.explain: `-R` applies the change recursively.

questions.q: Who can change which user owns a file?
options: Any member of the file's group
questions.explain: A regular owner can change the group, but only to a group they belong to.

questions.q: In `ls -l` output `-rw-r--r--.`, what does the trailing `.` mean?
options: The file is a hard link
The file has an SELinux context and no ACL
questions.explain: A `+` in that spot means the file has an ACL. Check with `getfacl`.

questions.q: Remove all permissions for "others" on secret.txt without touching owner and group permissions.
questions.explain: `=` with nothing after it sets that class to no permissions.

labs.title: Permissions workout
labs.scenario: Create /srv/project owned by harry and group sysmgrs. Owner: full access. Group: read and enter only. Others: nothing. Inside, create plan.txt readable and writable only by the owner. Test access as natasha and sarah.

labs.title: Fix a script that will not run
labs.scenario: Create /usr/local/bin/hello.sh containing `echo Hello $USER`. Run it and read the error. Fix the permissions so every user can run it but only root can edit it.

blocks.x: Linux is multi-user, so every file and directory records **who may do what** with it. Look at the left of `ls -l` output, for example `-rwxr-xr--`. That is ten characters: the first is the **type** (`-` file, `d` directory, `l` link), and the remaining nine are three groups of three permissions.

theory.h: The three who's and the three what's

blocks.x: Permissions are set for three classes of people:
**u** = the **user** who owns the file (owner).
**g** = the **group** that owns the file.
**o** = **others** (everyone else).
And three kinds of access:
**r** (read) = 4, **w** (write) = 2, **x** (execute) = 1.
So `rwxr-xr--` means: owner can read/write/execute, group can read/execute, others can only read.

theory.h: What r, w, x mean on directories (the tricky part)

blocks.x: On a **file** the meanings are obvious. On a **directory** they are different:
**r** lets you **list** the names inside (e.g. run `ls`).
**x** lets you **enter** the directory and reach files inside (traverse it). Without `x` you cannot `cd` in, even if you can read the name list.
**w** (plus x) lets you **create and delete** entries inside.
A common bug: a file is readable but a user still cannot open it — usually because a parent directory is missing `x` for them. Trace the whole path with `namei -l /path/to/file`.
`chmod` changes permissions two ways.

**Symbolic mode** spells out who/operator/what: `chmod g+w file` adds write for group, `chmod o-rwx file` removes all from others, `chmod u=rwx,go=rx file` sets exact values, and `chmod a+x file` adds execute for all (a = all three classes).

**Octal (numeric) mode** adds up r=4, w=2, x=1 for each class: `chmod 755 file` = rwx (7) for owner, r-x (5) for group, r-x (5) for others. `chmod 644` is the normal file default (rw-r--r--), `chmod 600` is owner-only. `chmod -R` applies changes recursively through a directory tree.
`chown harry file` changes the **owner** to harry (root only).
`chown harry:sysmgrs file` changes owner **and** group at once.
`chown :sysmgrs file` changes just the group (same as `chgrp sysmgrs file`).
`chown -R harry:sysmgrs /data` changes ownership through a whole tree.
A regular owner may change a file's group only to a group they belong to; only root can give a file to a different user.

days.title: Special permissions, umask and ACLs
days.objective: Manage default file permissions and diagnose and correct file permission problems.

questions.q: What does the SGID bit do on a directory?
options: Files inside it run with group privileges
New files created in it get the directory's group
Only the group owner may delete files in it
Group members get write access automatically
questions.explain: This is how you build shared team directories.

questions.q: What does the sticky bit do on a directory such as /tmp?
options: Users can only delete their own files, even with write permission on the directory
Files are never deleted at reboot
New files inherit the directory's owner
questions.explain: /tmp shows `drwxrwxrwt`. In octal the sticky bit is 1, e.g. `chmod 1777`.

questions.q: Set the SGID bit on /home/managers using symbolic mode.
questions.explain: Octal version: `chmod 2770 /home/managers` (2 = SGID, 4 = SUID, 1 = sticky).

questions.q: With umask 027, what permissions does a newly created regular file get?
questions.explain: Files start from 666, directories from 777, then the umask bits are removed: 666-027 = 640, 777-027 = 750.

questions.q: Set the umask of your current shell so new files are 600 and new directories 700.
questions.explain: Run `umask` with no argument to see the current value.

questions.q: How do you make a user's umask survive logout and reboot?
options: Set it with chmod on the home directory
Put the umask command in that user's ~/.bashrc or ~/.bash_profile
questions.explain: For every user, use a script in /etc/profile.d/ instead.

questions.q: Give user natasha read and write access to /var/tmp/fstab using an ACL.
questions.explain: View the result with `getfacl /var/tmp/fstab`.

questions.q: Use an ACL so that user harry has no access at all to /var/tmp/fstab.
questions.explain: A named-user ACL entry takes priority over the "other" permissions.

questions.q: `ls -l /usr/bin/passwd` shows `-rwsr-xr-x`. What does the `s` mean?
options: SUID: the program runs with the privileges of its owner (root)
questions.explain: This is how normal users can update /etc/shadow through passwd. A capital `S` means SUID is set but execute is not.

questions.q: A user cannot open /data/reports/q1.txt even though the file is mode 644. What is the most likely cause?
options: A parent directory is missing the x permission for that user
The file needs the sticky bit
The user needs to be in the wheel group
questions.explain: Check every directory on the path, e.g. `namei -l /data/reports/q1.txt`. Also check ACLs and SELinux.

labs.title: Collaborative directory (exam classic)
labs.scenario: Create /home/managers. Group owner: sysmgrs. Members of sysmgrs get read, write and access; others get no access. Files created inside must automatically belong to sysmgrs.

labs.title: File ACLs (exam classic)
labs.scenario: Copy /etc/fstab to /var/tmp/fstab. Owner root, group root, not executable by anyone. natasha can read and write, harry has no access, everyone else can read.

blocks.x: Beyond rwx there are three **special bits** that change behaviour, shown in place of an `x` in `ls -l`:

**SUID** (Set User ID, value 4) on an executable makes it run with the **owner's** privileges instead of yours. That is how `passwd` (owned by root) can update `/etc/shadow` when you run it. Shown as an `s` in the owner's execute slot (`-rwsr-xr-x`).
**SGID** (Set Group ID, value 2) on a **directory** makes new files inside inherit the directory's **group** — perfect for shared team folders. Shown as `s` in the group slot.
**Sticky bit** (value 1) on a directory means users can only **delete their own** files there, even if the directory is world-writable. `/tmp` uses it, shown as `t` in the others slot (`drwxrwxrwt`).
Set them in octal by prefixing a fourth digit: `chmod 2770 dir` (SGID), `chmod 1777 dir` (sticky), `chmod 4755 file` (SUID). Or symbolically: `chmod g+s dir`, `chmod +t dir`, `chmod u+s file`.

theory.h: umask: the default for new files

blocks.x: When you create a file, its starting permissions are decided by the **umask**, which *removes* bits from a base. New files start from 666 and new directories from 777, then the umask is subtracted.
With `umask 022`, files become 644 (666−022) and directories 755 — the common default.
With `umask 077`, files become 600 and directories 700 — private to you.
Run `umask` alone to see the current value. To make a umask permanent for one user, add the `umask` line to their `~/.bashrc`; for everyone, put a script in `/etc/profile.d/`.

theory.h: Access Control Lists (ACLs) for finer control

blocks.x: Standard permissions only cover one owner, one group, and others. **ACLs** let you grant a *specific* extra user or group their own permissions on a file.
`getfacl file` shows the ACL.
`setfacl -m u:natasha:rw file` gives user natasha read+write. `setfacl -m g:auditors:r file` grants a group.
`setfacl -m u:harry:--- file` gives harry no access at all (a named-user entry beats the "others" bits).
`setfacl -x u:natasha file` removes one entry; `setfacl -b file` removes all ACL entries.
On a directory, a **default** ACL applies to files created later: `setfacl -m d:u:harry:rwx dir`.
A file that has an ACL shows a `+` at the end of its `ls -l` permission string (e.g. `-rw-r--r--+`).

days.title: Processes and signals
days.objective: Identify CPU and memory intensive processes and kill processes; manage jobs.

questions.q: Which signal does `kill PID` send when you give no signal?
questions.explain: SIGTERM asks the program to exit cleanly. Use `kill -9` only when it refuses.

questions.q: Which signal can a process NOT catch or ignore?
questions.explain: SIGKILL and SIGSTOP are handled by the kernel directly.

questions.q: List all processes sorted by CPU usage, highest first.
questions.explain: Use `--sort=-%mem` to sort by memory instead.

questions.q: Kill every process owned by user harry.
questions.explain: `pgrep -u harry` lists the PIDs first so you can see what will be killed.

questions.q: In top, which key sorts processes by memory usage?
questions.explain: P sorts by CPU, M by memory, k kills a PID, r renices, q quits.

questions.q: Start `sleep 1000` as a background job.
questions.explain: The shell prints the job number and PID. `jobs` lists background jobs.

questions.q: What does Ctrl+Z do to the program running in the foreground?
options: Moves it to the background while it keeps running
Stops (suspends) it; `bg` resumes it in the background
questions.explain: Ctrl+C sends SIGINT to end it. Ctrl+Z sends SIGTSTP to pause it.

questions.q: Bring job number 1 back to the foreground.
questions.explain: `bg %1` resumes it in the background instead. `kill %1` sends it SIGTERM.

questions.q: A process shows state `D` in ps. What does that mean?
options: It is running on a CPU
Uninterruptible sleep, usually waiting for disk or network I/O
questions.explain: R running, S sleeping, T stopped, Z zombie, D uninterruptible sleep.

labs.title: Find and stop CPU hogs
labs.scenario: Start three CPU-heavy processes with `sha1sum /dev/zero &`. Find them with ps sorted by CPU and with top. Kill one by PID with SIGTERM, and kill the other two by name.
steps: for i in 1 2 3; do sha1sum /dev/zero & done
top          # press P, note a PID, press q

labs.title: Find the biggest memory users
labs.scenario: Save the 5 processes using the most memory (with PID, user, %MEM and command) to /root/topmem.txt.

labs.title: Job control drill
labs.scenario: Start `sleep 500` and `sleep 600` in the background and `sleep 700` in the foreground. Suspend the foreground job, resume it in the background, bring job 2 to the foreground and end it with Ctrl+C, then kill the rest by job number.

labs.title: Pause and resume a process with signals
labs.scenario: As harry, start `sleep 900`. As root, stop it with SIGSTOP, confirm the state is T, resume it with SIGCONT, then kill it with SIGKILL.

blocks.x: A running program is a **process**. Each has a unique number, the **PID** (Process ID), and belongs to a user. The kernel schedules processes onto the CPU. Understanding how to see, prioritise and stop processes is core system administration.

theory.h: Seeing what is running: ps and top

blocks.x: `ps` shows a snapshot of processes. The most common form is `ps aux` (every process, with user and resource use). `ps -ef` is another full listing. Add sorting: `ps aux --sort=-%cpu` (biggest CPU first) or `--sort=-%mem` (biggest memory).
`top` (or the friendlier `htop`) is a **live** view that refreshes every few seconds. Inside top: press **P** to sort by CPU, **M** by memory, **k** to kill a PID, **r** to renice, and **q** to quit.
Process **states** you will see: R (running), S (sleeping), T (stopped), Z (zombie), D (uninterruptible sleep, usually waiting on disk).
You control processes by sending them **signals** (messages).
`kill PID` sends **SIGTERM (15)** by default — a polite "please exit cleanly".
`kill -9 PID` sends **SIGKILL (9)** — force-quit, which a process cannot catch or ignore. Use it only when SIGTERM does not work.
Other useful signals: **SIGHUP (1)** often tells a daemon to reload; **SIGSTOP** pauses a process and **SIGCONT** resumes it.
`pkill name` and `killall name` kill by **name** instead of PID; `pgrep name` lists matching PIDs first so you can check before killing. `pkill -u harry` targets all of a user's processes.
A command normally runs in the **foreground**, holding your terminal. You can move work to the **background**:
Add `&` to start a command in the background: `sleep 1000 &`.
Press **Ctrl+Z** to **suspend** (pause) the foreground job; **Ctrl+C** sends SIGINT to end it.
`jobs` lists background jobs; `bg %1` resumes job 1 in the background; `fg %1` brings it to the foreground.
`nohup command &` runs something immune to hang-ups so it keeps running after you log out.
Every process has a **nice value** from **−20** (highest priority, greediest) to **19** (lowest, most generous to others); the default is 0.
`nice -n 10 command` starts a command with a nicer (lower) priority.
`renice -n 5 -p 1234` changes the priority of running PID 1234.
Only **root** can *raise* priority (give a more negative nice); regular users can only make their own processes nicer.

days.title: Controlling services with systemd
days.objective: Start, stop and check services; configure automatic startup.

questions.q: Start httpd now and also enable it at boot, in one command.
questions.explain: `enable` alone only affects the next boot. `--now` also starts it.

questions.q: What does `systemctl mask atd` do?
options: Stops it and deletes its unit file
Links the unit to /dev/null so it cannot be started at all, even manually
Disables it at boot but still allows manual start
questions.explain: Undo with `systemctl unmask atd`.

questions.q: Check whether sshd is enabled to start at boot.
questions.explain: `systemctl is-active sshd` tells you whether it's running now.

questions.q: List all units that are in a failed state.
questions.explain: Then run `systemctl status <unit>` and `journalctl -u <unit>` for details.

questions.q: What is the difference between `systemctl reload` and `systemctl restart`?
options: reload tells the service to re-read its config without stopping; restart stops and starts it
reload also enables the service at boot
restart only works if reload fails
questions.explain: Not every service supports reload; `systemctl reload-or-restart` covers both cases.

questions.q: You create or edit a unit file under /etc/systemd/system. What must you run next?
questions.explain: systemd caches unit files. daemon-reload makes it read them again.

questions.q: Where should administrators put their own unit files and overrides?
questions.explain: Package units live in /usr/lib/systemd/system. Files in /etc take priority. `systemctl edit unit` creates a drop-in override for you.

questions.q: Stop the atd service and stop it starting at boot, in one command.
questions.explain: Confirm with `systemctl status atd`.

questions.q: `systemctl status sshd` shows "Loaded: ... enabled; preset: enabled" and "Active: active (running)". What does that mean?
options: sshd is running now and will start at boot
sshd starts at boot but is not running now
sshd is running but will not start at boot
questions.explain: "enabled" is the boot setting, "active" is the current state. They are separate.

labs.title: Install and run a web server
labs.scenario: Install httpd, start it and enable it at boot, allow HTTP through the firewall, put "Hello RHCSA" in /var/www/html/index.html and fetch it with curl.
verify: systemctl is-enabled httpd; systemctl is-active httpd

labs.title: Mask and unmask a service
labs.scenario: Mask atd, try to start it and read the error, then unmask it and make sure it is running and enabled.
steps: systemctl start atd       # Unit atd.service is masked.

labs.title: Explore units
labs.scenario: List all installed service unit files and their boot state, show what multi-user.target pulls in, and print the unit file of sshd.

labs.title: Write your own service
labs.scenario: Create /usr/local/bin/heartbeat.sh that writes "alive" to the journal every 30 seconds in a loop. Create heartbeat.service to run it, enable it at boot, and read its messages in the journal.
steps: printf '#!/bin/bash\nwhile true; do echo alive; sleep 30; done\n' > /usr/local/bin/heartbeat.sh

blocks.x: On modern RHEL, **systemd** is the first process to start (PID 1) and it manages everything else. The things it manages are called **units**. The most common unit type is a **service** (a background program, or "daemon"), whose files end in `.service`. Other unit types include targets, sockets, and timers.

theory.h: systemctl: the one command to know

blocks.x: `systemctl` controls units. The verbs are intuitive:
`systemctl status sshd` — show whether it is running, plus recent log lines.
`systemctl start sshd` / `stop sshd` / `restart sshd` — control it **now**.
`systemctl reload sshd` — tell it to re-read its config **without** stopping (not all services support it; `reload-or-restart` covers both).
`systemctl enable sshd` — make it start **at boot**; `disable` undoes that. These do **not** affect the current run — that is why `enable --now sshd` (enable *and* start) is so handy.
`systemctl is-active sshd` and `is-enabled sshd` answer the two separate questions: running now? starting at boot?

theory.h: Enabled vs active — two different things

blocks.x: This trips up beginners: **enabled** is about the *next boot*, **active** is about *right now*. A service can be enabled but stopped, or running but not enabled. The exam usually wants services that are **both** running and enabled — so `systemctl enable --now name` is your go-to.
`systemctl mask atd` links a unit to `/dev/null` so it **cannot** be started at all, even manually — a strong "off switch". `systemctl unmask atd` reverses it.
`systemctl list-units --type=service` lists running services; `list-unit-files` shows every installed unit and its boot state; `--failed` shows what has failed.

`systemctl cat sshd` prints a unit's file; `systemctl daemon-reload` makes systemd re-read unit files after you add or edit one (files you write go in `/etc/systemd/system/`, which overrides the packaged copies in `/usr/lib/systemd/system/`).

days.title: Configure and secure SSH
days.objective: Access remote systems using SSH and configure key-based authentication.

questions.q: Generate a new SSH key pair with the default settings.
questions.explain: Keys are saved in ~/.ssh/. The .pub file is the public key you share.

questions.q: Copy your public key to the account harry on host servera.
questions.explain: It appends your key to ~harry/.ssh/authorized_keys and sets safe permissions.

questions.q: On the server, which file lists the public keys allowed to log in to an account?
questions.explain: known_hosts on the client stores the server fingerprints you have accepted.

questions.q: Which permissions does sshd expect on ~/.ssh and ~/.ssh/authorized_keys?
options: 700 on the directory and 600 on the file
questions.explain: If they are too open, sshd ignores the key (StrictModes) and falls back to a password.

questions.q: How do you stop root from logging in over SSH?
options: Set root's shell to nologin in /etc/ssh/ssh_config
Set `PermitRootLogin no` in the sshd config, then reload sshd
questions.explain: On RHEL 9 and 10 you can put the setting in a file under /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/. /etc/ssh/ssh_config is the client config, not the server.

questions.q: Check the sshd configuration for syntax errors before reloading.
questions.explain: No output means the syntax is valid. Then run `systemctl reload sshd`.

questions.q: Run `hostname` on servera as student without opening an interactive shell.
questions.explain: The command runs remotely and the output comes back to your terminal.

questions.q: What is OpenSSH's built-in default for PermitRootLogin, which RHEL 9 and 10 use?
options: prohibit-password: root can log in with a key but not with a password
questions.explain: Exam tasks often need root password login between exam nodes, or a key. Read the task carefully.

questions.q: Where are the SSH server's own host keys stored?
questions.explain: If a host is reinstalled, its host key changes and clients warn you. Remove the old line with `ssh-keygen -R host`.

labs.title: Key-based login between two machines
labs.scenario: On node1 as student, generate a key pair and set up key-based login to student@node2. Confirm you can run a command on node2 with no password prompt.
verify: ssh -o PasswordAuthentication=no student@node2 true && echo KEY-OK

labs.title: Harden the SSH server
labs.scenario: On node2: stop root logging in over SSH and stop password logins for everyone. Make sure your key login works BEFORE you reload sshd, then test both.
hints: Settings in /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/*.conf are read first, so the first value set wins.

labs.title: Remote commands and quick copies
labs.scenario: From node1, save the output of `df -h` on node2 to /root/node2-disk.txt on node1, and copy node2's /etc/os-release into /tmp on node1 in one command each.

labs.title: Use ssh-agent with a passphrase
labs.scenario: Create a second key ~/.ssh/lab_key with a passphrase, install it on node2, and load it into ssh-agent so you type the passphrase only once.

blocks.x: **SSH** (Secure Shell) lets you log in to and run commands on another machine over an **encrypted** connection. It replaced old plaintext tools like Telnet, which sent passwords in the clear. The client command is `ssh`; the server is the `sshd` service listening on TCP port **22**.
`ssh student@servera` opens an interactive shell on servera as student.
`ssh student@servera hostname` runs a single command remotely and returns just its output.

The first time you connect, SSH shows the server's **host key fingerprint** and asks you to accept it; it is then stored in `~/.ssh/known_hosts`. If a host is reinstalled its key changes and you will be warned — remove the stale entry with `ssh-keygen -R servera`.
Copy files over SSH with `scp file user@host:/path` (or `scp user@host:/path localfile` to pull), and `sftp user@host` for an interactive file transfer session.
Instead of typing a password every time, you can use a **key pair**: a private key you keep secret and a matching public key you place on the server.
`ssh-keygen` creates the pair in `~/.ssh/` (`id_rsa`/`id_ed25519` private, `.pub` public). Press Enter for defaults; you may add a passphrase for extra safety.
`ssh-copy-id student@servera` copies your public key into the server's `~/.ssh/authorized_keys` and fixes the permissions automatically.
After that, `ssh student@servera` logs in using the key, no password needed.
Permissions matter: the server ignores your key unless `~/.ssh` is `700` and `authorized_keys` is `600` (this is "StrictModes").
The server's config is `/etc/ssh/sshd_config` (and drop-in files in `/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/`). Two important settings:
`PermitRootLogin no` stops root logging in directly over SSH.
`PasswordAuthentication no` forces key-only login (set up your key **first**, or you will lock yourself out).
Always check the syntax with `sshd -t` before applying, then `systemctl reload sshd`. Note `/etc/ssh/ssh_config` is the **client** config — don't confuse it with the server's `sshd_config`.

days.title: System logs and the journal
days.objective: Locate and interpret system log files and journals; preserve system journals.

questions.q: Show journal entries for the sshd service only.
questions.explain: Add `-f` to follow, `-n 20` for the last 20 lines, `--since today` to limit time.

questions.q: Show only messages of priority err or worse from the current boot.
questions.explain: `-p` includes that level and everything more severe.

questions.q: Show journal messages from the last hour.
questions.explain: You can also give dates: `--since "2026-10-01 09:00" --until "2026-10-01 10:00"`.

questions.q: Which journald setting keeps the journal across reboots?
questions.explain: With the default Storage=auto, the journal is only kept if /var/log/journal exists. Otherwise it stays in /run/log/journal and is lost at reboot.

questions.q: Which file holds authentication and security messages on RHEL?
questions.explain: /var/log/auth.log is the Debian and Ubuntu name. SELinux denials go to /var/log/audit/audit.log.

questions.q: Send the test message "hello from logger" to syslog with priority user.notice.
questions.explain: Check it with `tail /var/log/messages` or `journalctl -n 5`.

questions.q: What does the rsyslog rule `authpriv.*  /var/log/secure` mean?
options: Messages of every priority from the authpriv facility go to /var/log/secure
questions.explain: Rule format: facility.priority followed by the target. Drop-in rules go in /etc/rsyslog.d/*.conf.

questions.q: Which list orders syslog priorities from most to least severe?
options: crit, emerg, alert, err, warning, info, notice, debug
err, warning, info, debug, notice, crit, alert, emerg
emerg, alert, crit, err, warning, notice, info, debug
debug, info, notice, warning, err, crit, alert, emerg
questions.explain: Numbers 0 to 7 in that same order.

questions.q: List every boot the journal has records for.
questions.explain: Only the current boot is listed unless the journal is persistent. `journalctl -b -1` shows the previous boot.

labs.title: Preserve the journal (exam objective)
labs.scenario: Configure the journal so it survives reboots. Reboot, then prove that the previous boot's messages are still there.
verify: journalctl --list-boots      # two or more boots listed

labs.title: Custom rsyslog rule
labs.scenario: Send messages of every facility at priority debug and above to a new file /var/log/messages-debug. Test it with logger.
steps: logger -p user.debug "Debug test from RHCSA practice"

labs.title: Investigate failed logins
labs.scenario: Make a few failed SSH logins to localhost, then use journalctl to show today's failed sshd attempts and count them.

labs.title: Filter the journal by fields
labs.scenario: Show journal entries for UID 1000 only, then only entries from the sshd command, then one entry in full verbose form.

blocks.x: RHEL records events in two ways. The **systemd journal** (managed by `systemd-journald`) is a structured, queryable log of everything systemd and its services produce. Alongside it, **rsyslog** writes traditional plain-text log files under `/var/log/`. Key files: `/var/log/messages` (general system messages) and `/var/log/secure` (authentication and security events like SSH logins).
`journalctl` queries the journal. Learn these filters:
`journalctl` alone shows everything (in the `less` pager); `-n 20` shows the last 20 lines; `-f` **follows** live like `tail -f`.
`journalctl -u sshd` limits output to one **unit** (service). Combine with `-f` to watch a service live.
`journalctl -p err` filters by **priority** (err and worse). Priorities from most to least severe: emerg, alert, crit, err, warning, notice, info, debug (numbered 0–7).
`journalctl -b` shows only the **current boot**; `-b -1` the previous boot; `--list-boots` lists them.
`journalctl --since "1 hour ago"` or `--since "2026-10-01 09:00" --until "10:00"` limits by time.
`journalctl _UID=1000` or `_COMM=sshd` filter by fields; `-o verbose` shows one entry in full detail.
By default (`Storage=auto`) the journal is kept in memory under `/run/log/journal` and is **lost on reboot** unless a directory exists to persist it. To keep it:
Create `/var/log/journal` (or set `Storage=persistent` in `/etc/systemd/journald.conf`), then restart `systemd-journald`.
After a reboot, `journalctl --list-boots` should show more than one boot, proving persistence works.

`logger` writes a message into the log system, useful for testing rules and scripts: `logger -p user.notice "hello"`. Check it landed with `journalctl -n 5` or `tail /var/log/messages`. rsyslog's routing rules live in `/etc/rsyslog.conf` and drop-in files in `/etc/rsyslog.d/*.conf`; a rule like `authpriv.*  /var/log/secure` means "all authpriv-facility messages go to that file".

blocks.x: A correct, synchronised clock is more important than beginners expect. Log timestamps, scheduled jobs, TLS certificates and cluster software all depend on accurate time. If two machines disagree on the time, investigating an incident by comparing their logs becomes almost impossible. RHEL keeps time in sync over the network using **NTP** (Network Time Protocol), implemented by the **chrony** service (`chronyd`).

theory.h: timedatectl: the clock and time zone

blocks.x: `timedatectl` is the single command for date, time and time zone:
`timedatectl` (or `timedatectl status`) shows the current time, the time zone, and whether NTP sync is active. Look for "System clock synchronized: yes".
`timedatectl list-timezones` lists all zone names; pipe to `grep Asia` to narrow it.
`timedatectl set-timezone Asia/Kolkata` sets the zone (this updates the `/etc/localtime` link).
`timedatectl set-ntp true` turns network time sync on (enabling and starting chronyd); `set-ntp false` turns it off.
`timedatectl set-time "2026-12-25 10:00:00"` sets the clock manually (only works with NTP off).
chrony's config is `/etc/chrony.conf`. The important line names a time source:
`server classroom.example.com iburst` syncs from one specific server; `iburst` speeds up the first sync.
`pool 2.rhel.pool.ntp.org iburst` uses a pool name that resolves to many servers.
After editing, apply with `systemctl restart chronyd` (and `enable` it for boot). To make a machine an NTP **server** for your LAN, add `allow 192.168.122.0/24`.

`chronyc sources` lists the time sources chrony is using. In the output, `^*` marks the server it is currently synced to, and `^?` means "not reachable yet" (wait a minute after a restart). Add `-v` for a legend.
`chronyc tracking` shows how accurate the local clock is and its offset from the reference.

blocks.x: On RHEL, the network is controlled by **NetworkManager**, and you configure it with the `nmcli` command. NetworkManager stores each network setup as a **connection profile** (a saved configuration), separate from the physical **device** (the network card, like `eth0`). One device can have several profiles; you activate whichever one you need.

theory.h: IP addresses, netmasks and gateways (the basics)

blocks.x: An **IP address** identifies a machine on a network, e.g. `192.168.122.11`.
A **netmask** (written as a prefix like `/24`) says how much of the address is the network part. `/24` equals `255.255.255.0`.
The **gateway** is the router the machine sends traffic to when the destination is on another network.
A **DNS server** turns names (like `servera`) into IP addresses.

theory.h: Viewing the network with ip and nmcli

blocks.x: `ip a` (short for `ip addr`) shows every interface and its addresses; `ip -br a` gives one tidy line each. `ip route` shows the routing table, including the `default via …` gateway line.
`nmcli con show` lists connection profiles; add `--active` to see which are live. `nmcli device status` shows devices and which profile each uses.

theory.h: Setting a static IP with nmcli

blocks.x: The pattern is to **modify** a profile, then **bring it up**:

`nmcli con mod "profile" ipv4.addresses 192.168.122.11/24 ipv4.gateway 192.168.122.1 ipv4.dns 192.168.122.1 ipv4.method manual` sets a static configuration. `ipv4.method manual` is essential — without it the profile may keep using DHCP.

`nmcli con up "profile"` re-activates the profile so the changes take effect (they do **not** apply until you do this — and if you are connected over SSH, changing the IP will drop your session, so use the console).
Use `+ipv4.addresses` to add a second address without removing the first.
Profiles are stored as keyfiles in `/etc/NetworkManager/system-connections/`.
`hostnamectl set-hostname server1.example.com` sets the machine's name permanently (writing `/etc/hostname`).

`/etc/hosts` is a simple local file mapping IP addresses to names; it is checked **before** DNS. Add a line like `192.168.122.12 server2` to reach a host by name without a DNS server. `getent hosts server2` shows what the system actually resolves.

days.title: Networking: IPv6, DNS and troubleshooting
days.objective: Configure IPv6 addresses, name resolution and network services at boot.

questions.q: Give connection eth0 the static IPv6 address fd00:10::10/64 with the manual method.
accept: nmcli con mod eth0 ipv6.addresses fd00:10::10/64 ipv6.method manual
nmcli connection modify eth0 ipv6.addresses fd00:10::10/64 ipv6.method manual
nmcli con mod eth0 ipv6.method manual ipv6.addresses fd00:10::10/64
questions.explain: Add `ipv6.gateway fd00:10::1` if the task gives a gateway, then `nmcli con up eth0`.

questions.q: What is the IPv6 loopback address?
questions.explain: `::` on its own means the all-zero (unspecified) address.

questions.q: Addresses beginning with fe80:: are what kind of IPv6 address?
options: Global addresses routed on the internet
Link-local, created automatically on every IPv6 interface
questions.explain: Your static address shows as "scope global" in `ip a` next to the fe80:: link-local one.

blocks.x: The internet is running out of the older **IPv4** addresses (the `192.168.x.x` style), so **IPv6** was created with vastly more addresses, written in hex groups like `fd00:10::11`. You configure it almost the same way as IPv4:
`nmcli con mod eth0 ipv6.addresses fd00:10::11/64 ipv6.method manual` then `nmcli con up eth0`.
The IPv6 loopback (this machine) is `::1`, the IPv4 equivalent of `127.0.0.1`.
Addresses starting `fe80::` are **link-local** — created automatically on every interface and only valid on the local link. Your real routable address shows as "scope global" in `ip a`.
DNS (Domain Name System) resolves names to IP addresses. Useful lookup tools:
`dig servera.example.com` gives detailed DNS answers; `dig servera +short` gives just the address. `dig example.com MX` looks up mail servers, `NS` name servers, `TXT` text records.
`host servera` is a simpler resolver; `nslookup` is another.
`getent hosts servera` resolves a name the way real applications do — using the full order in `/etc/nsswitch.conf` (usually files, then DNS) — so it reflects `/etc/hosts` **and** DNS.
The DNS servers the system uses appear in `/etc/resolv.conf`, but on RHEL you set them through NetworkManager (`ipv4.dns`), not by editing that file directly.

theory.h: A calm way to troubleshoot connectivity

blocks.x: When something "can't connect", work up the stack in order instead of guessing:
**Link** — is the interface up with an IP? `ip -br a`, `ip -br link`.
**Route** — is there a default gateway? `ip route`.
**Gateway** — can you reach it? `ping -c2 <gateway>`.
**DNS** — does the name resolve? `getent hosts <name>` or `dig <name>`.
**Service** — is the remote port open? `ss -tulpn` locally, or `nc -zv host 443` to a remote port.
`ss -tulpn` is the modern replacement for `netstat`: t=TCP, u=UDP, l=listening, p=process, n=numeric ports.

days.title: RPM and DNF packages
days.objective: Install and remove RPM software packages; query the RPM database.

questions.q: Find which installed package owns the file /etc/ssh/sshd_config.
questions.explain: `rpm -qf` only looks at installed packages; `dnf provides` also searches repositories.

questions.q: List the configuration files that belong to the chrony package.
questions.explain: -qc lists config files, -qd docs, -ql all files, -qi package info.

questions.q: Find which package provides the semanage command, even if it is not installed yet.
questions.explain: The answer is policycoreutils-python-utils. You will need it for SELinux tasks.

questions.q: What is the advantage of `dnf install ./pkg.rpm` over `rpm -ivh pkg.rpm`?
options: dnf also installs the dependencies from the enabled repositories
questions.explain: rpm only reports missing dependencies and stops.

questions.q: List every installed package with "http" in its name.
questions.explain: rpm -qa prints every installed package.

questions.q: What does `dnf history undo 12` do?
options: Reverses the changes made by transaction 12
questions.explain: `dnf history` lists transactions and `dnf history info 12` shows one.

questions.q: Install the package group "Development Tools".
questions.explain: `dnf group list` shows the available groups.

questions.q: What happens to the running kernel when `dnf update` installs a newer kernel?
options: Kernels are never updated by dnf
The new kernel is added next to the old ones and used after a reboot
The old kernel is removed immediately
questions.explain: Kernels are "install-only" packages, so you can boot an older one from GRUB if the new one fails.

questions.q: Remove the httpd package.
questions.explain: dnf also removes packages that depend on httpd. Read the list before confirming.

labs.title: Query the RPM database
labs.scenario: Answer with rpm commands only: which package owns /usr/bin/ls, which files does openssh-server install, where are its config files, and when was it installed?

labs.title: Install from a local RPM file
labs.scenario: Download the tree package as an .rpm file into /root/rpms without installing it. Inspect the file, then install it from the local file.

labs.title: Use dnf history
labs.scenario: Install the packages zsh and tmux in one transaction, find that transaction in the history, then undo it.

labs.title: Work with package groups
labs.scenario: List the available groups, show what "Development Tools" contains, and install it.

blocks.x: Instead of copying files around, Linux installs software as **packages**. On RHEL these are **RPM** packages (`.rpm` files). Each package bundles the program plus information about what other packages it needs (its **dependencies**). Two tools work with them: the low-level `rpm` (queries and installs a single file) and the high-level `dnf` (resolves dependencies and downloads from repositories).
`rpm` is best for asking questions about **already-installed** packages (the `-q` = query flag):
`rpm -qa` lists all installed packages (pipe to `grep` to search).
`rpm -qf /etc/ssh/sshd_config` says which package **owns** a given file.
`rpm -ql openssh-server` lists all files a package installed; `-qc` shows just its config files; `-qd` its documentation; `-qi` general info.
`rpm -qip file.rpm` and `-qlp file.rpm` query a `.rpm` **file** that is not installed yet (the `p` = package file).
`dnf` is what you use day to day because it handles dependencies and repositories:

`dnf install httpd` downloads httpd **and** anything it needs. `dnf install ./local.rpm` installs a local file but still pulls dependencies from repos (better than `rpm -ivh`, which just fails if something is missing).
`dnf remove httpd` uninstalls it (and packages that depend on it — read the list before confirming).
`dnf update` updates everything; `dnf search word` and `dnf provides */semanage` find packages (the second finds which package provides a command).
`dnf list installed`, `dnf info httpd`, and package **groups** via `dnf group list` / `dnf group install "Development Tools"`.
`dnf history` lists past transactions; `dnf history info last` details one; `dnf history undo last` reverses it.

Kernels are special "install-only" packages: a `dnf update` **adds** the new kernel alongside the old ones (used after a reboot) so you can still boot an older, working kernel from the GRUB menu if a new one misbehaves.

days.title: Repositories and Flatpak
days.objective: Configure access to RPM repositories and Flatpak repositories; install and remove Flatpak packages.

questions.q: Where do DNF repository definitions go?
questions.explain: Every file in /etc/yum.repos.d/ ending in `.repo` is read. The file name does not matter.

questions.q: Which set of lines is enough for a working repository section?
options: [id], name, baseurl, enabled=1 and gpgcheck (0 or 1 with a gpgkey)
questions.explain: A typo in baseurl is the most common exam mistake. Test with `dnf repolist` and install a package.

questions.q: Add a repository for http://repo.lab.example.com/BaseOS with dnf config-manager.
questions.explain: It writes a new .repo file. If the task asks for gpgcheck=0, edit the file afterwards.

questions.q: List the enabled repositories.
questions.explain: `dnf repolist all` includes the disabled ones.

questions.q: What is the baseurl for a BaseOS repository on a DVD mounted at /mnt/iso?
questions.explain: `file://` plus the absolute path `/mnt/iso/...` gives three slashes.

questions.q: Add the Flathub remote only if it is not already configured.
questions.explain: In the exam, use the remote name and URL the task gives you.

questions.q: List the configured Flatpak remotes.
questions.explain: `flatpak remote-ls <remote>` lists the apps a remote offers.

questions.q: Install the app org.gnome.Calculator from the flathub remote.
questions.explain: `flatpak list` shows installed apps; `flatpak run <app-id>` starts one.

questions.q: Where does `flatpak install` put apps if you do not pass --user?
options: System-wide, for all users (needs admin rights)
questions.explain: `--user` installs just for you, under ~/.local/share/flatpak.

questions.q: Uninstall the org.gnome.Calculator Flatpak app.
questions.explain: `flatpak uninstall --unused` removes runtimes that no app needs any more.

labs.title: Local repository from the RHEL ISO
labs.scenario: Attach the RHEL 10 ISO to your VM. Mount it permanently at /mnt/iso and create /etc/yum.repos.d/local.repo with BaseOS and AppStream repositories from it. Install httpd from it to prove it works.

labs.title: Network repositories (exam style)
labs.scenario: On node2, publish the ISO over HTTP by linking /mnt/iso into /var/www/html/rhel10. Then on node1, configure repos BaseOS and AppStream pointing to http://node2/rhel10/BaseOS and http://node2/rhel10/AppStream.
steps: dnf install -y httpd && systemctl enable --now httpd

labs.title: Flatpak end to end
labs.scenario: Install the flatpak package, add the Flathub remote, search for a calculator app, install it system-wide, list installed apps, and uninstall it. (Needs internet on the VM.)

labs.title: Enable and disable repositories
labs.scenario: Disable the AppStream repo, see that httpd can no longer be found, then enable it again. Also try a single command that ignores it only once.

blocks.x: A **repository** (repo) is a collection of packages that `dnf` can download from, plus an index of what's available. Without a repo, `dnf` has nowhere to fetch software. On the RHCSA exam you often have to point a machine at a repo yourself.
Repo definitions are `.repo` files in `/etc/yum.repos.d/`. A minimal working repo section needs just a few lines:
`[myrepo]` — a short id in square brackets.
`name=My Repo` — a human name.
`baseurl=…` — where the packages are. This can be `http://host/path`, or a local path as `file:///mnt/iso/BaseOS` (three slashes: `file://` + the absolute path).
`enabled=1` — turn it on.
`gpgcheck=0` (or `1` with a `gpgkey=` line) — whether to verify signatures.

You can also add one with `dnf config-manager --add-repo <url>`, and enable/disable with `dnf config-manager --set-enabled`/`--set-disabled`. Check your work with `dnf repolist` (add `all` to include disabled ones), then install a package to prove it works.

theory.h: Flatpak: a different kind of package

blocks.x: **Flatpak** is a newer, cross-distribution way to install desktop **applications**, sandboxed and independent of the system packages. It uses **remotes** (its version of repositories):
`flatpak remote-add --if-not-exists flathub https://dl.flathub.org/repo/flathub.flatpakrepo` adds the popular Flathub remote.
`flatpak remotes` lists configured remotes; `flatpak remote-ls flathub` lists apps a remote offers.

`flatpak install flathub org.gnome.Calculator` installs an app system-wide (add `--user` to install only for you); `flatpak list` shows what is installed; `flatpak run <app-id>` starts one; `flatpak uninstall <app-id>` removes it.

days.title: Archives and secure file transfer
days.objective: Archive, compress, unpack and uncompress files with tar, gzip and bzip2; securely transfer files between systems.

questions.q: Create the gzip-compressed archive /root/etc.tar.gz of /etc.
questions.explain: c = create, z = gzip, f = file name, v = list files as they are added.

questions.q: Create the bzip2-compressed archive /root/local.tar.bz2 of /usr/local.
questions.explain: j = bzip2. The bzip2 package must be installed.

questions.q: Which tar option compresses with xz?
questions.explain: Summary: -z gzip (.gz), -j bzip2 (.bz2), -J xz (.xz).

questions.q: List the contents of /root/etc.tar.gz without extracting it.
questions.explain: Modern tar detects the compression when reading, so -z is optional here.

questions.q: Extract /root/etc.tar.gz into the existing directory /tmp/restore.
questions.explain: `-C` changes to that directory before extracting.

questions.q: tar prints "Removing leading '/' from member names". What does that mean?
options: You must run tar as root
Paths are stored relative, so extracting never overwrites the original location by accident
questions.explain: When you extract, the files go under your current directory (or the -C directory).

questions.q: Copy /etc/hosts into /tmp on serverb, logging in as root over SSH.
questions.explain: Reverse the arguments to copy from the remote host. Add `-r` for directories.

questions.q: What does a trailing slash on the source mean in `rsync -av /var/www/ serverb:/backup/www`?
options: The contents of /var/www are copied into /backup/www, not the www directory itself
rsync deletes files on the target
questions.explain: Without the slash you get /backup/www/www.

questions.q: What does `gzip notes.txt` do?
options: Replaces notes.txt with the compressed notes.txt.gz
questions.explain: Use `gunzip notes.txt.gz` to reverse it, or `gzip -k` to keep the original.

labs.title: Compare compression types
labs.scenario: Archive /etc three times, with gzip, bzip2 and xz, into /root/backups. Compare the sizes and check each file's type.

labs.title: Backup archive (exam classic)
labs.scenario: Create /root/backup.tar.bz2 containing /usr/local, compressed with bzip2. Confirm it is valid and lists the expected files.

labs.title: Restore a single file
labs.scenario: From /root/backups/etc.tar.gz, restore only etc/hosts into /tmp/restore, and compare it with the live file.

labs.title: Move files between nodes
labs.scenario: Copy /root/backup.tar.bz2 from node1 to /tmp on node2 with scp. Sync /etc/yum.repos.d/ from node1 into /root/repos-copy on node2 with rsync. Use sftp to download /etc/hostname from node2.
steps: sftp root@node2      # then: get /etc/hostname   and   bye

blocks.x: Bundling many files into one **archive** makes them easy to move or back up, and **compression** makes that bundle smaller. On Linux the classic tool is `tar` (tape archive), which can also compress by calling gzip, bzip2 or xz.
tar's letters combine, and beginners find them clearer once named:
**c** = create, **x** = extract, **t** = list (test contents), **f** = the archive **f**ilename (always needed), **v** = verbose (show files as they are processed).
Compression: **z** = gzip (`.tar.gz`), **j** = bzip2 (`.tar.bz2`), **J** = xz (`.tar.xz`).

So `tar -czf /root/etc.tar.gz /etc` **c**reates a g**z**ipped archive **f**ile of `/etc`. `tar -xzf etc.tar.gz -C /tmp/restore` e**x**tracts it into a chosen directory (`-C` = change to that directory first). `tar -tzf etc.tar.gz` **lists** contents without extracting. Modern tar auto-detects compression on extract, so `z/j/J` is optional when reading. When tar prints "Removing leading '/'", it is storing paths **relative** so extracting never overwrites the originals by accident — they land under your current (or `-C`) directory.
`gzip file` compresses `file` into `file.gz` (replacing the original); `gunzip file.gz` reverses it. `gzip -k` keeps the original.
`zip -r archive.zip folder` and `unzip archive.zip` handle the cross-platform ZIP format.
`scp file user@host:/path` copies over SSH (encrypted). Add `-r` for directories. Reverse the arguments to pull: `scp user@host:/path localfile`.
`sftp user@host` opens an interactive session (`get`, `put`, `ls`, `bye`).

`rsync -av source/ user@host:/dest/` efficiently syncs directories, copying only what changed. A **trailing slash** on the source means "the contents of source" go into dest, rather than the source folder itself — a classic gotcha.

days.title: Accessing file systems and users on consoles
days.objective: Mount and inspect file systems; log in and switch users in multi-user targets.

questions.q: List all block devices with their filesystem types and UUIDs.
questions.explain: `lsblk` alone shows sizes and mount points.

questions.q: Show free space on mounted filesystems in human-readable units, including the filesystem type.
questions.explain: `df` reports filesystems; `du` reports what files use.

questions.q: Show the total disk space used by /var/log.
questions.explain: -s summary, -h human-readable. `du -h --max-depth=1 /var` lists subdirectories.

questions.q: Mount /dev/vdb1 on /mnt/data for now (not permanently).
questions.explain: For a permanent mount, add a line to /etc/fstab.

questions.q: `umount /mnt/data` says "target is busy". What is the usual cause?
options: A process, maybe your own shell, is using files or has its working directory there
questions.explain: `cd` out of it, then find other users with `lsof /mnt/data` or `fuser -vm /mnt/data`.

questions.q: Show the UUID of /dev/vdb1.
questions.explain: Use the UUID in /etc/fstab. It does not change if disks are renamed.

questions.q: On a text-only system in multi-user.target, how do you reach a second login console?
options: Press Ctrl+Alt+F2 (F2 to F6 give more consoles)
questions.explain: In a VM, send the key combination from the VM window's menu.

questions.q: Which command shows who is logged in and what each person is running?
questions.explain: `who` is shorter, `last` shows past logins.

questions.q: What is the difference between `sudo -i` and `su -`?
options: su - only works for regular users
sudo -i does not give a login shell
sudo -i asks for your own password and needs sudo rights; su - asks for root's password
questions.explain: Both give a root login shell. Type `exit` to return to your own user.

labs.title: Explore storage usage
labs.scenario: Show all disks and partitions, see which filesystems are mounted and how full they are, and save the 5 largest directories under /var to /root/var-usage.txt.

labs.title: Mount an ISO image
labs.scenario: Download or copy an ISO file (the RHEL ISO works) and mount it read-only through a loop device at /mnt/image. Browse it, then unmount it.

labs.title: Busy mount point
labs.scenario: Mount something at /mnt/image, cd into it from a second terminal, and try to unmount it. Find the process that blocks it, fix it, and unmount.
steps: # leave the directory in the other terminal (cd ~), then:

labs.title: Log in and switch users on text consoles
labs.scenario: Switch the system to multi-user.target for now. Log in as harry on tty2, become root with su -, check who is logged in, then return to graphical.target if you have a desktop.

blocks.x: Disks appear under `/dev` with names like `/dev/vda` (a whole disk) and `/dev/vda1` (a partition on it). A **filesystem** (like XFS or ext4) is the structure that lets a partition hold files. To use a filesystem you **mount** it onto an empty directory (the **mount point**); everything under that directory then lives on that filesystem.
`lsblk` lists block devices as a tree (disks, partitions, sizes, mount points); `lsblk -f` adds filesystem type and **UUID**.
`df -h` shows free space on mounted filesystems in human-readable units; `df -hT` adds the type. Remember: `df` reports **filesystems**.
`du -sh /var/log` shows how much space files **use** (`-s` summary, `-h` human); `du -h --max-depth=1 /var` breaks it down by subdirectory.
`blkid` prints each filesystem's UUID and type — the UUID is a stable id you use in `/etc/fstab` because device names (`/dev/vdb1`) can change between boots.
`mount /dev/vdb1 /mnt/data` attaches a filesystem for now (the mount point directory must already exist).

`umount /mnt/data` detaches it. If it says "target is busy", something is using it — often your own shell sitting inside it. `cd` out, then find other users with `lsof /mnt/data` or `fuser -vm /mnt/data`.
`findmnt /mnt/data` confirms what is mounted where.
Permanent mounts belong in `/etc/fstab` (covered in the storage days) using `UUID=` or `LABEL=` so they survive reboots.

theory.h: Logging in on text consoles and switching users

blocks.x: When there is no desktop, RHEL provides several text **consoles**. Switch between them with **Ctrl+Alt+F2** through **F6** (in a VM, send the keys from the VM window's menu). To see who is around and become another user:
`who` and `w` show who is logged in (`w` also shows what each person is running); `last` shows past logins.
`su - harry` becomes harry (needs harry's password); `sudo -i` gives a root login shell using **your** password (if you have sudo rights). Type `exit` to return to your own account.

days.title: Shell scripts: basics
days.objective: Process script inputs ($1, $2, etc.) and process the output of shell commands within scripts.

questions.q: What should the first line of a bash script be?
questions.explain: This "shebang" line tells the kernel which interpreter runs the file.

questions.q: Make script.sh executable for everyone.
questions.explain: Run it as `./script.sh`, or put it in /usr/local/bin so it's on the PATH.

questions.q: Inside a script, what are $1, $# and $@?
options: The first argument, the number of arguments, and all arguments
The first line, the line count, and all lines
The user, the group, and the home directory
The script name, the PID, and the exit code
questions.explain: $0 is the script's own name. Quote "$@" so arguments with spaces stay intact.

questions.q: What does $? contain?
options: The exit status of the last command (0 means success)
The PID of the last background job
questions.explain: Check it right after the command, because every command overwrites it.

questions.q: Store the output of the `hostname` command in a variable named host.
questions.explain: Prefer $( ); it nests cleanly and is easier to read.

questions.q: What happens with `count = 5` in bash?
options: An error: bash tries to run a command named count
questions.explain: Assignments must have no spaces around the =.

questions.q: What is the difference between "$HOME" and '$HOME'?
options: Double quotes expand the variable; single quotes keep the text literally
Single quotes expand it; double quotes do not
questions.explain: Use double quotes around variables to keep spaces intact and still expand them.

questions.q: Print the number of arguments that were passed to the script.
questions.explain: Useful for checking that the user passed what the script needs.

questions.q: What does `exit 1` do in a script?
options: Ends the script immediately with exit status 1 (failure)
questions.explain: By convention, 0 means success and anything else means an error.

labs.title: Your first system-info script
labs.scenario: Write /usr/local/bin/sysinfo that prints the hostname, kernel version, uptime and the number of logged-in users. Every user must be able to run it.

labs.title: A script with arguments
labs.scenario: Write /usr/local/bin/greet that prints "Hello, NAME" for its first argument. With no argument, print "Usage: greet NAME" to stderr and exit with status 1.

labs.title: Use command output in a script
labs.scenario: Write /root/diskcheck.sh that reads how full / is (as a number) and prints "WARNING" if it is over 80, otherwise "OK".
steps: # if [ "$used" -gt 80 ]; then echo "WARNING: / is ${used}% full"; else echo "OK: / is ${used}% full"; fi

labs.title: Dated backups
labs.scenario: Write /root/backup-etc.sh that creates /root/backups/etc-YYYY-MM-DD.tar.gz using today's date, and prints the archive size.

blocks.x: A **shell script** is just a text file containing the same commands you would type in the terminal, saved so you can run them again as one command. Instead of typing ten steps every time, you put them in a file and run the file. This is how administrators automate repetitive work.

theory.h: The shebang and making a script runnable

blocks.x: The first line of a script should be the **shebang**: `#!/bin/bash`. The `#!` tells the kernel which interpreter (here bash) should run the file. Without it, the system may not know how to execute your script. A fresh text file is not executable, so you must give it the execute permission:
`chmod +x script.sh` makes it runnable.
Run it with `./script.sh` (the `./` means "in the current directory"), or put it in a directory on your PATH like `/usr/local/bin/` so you can call it by name from anywhere.

A **variable** stores a value. Assign with no spaces around the `=`: `name="Purva"` (writing `name = "Purva"` fails because bash thinks `name` is a command). Read it back with a `$`: `echo "$name"`. Always quote variables in double quotes so spaces stay intact. **Command substitution** captures the output of a command into a variable: `today=$(date +%F)` stores today's date. The `$( )` form is preferred over the older backticks.
When you run `./greet.sh Purva`, the script receives that word as an input:
`$1`, `$2`, `$3` … are the first, second, third arguments.
`$0` is the script's own name.
`$#` is the **number** of arguments given.
`$@` is **all** the arguments (quote it as `"$@"` to keep each intact).
This lets one script behave differently depending on what you pass it.

Every command returns an **exit status**: `0` means success, any other number means failure. The special variable `$?` holds the status of the **last** command, so you can test whether it worked. In your own scripts, `exit 0` ends with success and `exit 1` (or any non-zero) signals an error. Send error messages to standard error with `>&2` by convention.

blocks.x: Scripts become useful when they can **decide**. The `if` statement runs code only when a test is true: ``` if [ "$x" = "yes" ]; then echo ok else echo no fi ``` The spaces inside `[ ]` are required, and the block ends with `fi` (if spelled backwards). `[ ]` is actually the `test` command in disguise.
Tests come in two flavours:

**Numbers**: `-eq` (equal), `-ne` (not equal), `-lt` (less than), `-le`, `-gt` (greater than), `-ge`. Example: `[ "$n" -gt 5 ]`. Note that inside `[ ]`, the symbol `>` means redirection, not comparison — so use `-gt`.
**Strings**: `=` and `!=`. `[ -z "$s" ]` is true when the string is empty; `[ -n "$s" ]` when it is not.
**Files**: `-f file` (a regular file exists), `-d dir` (a directory), `-e` (exists, any type), `-r`/`-w`/`-x` (readable/writable/executable), `-s` (not empty).

A **loop** repeats work. The `for` loop steps through a list: ``` for i in 1 2 3; do echo $i; done ``` The list can be numbers (`{1..5}`), files (`for f in /etc/*.conf`), or command output. A `while` loop repeats **as long as** a condition is true — the classic pattern reads a file line by line: ``` while read line; do echo "$line"; done < users.txt ``` This safely handles each line even if it contains spaces.

`&&` runs the next command only if the previous **succeeded**; `||` runs it only if the previous **failed** — e.g. `[ -r /etc/hosts ] && echo yes`. For choosing between many fixed values, `case` is cleaner than a chain of ifs, and each branch ends with `;;`, with the whole block closed by `esac`.

blocks.x: Sometimes a task should run **later** or **repeatedly** without you being there. RHEL offers two classic tools:
**at** runs a command **once** at a future time.
**cron** runs commands **repeatedly** on a schedule.
(A third, modern option — systemd timers — is covered on the next day.)

theory.h: Scheduling a one-off job with at

blocks.x: `at` reads the command from standard input and runs it once:
`echo "command" | at now + 5 minutes` schedules it 5 minutes from now. Other time forms: `at 16:30`, `at 9am tomorrow`, `at noon + 2 days`.
`atq` (or `at -l`) lists pending jobs; `at -c 3` shows the full script of job 3; `atrm 3` (or `at -d 3`) deletes it.
The `atd` service must be running for jobs to fire.

Each user has a **crontab** (cron table). Edit yours with `crontab -e`; list it with `crontab -l`; remove it with `crontab -r`. As root you can manage another user's with `-u`: `crontab -e -u natasha`. A crontab line has **five time fields** then the command: ``` minute  hour  day-of-month  month  day-of-week   command ```

`*` means "every". `30 14 * * *` = 14:30 every day. `*/10 * * * *` = every 10 minutes. `0 2 * * 0` = 02:00 every Sunday (0 or 7 = Sunday). `30 23 1,15 * *` = 23:30 on the 1st and 15th (commas list values, dashes give ranges).

Besides per-user crontabs, the system has `/etc/crontab` and drop-in files in `/etc/cron.d/`. These have one **extra** field — the **user** to run as — between the time and the command: ``` 30 2 * * 0  root  /usr/local/bin/backup.sh ``` There are also ready-made directories `/etc/cron.hourly`, `/etc/cron.daily`, etc., where any script is run on that schedule. Who may use cron is controlled by `/etc/cron.allow` and `/etc/cron.deny`.

blocks.x: A **systemd timer** does the same job as cron but is integrated with systemd, so it gets logging, dependencies and better control. A timer always comes in **two files** with the same base name:
a **.service** unit that says *what* to run,
a **.timer** unit that says *when* to run it.
The timer starts its matching service. Put both in `/etc/systemd/system/`.
The `.timer` file's key line is `OnCalendar=`, which uses the format `DayOfWeek Year-Month-Day Hour:Minute:Second`:
`OnCalendar=*-*-* 02:00:00` runs every day at 02:00. Shortcuts like `daily`, `weekly`, `hourly` also work.
`OnBootSec=15min` runs 15 minutes after boot; pair it with `OnUnitActiveSec=1h` to then repeat every hour.
`Persistent=true` means if the machine was **off** at the scheduled time, the job runs soon after the next boot (like anacron).
The `[Install]` section should say `WantedBy=timers.target`, and you enable the **timer** (not the service): `systemctl enable --now backup.timer`.
`systemctl list-timers` shows all timers with their next and last run times.
`systemd-analyze calendar "Mon..Fri *-*-* 09:00"` checks what a calendar expression means and when it fires next — great for testing before you commit.
After creating or editing any unit file, run `systemctl daemon-reload` so systemd re-reads it.

systemd can also create and clean up temporary files/directories using rules in `/etc/tmpfiles.d/*.conf`. A rule like `d /run/myapp 0755 root root 1d` means "create this directory at boot and delete files in it older than 1 day". Apply now with `systemd-tmpfiles --create` and clean with `systemd-tmpfiles --clean`.

blocks.x: Different workloads want different settings — a laptop wants power saving, a database server wants throughput. The **tuned** service bundles these into **profiles** so you can switch with one command:
`tuned-adm active` shows the current profile.
`tuned-adm list` lists all available profiles.
`tuned-adm recommend` suggests the best profile for this machine (on a VM it usually recommends `virtual-guest`).
`tuned-adm profile virtual-guest` applies a profile; the choice persists while the tuned service is enabled.
Make sure the service runs: `systemctl enable --now tuned`.

Every process has a **nice value** from **−20** (highest priority, takes the most CPU) to **19** (lowest, most generous to others). The default is 0. A "nicer" process (higher number) yields CPU to others.
`nice -n 10 command` starts a command with nice value +10.
`renice -n 5 -p 1234` changes running PID 1234 to nice value 5.
Only **root** can lower a nice value (give higher priority / a negative number); a normal user can only raise their own processes' nice value.
The nice value shows in the **NI** column of `top` and `ps -o pid,ni,comm`.

For controlled tests you can bind a process to specific CPUs with `taskset -c 0 command`. Combined with nice, this shows clearly how priority affects CPU sharing when two processes compete on the same core.

theory.h: What SELinux is and why it exists

blocks.x: Standard permissions (rwx) are **discretionary** — the file owner decides access. **SELinux** (Security-Enhanced Linux) adds a second, **mandatory** layer that the system enforces regardless of the owner. Even if a service is tricked into misbehaving, SELinux policy limits what it can touch. It is a major reason RHEL is considered secure, and the exam expects you to keep it **enforcing** and fix problems, not switch it off.
SELinux has three modes:
**Enforcing** — policy is applied and violations are blocked (and logged).
**Permissive** — policy is **not** enforced, but violations are still **logged**. Useful for troubleshooting.
**Disabled** — off entirely (avoid on the exam).

Check the mode with `getenforce` or the fuller `sestatus`. Switch temporarily with `setenforce 0` (permissive) or `setenforce 1` (enforcing) — but note `setenforce` can only toggle between enforcing and permissive, not fully disable. The **permanent** setting lives in `/etc/selinux/config` (the `SELINUX=` line); fully disabling requires a reboot.

Every file and process carries an SELinux **context** of the form `user:role:type:level`, for example `system_u:object_r:httpd_sys_content_t:s0`. In the everyday "targeted" policy, the part that matters most is the **type** (ending in `_t`). Policy rules say which process types may access which file types — e.g. the web server runs as `httpd_t` and is only allowed to read files labelled `httpd_sys_content_t`.
`ls -Z file` shows a file's context; `ps -eZ | grep httpd` shows process contexts; `id -Z` shows your own.

This is the classic beginner trap: when you **move** a file with `mv`, it **keeps its original context**, which may be wrong for its new location — so a service is denied access. **Copying** (`cp`) usually gives the destination's default context. The correct fix is to relabel to the policy default with `restorecon` (covered next day). A denial in permissive mode is allowed but logged, which is exactly how you diagnose these problems safely.

labs.scenario: Create /var/www/html/bad.html in /root and move it into place so it gets the wrong context. Request it, find the denial in the audit log, read the sealert advice, and fix it.

blocks.x: When a file has the wrong SELinux type, you need to relabel it — and make that relabel **stick** even after a full filesystem relabel. There are two tools, and using the right one matters:
`chcon -t type file` changes the label **now**, but it is **temporary** — a relabel or `restorecon` will revert it. Avoid it for anything permanent.

`semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_sys_content_t '/web(/.*)?'` **records** a rule in the policy so the path always gets that type. The `(/.*)?` is a regular expression meaning "this directory and everything under it".

`restorecon -Rv /web` then **applies** the recorded rules to the files, setting each to its correct type (`-R` recursive, `-v` verbose). The exam answer is almost always **semanage fcontext + restorecon**, never chcon.
Some policy behaviour is optional and controlled by **booleans** — named on/off switches. For example `httpd_enable_homedirs` lets the web server read users' home directories.
`getsebool -a | grep httpd` lists httpd-related booleans and their state; `semanage boolean -l` adds a description.
`setsebool -P httpd_enable_homedirs on` turns one **on permanently** (the `-P` writes it to disk; without `-P` the change is lost at reboot).
`semanage boolean -l -C` shows only the booleans you have changed from their defaults.
SELinux also controls which **ports** a service may use. If you make a service listen on a non-standard port, SELinux will block the bind until the port is labelled correctly:
`semanage port -l | grep http` shows which ports carry the `http_port_t` type (80, 443, 8008, 8009, 8443 by default).
`semanage port -a -t http_port_t -p tcp 8888` **adds** port 8888 as an http port. If the port already has another type, use `-m` (modify) instead of `-a`.
The `semanage` command comes from the **policycoreutils-python-utils** package — install it if `semanage` is missing.

When something is blocked, the reason is logged as an **AVC denial** in `/var/log/audit/audit.log`. Search recent ones with `ausearch -m AVC -ts recent`, and get a plain-language explanation and suggested fix with `sealert -a /var/log/audit/audit.log` (from the setroubleshoot-server package). A methodical order — check the file context, the port label, then the relevant boolean — solves the large majority of SELinux problems without ever disabling it.

blocks.x: A physical disk (like `/dev/vdb`) is usually divided into **partitions** (`/dev/vdb1`, `/dev/vdb2`). A **partition table** at the start of the disk records where each partition begins and ends. Modern systems use the **GPT** (GUID Partition Table) format, which replaced the old MBR and supports large disks and many partitions.
`lsblk` shows disks and partitions as a tree — always start here to see the layout.
`parted` edits partition tables. Two commands you must know:
`parted /dev/vdb mklabel gpt` writes a **new, empty** GPT table. **Warning:** this erases every existing partition — only run it on a blank disk.

`parted /dev/vdb mkpart data xfs 1MiB 1025MiB` creates a partition. On GPT the first argument is a **name**, then a filesystem hint, then the start and end. Always use **MiB** units and start the first partition at 1MiB so it is properly **aligned** and leaves room for the GPT header.
`parted /dev/vdb print` shows the table; add `unit MiB print free` to see free space so you know where to start the next one.
After creating a partition, run `udevadm settle` so the device file (`/dev/vdb1`) appears before you format it.
Creating a partition does not make it usable — you must put a **filesystem** on it and mount it:
`mkfs.xfs /dev/vdb1` formats it as XFS (RHEL's default). `blkid /dev/vdb1` then shows its **UUID**.
`mount /dev/vdb1 /mnt/data` mounts it for now.

For a mount to survive reboots, add a line to `/etc/fstab` with **six fields**: ``` device        mountpoint   type   options    dump  fsck UUID=1b2c...  /mnt/data    xfs    defaults   0     0 ``` Use `UUID=` (or `LABEL=`) rather than `/dev/vdb1`, because device names can change between boots but the UUID does not. After editing fstab, **always test** with `systemctl daemon-reload` then `mount -a` (which mounts everything not yet mounted) before you reboot — a broken fstab line drops the boot into emergency mode. Run `findmnt --verify` for a deeper check.

blocks.x: **Swap** is disk space the kernel uses as overflow when physical RAM fills up — inactive memory pages are moved to swap so RAM is freed for active work. It is not a replacement for RAM, but it prevents out-of-memory crashes. Swap can live on a **partition**, a **logical volume**, or a **file**.
The process mirrors making a filesystem, but with swap-specific tools:
Create the partition with a swap hint: `parted /dev/vdb mkpart swap1 linux-swap 1025MiB 1537MiB`, then `udevadm settle`.
`mkswap /dev/vdb2` initialises it as swap (and prints a new UUID).
`swapon /dev/vdb2` turns it on now; `swapoff /dev/vdb2` turns it off.

Add a line to `/etc/fstab` — the mount-point field is `none` (or `swap`) and the type is `swap`: ``` UUID=<uuid>  none  swap  defaults  0 0 ``` Test it without rebooting using `swapon -a` (which activates all swap listed in fstab); `mount -a` ignores swap entries, so this separate step matters.
`swapon --show` (or `swapon -s`, or `cat /proc/swaps`) lists active swap areas; `free -h` shows total swap alongside RAM.
If you have several swap areas, give one priority with the `pri=N` option in fstab (higher numbers are used first): `UUID=... none swap pri=10 0 0`.
"Add swap non-destructively" — a common exam phrase — means add new swap using free space **without** deleting or disturbing existing partitions or swap.

questions.q: A VG has an extent size of 16 MiB. How big is an LV of 60 extents?
questions.explain: Size = extents x extent size = 60 x 16 MiB.
