labs.scenario: Completely remove labvg and its PVs, leaving the system booting cleanly.
steps: vim /etc/fstab             # delete the two labvg lines

blocks.x: Plain partitions are rigid — resizing them is awkward. **LVM** (Logical Volume Manager) adds a flexible layer so you can grow, shrink and combine storage easily. It has three levels:
**Physical Volumes (PV)** — the raw partitions or disks you hand to LVM.
**Volume Group (VG)** — a pool made by combining one or more PVs.
**Logical Volumes (LV)** — the usable "virtual partitions" you carve out of the VG, format and mount.
Space in a VG is measured in fixed chunks called **physical extents** (PE), 4 MiB by default.

theory.h: Building an LVM stack step by step

blocks.x: The commands follow the three levels in order:
`pvcreate /dev/vdb1` marks a partition as a physical volume. Check with `pvs`.
`vgcreate vgdata /dev/vdb1` creates a volume group from it. Add `-s 16M` to set a custom extent size. Check with `vgs` or `vgdisplay`.

`lvcreate -n lvdata -L 500M vgdata` creates a 500 MiB logical volume named lvdata. Use `-L` for a size, or `-l 60` for a number of **extents**, or `-l 100%FREE` to use all remaining space. Check with `lvs`.
Then treat the LV like any partition: `mkfs.xfs /dev/vgdata/lvdata`, make a mount point, and add it to `/etc/fstab`.

A logical volume can be reached by two equivalent paths: `/dev/vgdata/lvdata` and `/dev/mapper/vgdata-lvdata` — both work in fstab, and because LV names are stable they are as reliable as a UUID. When a task gives extents and an extent size, size = extents × extent size (e.g. 60 extents × 16 MiB = 960 MiB). `-L` rounds up to a whole number of extents.
The short summaries are `pvs`, `vgs`, `lvs`; the detailed versions are `pvdisplay`, `vgdisplay`, `lvdisplay`. `vgdisplay` shows the "PE Size" (extent size) and how many free extents remain.

days.title: LVM: extending volumes

questions.q: Grow /dev/vgdata/lvdata by 200 MiB and grow its filesystem in the same command.
questions.explain: `-r` runs the right grow tool for XFS or ext4 after the LV grows.

questions.q: Grow the mounted XFS filesystem at /mnt/data to fill its (already extended) LV.
questions.explain: xfs_growfs takes the mount point. XFS grows while mounted.

questions.q: Grow the ext4 filesystem on /dev/vgdata/lvdb to fill its LV.
questions.explain: resize2fs takes the device. ext4 can grow while mounted.

questions.q: Can an XFS filesystem be made smaller?
questions.explain: To shrink XFS you must back up, recreate the filesystem smaller, and restore. ext4 can shrink while unmounted.

questions.q: Add the physical volume /dev/vdc1 to the volume group vgdata.
questions.explain: Run `pvcreate /dev/vdc1` first if it is not a PV yet (vgextend can also do it for you).

questions.q: A task says: "Resize LV vo to 230 MiB (anything from 217 to 243 MiB is fine)". The extent size is 16 MiB. What does `lvextend -L 230M` give?
options: An error, because 230 is not a multiple of 16
240 MiB, because LVM rounds up to a whole number of extents (15)
questions.explain: 230 / 16 = 14.4, rounded up to 15 extents = 240 MiB, which is inside the allowed range.

questions.q: What is the difference between `lvextend -L 1G` and `lvextend -L +1G`?
options: -L 1G sets the total size to 1 GiB; -L +1G adds 1 GiB to the current size
questions.explain: Read the task carefully: "resize to" is an absolute size, "grow by" is relative.

questions.q: You grew the LV but `df -h` still shows the old size. Why?
options: The VG needs to be reactivated
You must remount with the grow option
The filesystem was not grown; run xfs_growfs or resize2fs, or use lvextend -r next time
questions.explain: The LV and the filesystem are separate layers.

questions.explain: The VG needs enough free space on its other PVs. It can run while mounted.

questions.q: After pvmove, which command removes /dev/vdb1 from vgdata?
questions.explain: Then `pvremove /dev/vdb1` wipes its LVM label.

labs.title: Resize a logical volume (exam classic)
labs.scenario: Setup: create VG vgexam (16 MiB extents) and LV vo of 176 MiB with XFS mounted at /mnt/vo, with a test file inside. Task: resize vo to 230 MiB (217 to 243 MiB is fine) without losing data.
steps: vgcreate -s 16M vgexam /dev/vdb4      # setup, on a spare partition or disk

labs.scenario: Try to grow an LV beyond the VG's free space and read the error. Add a new PV to the VG, then grow the LV and its filesystem by 500 MiB.

blocks.x: The big advantage of LVM is easy resizing. Growing an LV is a **two-part** job: enlarge the LV, then enlarge the filesystem on it. The safe way does both at once:

`lvextend -r -L +200M /dev/vgdata/lvdata` grows the LV by 200 MiB **and** (thanks to `-r`, "resize filesystem") grows the filesystem to match. Without `-r` you would have to run the filesystem grow tool separately.
`-L +200M` **adds** 200 MiB; `-L 1G` **sets** the total to 1 GiB. Read the task: "grow by" is relative (`+`), "resize to" is absolute.
If you extend the LV without `-r`, `df -h` still shows the old size until you grow the filesystem:
**XFS**: `xfs_growfs /mnt/data` — note it takes the **mount point**, and XFS grows only while mounted.
**ext4**: `resize2fs /dev/vgdata/lvdata` — takes the **device**.
Important limitation: **XFS can only grow, never shrink.** ext4 can shrink (while unmounted). To make XFS smaller you must back up, recreate it smaller, and restore.

theory.h: When the volume group is full

blocks.x: If the VG has no free space, you cannot grow an LV until you add capacity:
`vgextend vgdata /dev/vdc1` adds another physical volume to the group (run `pvcreate` on it first if needed).
To remove a PV, first move its data off with `pvmove /dev/vdb1`, then `vgreduce vgdata /dev/vdb1`, then `pvremove /dev/vdb1`.
To tear an LVM stack down cleanly, always work top-down: unmount, remove the fstab line, `lvremove`, `vgremove`, `pvremove`.

blocks.x: RHEL supports several filesystems, and the exam expects you to create and mount each:
**XFS** — RHEL's default; robust and fast; can only grow.
**ext4** — the long-standing Linux default; can grow **and** shrink.
**VFAT** — the FAT filesystem for compatibility with other systems (USB sticks, EFI). It stores **no** Linux ownership or permissions.
The tools: `mkfs.xfs` (from xfsprogs), `mkfs.ext4` (from e2fsprogs), and `mkfs.vfat` (from dosfstools). Add `-f` to overwrite an existing filesystem.
A **label** is a friendly name you can mount by, as an alternative to the UUID:
XFS: set with `xfs_admin -L DATA /dev/vdb1` (unmounted) or at creation `mkfs.xfs -L DATA`.
ext4: `e2label /dev/vdb2 BACKUP` or `tune2fs -L`.
VFAT: `fatlabel /dev/vdb5 WINDATA`, or at creation `mkfs.vfat -n WINDATA`. Note VFAT's label option is `-n`, while XFS/ext4 use `-L`.
Then mount by `LABEL=DATA` in fstab instead of the UUID.

Because VFAT has no concept of Linux ownership, you assign it at mount time with options: `mount -o uid=2000,gid=2000 /dev/vdb5 /mnt/usb`. In fstab: `UUID=1A2B-3C4D /mnt/usb vfat uid=2000,gid=2000 0 0` (VFAT UUIDs are short, like `1A2B-3C4D`).

`nofail` lets the boot continue even if that device is missing (good for removable or network disks); `noauto` means "do not mount at boot at all"; `ro`/`rw` for read-only/read-write; remount live with `mount -o remount,ro /mnt/data`.
Inspect: `xfs_info /mnt/data` for XFS geometry; `tune2fs -l /dev/...` for ext4; `findmnt -o TARGET,OPTIONS /mnt/data` to see how something is mounted.

labs.scenario: On node2, share /shares/docs (read-write) and /rhome with your lab subnet. Create remote user home directories /rhome/remoteuser1 and /rhome/remoteuser2 owned by UIDs 5001 and 5002. Open the firewall.

mount -t nfs node2:/wrong /mnt/docs        # access denied / No such file

blocks.x: **NFS** (Network File System) lets a server **share** (export) a directory over the network so client machines can **mount** it and use it as if it were local. It is the standard way to share files between Linux systems. The client tools come from the **nfs-utils** package.

theory.h: Mounting an NFS share on the client

blocks.x: `mount -t nfs node2:/shares/docs /mnt/docs` mounts the export now (the mount point must exist). The syntax is `server:/exported/path`.
`showmount -e node2` lists what a server exports (needs the server's supporting services reachable).
RHEL defaults to **NFSv4**; force a version with `-o nfsvers=4.2` or `-o vers=3` if a task asks.
`findmnt -t nfs4` shows mounted NFS filesystems and their options.

Add it to `/etc/fstab` with the type `nfs` and the `_netdev` option (which tells the system to wait for the network before mounting): ``` node2:/shares/docs  /mnt/docs  nfs  defaults,_netdev  0 0 ``` The dump and fsck fields are `0 0` because there is nothing local to check. Test with `mount -a` and confirm with `findmnt /mnt/docs`.

On the server, exports are defined in `/etc/exports`, one line each: `/shares/docs 192.168.122.0/24(rw,sync)`. Apply changes with `exportfs -rv`, run the `nfs-server` service, and open the firewall for the `nfs` service (plus `rpc-bind` and `mountd` if clients use `showmount`). Understanding the server helps you troubleshoot a failing client mount — a hang usually means a firewall or export problem.

questions.q: Where do you add your own master map entries on RHEL?
options: In a file ending in .autofs under /etc/auto.master.d/
questions.explain: Example /etc/auto.master.d/shares.autofs: `/shares  /etc/auto.shares`.

options: At /shares/work, the first time something accesses it

blocks.x: Mounting every network share in `/etc/fstab` means they are all mounted at boot and stay mounted, even when unused. **autofs** mounts a share **on demand** — only when someone accesses it — and unmounts it automatically after a period of inactivity. This is ideal for home directories and shares that are not always needed. It is provided by the **autofs** package and service.

theory.h: The master map and the mount maps

blocks.x: autofs configuration has two layers:
The **master map** entries live in files under `/etc/auto.master.d/` ending in `.autofs`. Each line links a **base directory** to a **mount map** file, e.g. `/shares  /etc/auto.shares`.

The **mount map** (e.g. `/etc/auto.shares`) lists the actual mounts: `work  -rw,sync  node2:/shares/work`. Here `work` becomes a subdirectory of the base directory, so this mounts at `/shares/work` the first time it is accessed.
You do **not** create the subdirectories yourself — autofs manages the base directory entirely. Enable it with `systemctl enable --now autofs`; after editing maps, `systemctl reload autofs`.
The example above is an **indirect map**: keys become subdirectories under one base. `ls /shares` shows nothing until you actually access `/shares/work`.
A **direct map** uses `/-` as the base in the master map, and each key is a full path: `/mnt/docs  -ro  node2:/shares/docs`.

A **wildcard map** uses `*` and `&` to serve any key automatically — perfect for home directories: `*  -rw,sync  node2:/rhome/&` mounts `node2:/rhome/<name>` whenever `/rhome/<name>` is accessed. The `&` is replaced by whatever key was requested.

A very common exam task combines a user with no local home and an autofs wildcard map, so the user's home is fetched from an NFS server on login. Create the user with `useradd -M` (no local home) and a matching home path, add the master and wildcard map entries, and confirm with `su - user` (which triggers the mount) and `findmnt`.

blocks.x: systemd groups the system into **targets** — named states that pull in a set of services. A target is roughly the modern replacement for old "runlevels". The two you care about most:
**multi-user.target** — a full multi-user system with networking, but **no graphical desktop** (text login).
**graphical.target** — everything in multi-user plus the desktop.
Special targets help with repair: **rescue.target** (single-user, root shell, local filesystems mounted) and **emergency.target** (the most minimal — only the root filesystem, mounted read-only).

theory.h: Viewing and setting the default target

blocks.x: `systemctl get-default` shows which target the system boots into.
`systemctl set-default multi-user.target` changes it permanently (this just re-points the `/etc/systemd/system/default.target` symlink).
`systemctl isolate multi-user.target` switches to a target **right now** without rebooting, stopping anything not needed by it (run it from the console, since switching can stop your SSH session).

To enter a target for a **single** boot (say, to repair something), interrupt the boot loader: at the GRUB menu press **e** to edit, find the line starting with `linux`, add `systemd.unit=rescue.target` at the end, and press **Ctrl+X** to boot. The change applies only to that boot.

Knowing the order tells you where to intervene when boot fails: 1. **Firmware (BIOS/UEFI)** powers on and finds the boot device. 2. **GRUB2** (the boot loader) loads and shows its menu. 3. The **kernel and initramfs** load and mount the real root filesystem. 4. **systemd** (PID 1) starts and brings the system up to the default target.

blocks.x: If you don't know the root password, you regain access by interrupting the boot into the initramfs, before the real system takes over. This is a signature RHCSA task, and the steps are worth memorising:
Reboot and at the GRUB menu press **e**. On the line starting with `linux`, add **`rd.break`** at the end, then **Ctrl+X**.
You land in a tiny emergency shell where the real root filesystem is mounted **read-only** at `/sysroot`.
`mount -o remount,rw /sysroot` — remount it writable.
`chroot /sysroot` — make `/sysroot` act as `/` so paths like `/etc/shadow` are the real ones.
`passwd root` — set the new password.
`touch /.autorelabel` — **crucial**: the changed `/etc/shadow` needs the correct SELinux label, and this flag makes the next boot relabel the filesystem. Skipping it can lock everyone out.
`exit`, then `exit` again — the system relabels (this takes a few minutes) and reboots. Log in with the new password.
A bad line in `/etc/fstab` (a wrong UUID, a missing device) stops the boot and drops you into **emergency mode**, asking for the root password. To fix it:
Enter the root password. The root filesystem is mounted **read-only**, so run `mount -o remount,rw /` first.
Edit `/etc/fstab` to correct or comment out the bad line (check real UUIDs with `blkid`).
`systemctl daemon-reload` then `mount -a` to test the fix before rebooting.
The lesson: after **every** fstab change, test with `mount -a` immediately — never discover the mistake at the next reboot.

For a device that may not always be present (a removable disk, an NFS share), add the **`nofail`** mount option in fstab. Then, if the device is missing at boot, the system logs it and continues instead of dropping into emergency mode.

blocks.x: **GRUB2** is the boot loader — the program that runs after the firmware, shows the menu of installed kernels, and loads the one you choose. Being able to edit its settings and kernel options is a required skill.

theory.h: Editing kernel options safely with grubby

blocks.x: Rather than hand-editing generated files, use `grubby` to manage kernel entries and their command-line options:
`grubby --default-kernel` shows which kernel boots by default; `grubby --info=ALL` lists every entry with its options.
`grubby --update-kernel=ALL --args="console=ttyS0"` adds a kernel argument to **all** kernels; use `--update-kernel=DEFAULT` to affect only the default one.
`grubby --remove-args="quiet"` removes an argument.
`grubby --set-default /boot/vmlinuz-<version>` makes a specific kernel the default.

Changes take effect at the next boot; confirm with `cat /proc/cmdline` afterward. The individual menu entries live in `/boot/loader/entries/*.conf` (Boot Loader Specification files), which grubby edits for you.
Global settings like the menu timeout live in `/etc/default/grub` (e.g. `GRUB_TIMEOUT=10`). This file is a **source**, not the live config — after editing it you must regenerate the real config:
`grub2-mkconfig -o /boot/grub2/grub.cfg` rebuilds it (this path is correct for both BIOS and UEFI on RHEL 9/10).

For a temporary change (testing), don't edit files at all — at the GRUB menu press **e**, add the option to the `linux` line, and press **Ctrl+X**. It applies to that boot only and is forgotten afterward.

blocks.x: **firewalld** is RHEL's firewall management service. It decides which incoming network connections are allowed. You manage it with the `firewall-cmd` command, and it organises rules into **zones** — each zone is a trust level (public, trusted, drop, internal, dmz…) that can be attached to network interfaces or source addresses.

theory.h: The permanent vs runtime rule (the #1 gotcha)

blocks.x: firewalld keeps two rule sets: the **runtime** rules (active now, lost at reboot) and the **permanent** rules (saved to disk, loaded at boot). This trips up everyone:
`firewall-cmd --add-service=http` changes only the **runtime** — gone after reboot.
`firewall-cmd --permanent --add-service=http` saves it **permanently** but does **not** apply it now.

The reliable pattern is: add with `--permanent`, then `firewall-cmd --reload` to make the permanent rules active immediately. `firewall-cmd --runtime-to-permanent` saves current runtime rules as permanent if you tested them live.
Allow a named service: `firewall-cmd --permanent --add-service=http` (a service is a predefined set of ports; see `firewall-cmd --get-services`, defined in `/usr/lib/firewalld/services/*.xml`).
Open a specific port: `firewall-cmd --permanent --add-port=8080/tcp`.
Remove: `--remove-service=` / `--remove-port=`.
Inspect: `firewall-cmd --list-all` (current zone), `--list-all-zones` (all), `--get-default-zone`, `--get-active-zones`.
Put a source address into a zone: `firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=trusted --add-source=192.168.122.12` gives that host full access.

For finer control, a **rich rule** combines source, service, action and logging: `firewall-cmd --permanent --add-rich-rule='rule family="ipv4" source address="192.168.50.0/24" service name="ssh" reject'` refuses SSH from one subnet. Note **reject** replies "refused" while **drop** silently discards. `man firewalld.richlanguage` has copyable examples.

theory.h: Security is layered — check all three

blocks.x: When a network service does not work, three separate layers can be blocking it, and a real administrator checks each in order: 1. **The service itself** — is it running, and listening on the right port? (`systemctl status`, `ss -tulpn`). 2. **SELinux** — is the port labelled and are the file contexts correct? A "Permission denied" when a service tries to **bind** to a new port is usually SELinux, not the firewall. 3. **The firewall** — is the port open to other machines? A service that works with `curl localhost` but not from another host points to the firewall. The firewall never stops a *local* service from starting; it only blocks *incoming* traffic. Keep this mental model and you will fix problems methodically instead of guessing.

theory.h: Running a service on a non-standard port

blocks.x: Putting, say, a web server on port 8888 needs all three layers aligned:
Configure the service to listen on 8888 (edit its config).
Tell SELinux the port is allowed: `semanage port -a -t http_port_t -p tcp 8888`.
Open the firewall: `firewall-cmd --permanent --add-port=8888/tcp && firewall-cmd --reload`.
Restart the service. Then test with `curl http://host:8888/` from another machine.

theory.h: SSH on an extra port and diagnosing

blocks.x: The same pattern applies to running sshd on an additional port: add `Port 2222` to the sshd config, label it with `semanage port -a -t ssh_port_t -p tcp 2222`, open `2222/tcp` in the firewall, and restart sshd. To diagnose, `ss -tlnp | grep 2222` confirms something is listening, and a capture with `tcpdump` shows whether a connection gets no reply (blocked) versus a reset (refused). The golden rule: fix contexts, ports and firewall rules — never "fix" a problem by turning SELinux or the firewall off.

A backup stored off the disk

A point-in-time copy of a logical volume that only stores changed blocks

options: Taking a consistent backup while the origin keeps changing
questions.explain: Back up from the frozen snapshot, then remove it.

questions.q: Create a 1 GiB snapshot named datasnap of the logical volume /dev/vgdata/lvdata.
questions.explain: -s makes it a snapshot; the origin is the last argument.

questions.q: Show all logical volumes including snapshots, with their origin and usage.
questions.explain: `lvs -a` reveals hidden internal volumes; add columns to see snapshot detail.

questions.q: Merge the snapshot /dev/vgdata/datasnap back into its origin.
questions.explain: After merging, the snapshot is automatically removed.

labs.title: Snapshot, break, and roll back (exam-plus)
labs.scenario: On lvdata (mounted at /mnt/data with a file inside), take a snapshot, deliberately corrupt the data, then roll back using the snapshot and prove the file returned.

labs.title: Consistent backup from a snapshot
labs.scenario: Snapshot lvdata, mount the snapshot read-only, back it up with tar, then remove the snapshot.
verify: tar -tzf /root/data-backup.tar.gz | head; lvs | grep -c bsnap   # 0 left

labs.title: Watch a snapshot fill up
labs.scenario: Create a small (100 MiB) snapshot, then write more than 100 MiB into the origin and observe the snapshot become invalid.
steps: lvs -a -o +data_percent      # tiny shows 100% then goes invalid
verify: lvs shows the snapshot invalidated (Attr has an 'I'); you understand sizing

blocks.x: A **snapshot** captures a logical volume at a moment in time so you can roll back to it later. It is clever about space: it uses **copy-on-write**, meaning it starts almost empty and only stores the **original** version of blocks that change on the source volume afterward. So a snapshot begins tiny and grows as the origin is modified.
`lvcreate -s -n datasnap -L 1G /dev/vgdata/lvdata` creates a 1 GiB snapshot of lvdata (`-s` = snapshot; the origin is the last argument).
`lvs -a -o +origin,data_percent` shows snapshots with their **Origin** and **Data%** columns. Watch Data% closely.
**If a snapshot fills to 100%, it becomes invalid and is dropped** — so size it for the amount of change you expect during its life. (lvm.conf can enable auto-extend.)
To restore the origin to the snapshot's state, **merge** the snapshot back:

`lvconvert --merge /dev/vgdata/datasnap`. If the origin is currently in use, the merge completes at the next activation/reboot; after merging, the snapshot is removed automatically. Unmount the origin first for an immediate merge.

A common professional use is taking a **consistent backup**: snapshot the volume (freezing a moment), mount the snapshot read-only, back it up with tar while the real volume keeps changing, then remove the snapshot. Remember snapshots are a fast local "undo", **not** a substitute for real off-machine backups.

days.title: Advanced LVM: thin, striped and RAID volumes
days.objective: Build thin-provisioned, striped and mirrored/RAID logical volumes.

questions.q: What is thin provisioning in LVM?
options: Volumes that are always exactly their physical size
Logical volumes can present more space than is physically allocated, using a shared thin pool
questions.explain: Space is consumed from the pool only as data is written.

questions.q: What is the main risk of thin provisioning?
options: Over-provisioning: if the pool fills, writes to any thin volume fail
questions.explain: Monitor the pool's Data% and Meta% and extend before it fills.

questions.q: A striped logical volume (`--type striped -i 2`) improves:
options: Performance, by spreading I/O across multiple physical volumes
questions.explain: Striping has no redundancy; losing one PV loses the volume.

questions.q: Which LVM RAID type gives mirroring (redundancy) across two devices?
questions.explain: raid1 keeps a full copy on each leg; it survives one device failing.

questions.q: In `lvcreate --type raid5 -i 3`, what does -i specify?
options: The number of data stripes (RAID 5 also adds one parity's worth of space)
questions.explain: RAID 5 needs at least 3 devices and tolerates one failure.

questions.q: Which command shows the underlying devices and segment type of LVs?
questions.explain: It reveals which PVs each stripe/leg sits on.

questions.q: Create a 1 GiB thin pool named tpool in volume group vgdata.
questions.explain: -T (or --type thin-pool) builds the pool that thin volumes draw from.

questions.q: Create a 5 GiB thin volume named tvol from the thin pool vgdata/tpool.
questions.explain: -V is the virtual size, which may exceed the pool's real size.

questions.q: Create a striped LV named fast across 2 PVs, 1 GiB total, 64 KiB stripe size.
questions.explain: -i = number of stripes (PVs), -I = stripe size in KiB.

questions.q: Create a mirrored (raid1) LV named safe of 500 MiB in vgdata.
questions.explain: -m 1 means one mirror copy (two legs total).

labs.title: Thin provisioning end to end
labs.scenario: In vgdata create a 1 GiB thin pool, a 4 GiB thin volume, format and mount it, and watch pool usage grow as you write.
steps: lvs vgdata      # tpool Data% climbs toward 300 MiB used
verify: df -h /mnt/thin shows 4G; lvs shows the pool is only partly used

labs.title: Build and inspect a RAID1 volume
labs.scenario: Create a raid1 LV across two PVs, format and mount it, then show its legs and sync status.
verify: lvs -a shows two rimage/rmeta legs and 100% sync

labs.title: Extend a thin pool before it fills
labs.scenario: Simulate a nearly full thin pool and extend the pool (not just the volume) to avoid write failures.
steps: lvs vgdata      # Data% drops as capacity grows
verify: the pool has more free space and thin volumes keep working

labs.title: Compare striped vs linear (concept + build)
labs.scenario: Create one linear and one striped LV of the same size and explain when you would choose each.
verify: # linear = simple/flexible; striped = faster I/O, no redundancy

blocks.x: Normally an LV reserves its full size up front. **Thin provisioning** lets logical volumes share a common **thin pool** and consume space only as they actually write data — so you can present more logical space than physically exists (over-provisioning):
`lvcreate --type thin-pool -L 1G -n tpool vgdata` creates the pool.
`lvcreate -V 5G -T vgdata/tpool -n tvol` creates a thin volume whose **virtual** size (5 G) exceeds the pool (1 G).
The risk: if the **pool** fills, writes to any thin volume fail. Watch the pool's Data% and Meta% with `lvs`, and extend the **pool** in time with `lvextend -L +1G vgdata/tpool`.
A **striped** LV spreads data across several physical volumes so reads and writes happen in parallel — faster I/O, but **no redundancy** (losing one PV loses the volume):
`lvcreate --type striped -i 2 -I 64 -L 1G -n fast vgdata` uses `-i` stripes across 2 PVs with a `-I` 64 KiB stripe size.
LVM can build RAID levels directly:
`raid1` (`lvcreate --type raid1 -m 1 -L 500M -n safe vgdata`) mirrors data across two legs and survives one device failing (`-m 1` = one mirror copy).
`raid5` (`--type raid5 -i 3`) stripes with parity across at least 3 devices and tolerates one failure.
Inspect the underlying devices and sync state with `lvs -a -o +devices,segtype,sync_percent`.

questions.q: What is Stratis?

questions.q: How do you make a Stratis filesystem mount at boot in /etc/fstab?

questions.q: What does LVM-VDO provide?

questions.explain: VDO is ideal for backups/VM images with lots of repeated data.

questions.q: Where does LVM keep automatic backups of volume-group metadata?
questions.explain: These let you restore a VG's metadata after accidental damage.

questions.q: Which command restores a volume group's metadata from an LVM backup file?
questions.explain: Pair it with vgcfgbackup, which writes the current metadata to a file.

questions.q: To physically move a volume group's disks to another system, you first:
options: Deactivate its LVs and run vgexport, then vgimport on the new host
questions.explain: vgexport marks the VG as movable; vgimport reactivates it elsewhere.

questions.q: Create a Stratis pool named mypool from the disk /dev/vdb.
questions.explain: Install stratisd/stratis-cli and enable stratisd first.

questions.q: Create a Stratis filesystem named data in the pool mypool.

verify: stratis filesystem list; findmnt /mnt/stratis; reboot and re-check

labs.title: Grow a Stratis pool

verify: the pool's total size increased with no downtime

labs.title: Deduplication with LVM-VDO
labs.scenario: Create a VDO volume, format and mount it, write duplicate data, and show that physical usage stays low.
steps: for i in $(seq 1 5); do cp /root/bigfile /mnt/vdo/copy$i; done
verify: logical data far exceeds the physical space actually used

labs.title: Recover a damaged volume group
labs.scenario: Back up vgdata's metadata, "accidentally" remove an LV, then restore the metadata from the archive.
steps: lvs vgdata      # note an LV to sacrifice, e.g. lvtest
ls /etc/lvm/archive/ | grep vgdata      # find the pre-removal archive
verify: lvs vgdata shows lvtest restored (reactivate with vgchange -ay vgdata)

blocks.x: **Stratis** is a newer local storage manager that layers on top of LVM and device-mapper to give you pools and thin XFS filesystems with simple commands, without managing PVs/VGs/LVs by hand. Manage it with the `stratis` command and the `stratisd` service:
`stratis pool create mypool /dev/vdb` builds a pool; `stratis pool add-data mypool /dev/vdc` grows it live.
`stratis filesystem create mypool data` makes a filesystem at `/dev/stratis/mypool/data`.
Because the device is not ready until `stratisd` runs, its `/etc/fstab` line needs the option `x-systemd.requires=stratisd.service` so the mount waits for the service.

**LVM-VDO** stores data with inline **deduplication** (identical blocks stored once) and **compression**, so a volume can hold far more logical data than its physical size — ideal for backups and VM images with lots of repetition:
`lvcreate --type vdo -n vdolv -L 10G -V 30G vgdata` creates a VDO volume; check savings with `lvs -o+vdo_used_size,data_percent`.
LVM automatically backs up each volume group's metadata to `/etc/lvm/backup` (current) and `/etc/lvm/archive` (historical). If you damage a VG — say you delete an LV by mistake — you can restore it:
`vgcfgbackup vgdata` writes current metadata to a file.
`vgcfgrestore -f /etc/lvm/archive/vgdata_XXXX.vg vgdata` restores from an archive (then reactivate with `vgchange -ay vgdata`).
To physically move a VG's disks to another machine, deactivate its LVs and use `vgexport`, then `vgimport` on the new host.

The service should run as root

questions.explain: This logs (but allows) only that domain's denials — great for targeted troubleshooting.

verify: the action is now allowed and semodule -l shows "custom"

labs.title: Targeted permissive domain

steps: # reproduce the app behavior, collect denials with ausearch
verify: only httpd_t was permissive; the rest stayed enforcing

labs.title: Use sealert for a guided fix
labs.scenario: Install setroubleshoot, reproduce a denial, and use sealert to get a step-by-step suggested fix.
verify: you can read the suggested commands and apply the correct one

blocks.x: When SELinux blocks something in enforcing mode, it records an **AVC** (Access Vector Cache) denial in `/var/log/audit/audit.log`. Reading and understanding these is the core troubleshooting skill:
`ausearch -m AVC -ts recent` searches for recent denials (`-m AVC` filters the message type, `-ts recent` the time window).
Pipe a denial to `audit2why` for a plain-language explanation of **why** it happened — often pointing at a boolean or a wrong context.
If no boolean or correct label fixes a legitimate denial, you can generate a small custom policy **module** that permits exactly those actions:
`audit2allow -a -M mymodule` reads the denials and produces `mymodule.pp` (always review the human-readable `mymodule.te` it also writes).
`semodule -i mymodule.pp` loads it; `semodule -l` lists loaded modules; `semodule -r mymodule` removes it.
This is a **last resort** — always try labels and booleans first, because they are the intended fix.

theory.h: Guided fixes and targeted permissive mode

blocks.x: `sealert -a /var/log/audit/audit.log` (from setroubleshoot-server) analyses denials and prints suggested commands.

`semanage permissive -a httpd_t` puts a **single** domain (here the web server) into permissive mode so you can collect all its denials while the rest of the system stays enforcing — much safer than `setenforce 0`. Remove it afterward with `semanage permissive -d httpd_t`.

theory.h: The right order to fix a denial

blocks.x: For a real problem, work through: (1) is the **file context** correct? fix with `restorecon`; (2) is a **boolean** needed? set it; (3) is a **port** label needed? add it. Only if none of those apply do you build a custom module. Fixing labels — never disabling SELinux — is always the exam-correct answer.

labs.title: Boolean-driven feature

theory.h: chcon vs semanage fcontext (again, because it matters)

blocks.x: This distinction is the heart of SELinux file management:
`chcon -t type file` changes a label **now** but does not survive a relabel — temporary.
`semanage fcontext -a -t type 'regex'` records a **permanent** rule in policy; `restorecon -Rv path` then applies it. Always prefer semanage + restorecon.
File-context rules use regular expressions; `'/web(/.*)?'` covers the directory `/web` and everything under it.
To let a service use a non-default port, add the port to the correct type:
`semanage port -a -t http_port_t -p tcp 8888` (use `-m` to modify a port that already has a different type).
`semanage port -l | grep http` lists the ports a type already covers; `semanage port -l -C` shows only your changes.
Booleans switch optional policy behaviour on and off without editing policy:

`getsebool -a | grep httpd` lists them; `setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect on` enables one permanently (`-P` = persistent). Common ones let the web server reach the network or read home directories.
`semanage boolean -l -C` reviews only the ones you changed.
SELinux can also limit what a **login** may do, beyond normal permissions, by mapping Linux users to SELinux users (`user_u`, `staff_u`, `sysadm_u`):

`semanage login -a -s staff_u operator` maps the Linux user `operator` to the `staff_u` SELinux user; `semanage login -l` shows the mappings. A user mapped to `user_u`, for example, is confined even if they gain root-like tools. Check a logged-in user's context with `id -Z`.

blocks.x: A recap that catches everyone: **moving** a file with `mv` preserves its **old** context, so a service may be denied; **copying** picks up the destination's default. The universal fix is `restorecon -Rv /path`, which sets each file to the type the policy defines — persistent and correct, unlike a manual `chcon`.
`matchpathcon /web/index.html` (or `restorecon -n -v` for a dry run) shows the **expected** label so you can spot a mismatch against `ls -Z`.
After widespread context damage (or a password reset), you can trigger a **full relabel** on the next boot:
`touch /.autorelabel` then reboot — the system relabels everything and removes the flag. It can take a few minutes.
`restorecon -Rnv /var/www` is a safe **dry run** that lists what would change without changing anything; drop the `-n` to apply.
Container isolation is reinforced by SELinux. When you mount a host directory into a container you must relabel it so the container process (type `container_t`) may access it:

`podman run -v /srv/data:/data:Z ...` — the **:Z** relabels the host directory with a **private** container context (`container_file_t`) for that one container; lowercase **:z** labels it **shared** among containers.

For a permanent host label, use `semanage fcontext -a -t container_file_t '/srv/data(/.*)?'` and `restorecon`. This layering — namespaces plus SELinux — is why rootless containers on RHEL are considered well isolated.

blocks.x: A **container** is a lightweight, isolated package that holds an application plus everything it needs to run, sharing the host's kernel instead of running a whole separate operating system like a virtual machine. This makes containers fast to start and small. On RHEL the tool is **Podman**, which is **daemonless** (no background service like Docker needs) and can run **rootless** (as an ordinary user) — both reasons the RHCSA favours it. Most Docker commands work identically with `podman`.

An **image** is the read-only template; a **container** is a running instance of an image. Images come from **registries** (online image stores). A full image name is `registry/namespace/name:tag`, e.g. `registry.access.redhat.com/ubi9/ubi:latest`, where the **tag** is the version.
`podman search ubi9` searches the configured registries. Which registries are searched for a bare name is set in `/etc/containers/registries.conf` (the `unqualified-search-registries` list).
`podman pull registry.access.redhat.com/ubi9/ubi` downloads an image; `podman images` lists what you have stored locally. Rootless images live under `~/.local/share/containers/storage`.
`podman login registry.redhat.io` authenticates to a registry that needs credentials.
**skopeo** works on remote images without pulling them — perfect for checking before you download:
`skopeo inspect docker://registry.access.redhat.com/ubi9/ubi` shows an image's metadata (layers, labels, digest).
`skopeo copy` can copy images between registries and local storage.

blocks.x: The core command is `podman run`:

`podman run -d --name web -p 8080:80 nginx` runs nginx in the background (`-d` detached), names it `web`, and maps host port 8080 to the container's port 80 (`-p host:container`). Reach it at `http://host:8080`.
`podman run --rm image cmd` runs a one-off command and removes the container when it exits (`--rm`).
`podman run -it --name shell image bash` runs **interactively** (`-i` keep input open, `-t` give a terminal) — you get a shell inside the container. It stops when you exit.
`-e VAR=value` sets an environment variable inside the container.
`podman ps` shows **running** containers; `podman ps -a` includes **stopped** ones.
`podman stop web` / `podman start web` / `podman restart web` control a container.
`podman rm web` removes a stopped container (`podman rm -f web` stops and removes in one step). A stopped container keeps existing — and using space — until you remove it.
`podman logs web` shows its output (`-f` to follow live) — the first place to look when a container misbehaves.
`podman exec -it web bash` opens a shell **inside** an already-running container to look around.
`podman inspect web` prints detailed JSON; filter one field with `--format '{{.State.Status}}'`.

days.title: Containers: persistent storage and environment

questions.q: Why does data written inside a container usually disappear when the container is removed?
options: The container's writable layer is ephemeral; only mounted volumes persist
questions.explain: Persistent data must live on a mounted host directory or named volume.

questions.q: Which podman option bind-mounts a host directory into a container?
questions.explain: -p is for ports; -v (or --volume) is for storage.

questions.q: On an SELinux-enforcing host, what does the :Z suffix on a volume do?
options: Relabels the host directory with a private container context so the container can access it
questions.explain: Without :Z (or :z), SELinux typically denies the container access to the host files.

questions.q: The difference between :z and :Z on a volume is:
options: :z labels it shared among containers; :Z labels it private to one container
questions.explain: Use :Z when only one container should use the directory.

questions.q: A "named volume" (podman volume create) differs from a bind mount because it:
options: Is managed by Podman under its storage, not a specific host path you choose
questions.explain: Bind mounts point at an exact host directory; named volumes are Podman-managed.

questions.q: Which permanent SELinux type should a host directory served by a container have?
questions.explain: Set it with semanage fcontext + restorecon so it survives a relabel (better than relying on :Z alone).

questions.q: Run a container mounting host /srv/web into /usr/share/nginx/html with a private SELinux relabel.
questions.explain: :Z relabels /srv/web to container_file_t for this container.

questions.q: Create a Podman-managed named volume called appdata.
questions.explain: Inspect it with `podman volume inspect appdata`; list with `podman volume ls`.

questions.q: Permanently label the host directory /srv/web for container use.
questions.explain: Then apply it with `restorecon -Rv /srv/web`.

labs.title: Persistent web content (exam-style)
labs.scenario: Serve content from host /srv/web through an nginx container so the page survives removing and recreating the container.
verify: curl http://localhost:8080 still shows "Hello from the host"

labs.title: Use a named volume
labs.scenario: Create a named volume, mount it in a container, write data, remove the container, and confirm the data persists in a new container.
steps: podman run --rm -v appdata:/data registry.access.redhat.com/ubi9/ubi bash -c 'echo persisted > /data/file.txt'
verify: the second container reads "persisted" written by the first

labs.title: Prove the SELinux label matters
labs.scenario: Mount a host dir WITHOUT :Z and observe the denial, then fix it with the label.
verify: curl http://localhost:8081 now serves the file

labs.title: Inspect a container's mounts
labs.scenario: Run a container with a bind mount and use inspect to confirm the mount source, destination and mode.
verify: you can read the mount details from inspect

blocks.x: A container has a writable layer, but it is **ephemeral** — remove the container and anything written inside is gone. To keep data you must store it **outside** the container using a volume. There are two kinds:
A **bind mount** maps a specific host directory in: `-v /srv/web:/usr/share/nginx/html`.
A **named volume** is Podman-managed storage: `podman volume create appdata`, then `-v appdata:/data`. List with `podman volume ls`.
On an SELinux-enforcing host (the default), a container is **denied** access to host files unless they carry a container label. Add a suffix to the volume:
`:Z` relabels the host directory with a **private** context (`container_file_t`) for that one container.
`:z` labels it **shared** among containers.

So `-v /srv/web:/usr/share/nginx/html:Z` is what makes a bind mount actually work. Without it you will see a 403/permission error and an AVC denial. For a permanent host label, use `semanage fcontext -a -t container_file_t '/srv/web(/.*)?'` and `restorecon`.

Applications are often configured through environment variables. Pass them at run time with `-e NAME=value` (repeat for several), and confirm inside with `podman exec name printenv NAME` or `podman inspect name --format '{{.Config.Env}}'`.

questions.q: What is a Containerfile?
options: A text file of instructions (FROM, RUN, COPY, CMD...) that defines how to build an image

questions.q: The first instruction in a Containerfile is normally:

questions.q: What is the difference between CMD and ENTRYPOINT?
options: ENTRYPOINT sets the fixed executable; CMD sets default arguments that are easy to override
questions.explain: A common pattern is ENTRYPOINT for the program and CMD for default args.

options: RUN runs at start, CMD at build
RUN executes during the BUILD (creating a layer); CMD runs when the container STARTS
questions.explain: Use RUN to install software; use CMD/ENTRYPOINT to define the runtime process.

questions.explain: COPY src dest; ADD can also fetch URLs/untar, but COPY is preferred for clarity.

questions.explain: Confirm with `podman images | grep webapp`.

questions.explain: ENV values are present at both later build steps and runtime.

theory.h: Building your own image from a Containerfile

blocks.x: A **Containerfile** (same format as a Dockerfile) is a recipe of instructions that build a custom image. The common instructions:
**FROM** — the base image to build on (always first): `FROM registry.access.redhat.com/ubi9/ubi`.
**RUN** — run a command **during the build**, creating a new layer: `RUN dnf install -y httpd && dnf clean all`.
**COPY** — copy files from your build directory into the image: `COPY index.html /var/www/html/index.html`.
**ENV** — set an environment variable baked into the image.
**EXPOSE** — document the port the app listens on.
**CMD** / **ENTRYPOINT** — what runs when the container **starts**. ENTRYPOINT is the fixed executable; CMD supplies default arguments that are easy to override.

theory.h: RUN vs CMD — build time vs run time

blocks.x: The key distinction: **RUN** happens while the image is being **built** (installing software); **CMD/ENTRYPOINT** happens when a container **starts** from the finished image. Mixing these up is the usual beginner error.
`podman build -t webapp:1.0 .` builds an image tagged `webapp:1.0` from the Containerfile in the current directory (the trailing `.` is the build context).
`podman history webapp:1.0` shows the layers each instruction created.
`podman tag webapp:1.0 webapp:latest` adds another tag; `podman save -o webapp.tar webapp:1.0` exports the image to a file.

questions.explain: Other common keys: Image=, Volume=, Environment=.

questions.explain: RHEL 10 favors Quadlet, but knowing generate systemd is still useful.

questions.explain: Check with `loginctl show-user $USER | grep Linger`.

theory.h: Running a container as a systemd service

blocks.x: For a container that should start automatically at boot and be managed like any service, integrate it with systemd. On RHEL 10 the modern method is **Quadlet**: you write a small `.container` unit and systemd generates the service for you.
Put the file in `~/.config/containers/systemd/` (rootless) or `/etc/containers/systemd/` (rootful).
A minimal `webapp.container`:

``` [Container] Image=docker.io/library/nginx:latest PublishPort=8080:80 [Install] WantedBy=default.target ``` Key `[Container]` keys: `Image=`, `PublishPort=host:container`, `Volume=/host:/ctr:Z`, `Environment=`.
A Quadlet file named `webapp.container` produces a service called `webapp.service`:
After creating or editing the unit, `systemctl --user daemon-reload` (rootless) regenerates the service.
`systemctl --user start webapp.service` starts it; check with `systemctl --user status webapp.service`.
By default, a rootless user's services stop when their last login session ends. To make them run at boot and keep running after logout, enable **lingering**:
`loginctl enable-linger $USER`. Confirm with `loginctl show-user $USER | grep Linger`.

On RHEL 9 you may still see `podman generate systemd --new --name web --files`, which writes a systemd unit for an existing container; you copy it to `~/.config/systemd/user/` and `systemctl --user enable --now` it. Quadlet is the current, preferred approach, but recognise both.

questions.q: What is a Podman "pod"?

questions.explain: Containers in a pod reach each other on localhost and share published ports.

questions.q: Which command removes all stopped containers, unused images and networks to reclaim space?

questions.q: `podman stats` shows:

questions.explain: Useful for spotting a runaway container.

questions.q: A container keeps exiting immediately. The best first troubleshooting step is:
options: Check its logs with podman logs <name>
questions.explain: The logs usually show the crash reason (bad config, missing file, permission).

questions.q: `podman inspect` with `--format` is used to:
options: Extract a specific field (like the IP or state) from a container's JSON
questions.explain: e.g. `--format '{{.NetworkSettings.IPAddress}}'`.

questions.q: What does `podman auto-update` do (with a label on the container)?
options: Checks the registry and restarts the container if a newer image is available
questions.explain: It pairs with a systemd timer for hands-off image updates.

questions.q: Create a pod named webpod that publishes host port 8080.
questions.explain: Then run containers with `--pod webpod`.

questions.q: Show live resource usage for all running containers.
questions.explain: --no-stream prints one snapshot instead of a live view.

questions.q: Copy /etc/os-release out of the running container "web" to the current directory.
questions.explain: Works while the container is running or stopped.

labs.title: Build a two-container pod (exam-plus)
labs.scenario: Create a pod publishing port 8080, run a web container inside it, and confirm it is reachable and that both share the pod's network.
verify: podman ps shows the container in webpod and the site responds

labs.title: Troubleshoot a crashing container
labs.scenario: Deliberately run a container with a bad command, read the logs to find why it exits, then fix it.
steps: podman logs broken                # shows "no such file or directory"
verify: podman ps shows "fixed" running; you diagnosed the failure from logs

labs.scenario: List everything using space, then prune stopped containers and unused images safely.

verify: podman system df shows reclaimed space

labs.title: Extract and edit a config from a container
labs.scenario: Copy a config file out of a running container, inspect the container's IP, and copy an edited file back in.
verify: the file is copied both ways and you retrieved the container IP

blocks.x: A **pod** groups several containers that share networking — the same idea as a Kubernetes pod. Containers in a pod reach each other on `localhost` and share the pod's published ports:
`podman pod create --name webpod -p 8080:80` creates a pod; `podman run -d --pod webpod --name web nginx` adds a container to it; `podman pod ps` lists pods.
`podman stats` shows live CPU/memory/I/O per container (`--no-stream` for one snapshot).
`podman cp web:/etc/nginx/nginx.conf ./nginx.conf` copies files out of (or into) a container, like `docker cp`.
`podman system df` shows space used; `podman container prune` removes stopped containers and `podman image prune -a` removes unused images to reclaim space.
`podman auto-update` checks the registry and restarts a labelled container if a newer image exists (pairs with a systemd timer).
When a container keeps exiting, the method is simple and reliable:
`podman ps -a` shows its exit code; `podman logs <name>` almost always reveals the cause (a bad command, a missing file, a permission problem).
`podman inspect <name> --format '{{...}}'` extracts specific details (IP address, state).
Resist the urge to reboot the host or disable SELinux — read the logs, fix the real cause (often a volume label or a wrong command), and re-run.

questions.q: What does the `+` prefix do in `nmcli con mod eth0 +ipv4.addresses 10.0.0.5/24`?
options: Appends to the list property without removing existing values
questions.explain: Use `-` to remove one item; no prefix replaces the entire list.

questions.q: A change made with `nmcli con mod` takes effect when you:
questions.explain: Editing over SSH and changing the IP drops your session; use the console.

questions.q: Which property makes a connection come up automatically at boot?
questions.explain: Check it with `nmcli -f connection.autoconnect con show <name>`.

questions.q: How do you add a static route "reach 192.168.50.0/24 via 192.168.1.254" to a profile?
questions.explain: This route persists in the profile, unlike a bare `ip route add`.

options: The priority of this connection's routes (lower wins) when multiple paths exist
questions.explain: Useful when a host has two uplinks and you prefer one.

questions.q: Show all connection profiles NetworkManager knows about.
questions.explain: `nmcli device status` shows devices and which profile each uses.

questions.explain: Apply it with `nmcli con up eth0`.

questions.explain: Add `ipv4.gateway` and `ipv4.dns` as the task requires.

questions.explain: Then `nmcli con up <name>` to apply.

labs.scenario: Create a static profile and keep the DHCP one; switch between them and confirm the active address each time.
steps: nmcli con add con-name static-lab type ethernet ifname eth0 ipv4.addresses 172.16.0.10/24 ipv4.method manual
nmcli con up static-lab && ip -br a
nmcli con up "System eth0" && ip -br a
verify: nmcli con show --active shows which profile is live each time

labs.scenario: On a host with two connections, set route metrics so one is preferred, and confirm the default route uses it.

verify: ip route shows the default via the lower-metric (primary) connection

labs.title: Inspect a profile in detail
labs.scenario: Show all IPv4 settings of a connection and the DNS it applies.
steps: nmcli dev show eth0 | grep -i dns
verify: you can read the profile's addresses, gateway, routes and DNS

blocks.x: NetworkManager separates the **device** (the network card, e.g. `eth0`) from the **connection profile** (a saved configuration). One device can have several profiles; you activate whichever you need. On RHEL 9/10, profiles are stored as **keyfiles** in `/etc/NetworkManager/system-connections/` ending in `.nmconnection`. After hand-editing a keyfile, run `nmcli con reload`.
Many settings are **lists** (addresses, DNS servers, routes). nmcli lets you add or remove single items without replacing the whole list:
`nmcli con mod eth0 +ipv4.addresses 10.0.0.5/24` **appends** a second address.
`nmcli con mod eth0 -ipv4.dns 8.8.8.8` removes one DNS entry.
No prefix replaces the entire list.
Changes only take effect when you re-activate the profile: `nmcli con up eth0`.
Add a persistent route with `nmcli con mod eth0 +ipv4.routes "192.168.50.0/24 192.168.1.254"` (reach that subnet via that gateway). This survives reboots, unlike a bare `ip route add`.
On a host with two uplinks, `ipv4.route-metric` sets which is preferred — **lower wins**. Set a lower metric on the primary connection so its default route is chosen.
`nmcli con mod eth0 connection.autoconnect yes` makes a profile come up at boot.
`nmcli -f ipv4 con show eth0` shows all IPv4 settings of a profile; `nmcli dev show eth0 | grep -i dns` shows the DNS it applies.

days.title: Networking: link aggregation (bonding)
days.objective: Combine NICs into a bond for redundancy or throughput.

questions.q: What is network bonding?
options: Combining two or more NICs into one logical interface for redundancy or bandwidth
questions.explain: On RHEL 9/10 use bonding; the older "teaming" (teamd) was removed.

questions.q: Which bond mode gives simple failover with one active NIC at a time?
questions.explain: active-backup needs no special switch support; 802.3ad (LACP) needs a configured switch.

questions.q: What does the miimon bond option do?
options: Sets how often (ms) to check link state for failover
questions.explain: e.g. miimon=100 checks every 100 ms.

questions.q: In a bond, the member interfaces are called:
questions.explain: Each port is its own connection profile with the bond as its controller/master.

questions.q: Which file shows a bond's live status and active port?
questions.explain: It lists the mode, each port's link state, and the currently active port.

questions.q: Why use active-backup mode for a server with two switches?
options: It survives a switch or cable failure with no special switch config
questions.explain: Redundancy without LACP; throughput bonding (802.3ad) needs switch support.

questions.q: Create a bond interface bond0 in active-backup mode with miimon 100.
accept: nmcli con add type bond con-name bond0 ifname bond0 bond.options "mode=active-backup,miimon=100"
questions.explain: Give it an IP with `ipv4.addresses`/`ipv4.method manual` as the task requires.

questions.q: Add the NIC eth1 as a port of bond0.
accept: nmcli con add type ethernet con-name bond0-port1 ifname eth1 master bond0
questions.explain: Repeat for eth2 as bond0-port2; the ports have no IP of their own.

questions.q: Show the live status and active port of bond0.
questions.explain: Also `nmcli device status` shows the bond and its ports.

blocks.x: **Bonding** combines two or more network cards into one logical interface (`bond0`) for **redundancy** (survive a cable/switch failure) or **more bandwidth**. On RHEL 9/10 use bonding — the older "teaming" (teamd) was removed. The member interfaces are called **ports**, and the bond that controls them is the **controller**.
The bonding **mode** decides how the ports are used:
**active-backup (mode 1)** — one port is active at a time; if it fails, another takes over. Needs **no** special switch configuration — the safe default for redundancy.
**802.3ad (mode 4, LACP)** — aggregates ports for throughput, but the switch must be configured for it.
**balance-rr (mode 0)** — round-robin across ports.
The `miimon` option sets how often (in milliseconds) the link is checked for failover, e.g. `miimon=100`.
Create the bond: `nmcli con add type bond con-name bond0 ifname bond0 bond.options "mode=active-backup,miimon=100"` (add `ipv4.addresses`/`ipv4.method manual` for a static IP).
Add each NIC as a port: `nmcli con add type ethernet con-name bond0-p1 ifname eth1 master bond0` (repeat for eth2). Ports have no IP of their own.
Bring it up with `nmcli con up bond0`.
`cat /proc/net/bonding/bond0` shows the mode, each port's link state, and which port is currently active.
To test failover, bring the active port down (`nmcli con down bond0-p1`) and confirm the bond switches to the other while connectivity continues (`ping`).

questions.q: A firewalld "zone" represents:

questions.q: What does a rich rule let you do that a simple service/port rule cannot?

questions.q: What does `firewall-cmd --add-masquerade` enable?
options: Source NAT, so traffic from an internal network is translated to the host's address
questions.explain: Needed when the host routes traffic for a private network to the internet.

questions.q: A firewalld port-forward rule sends traffic arriving on one port to:

questions.explain: Use `--add-forward-port=port=80:proto=tcp:toport=8080`.

questions.q: Which command permanently rejects SSH only from 192.168.50.0/24?

questions.explain: `man firewalld.richlanguage` has copyable examples for the exam.

questions.q: What is the difference between "reject" and "drop" in a rule?

questions.explain: drop makes the host appear offline to that source.

questions.q: Add a rich rule that logs and drops all traffic from 10.0.0.66.
accept: firewall-cmd --permanent --add-rich-rule='rule family="ipv4" source address="10.0.0.66" log prefix="DROP66 " level="info" drop'
questions.explain: Reload after; check /var/log/messages or the journal for the log prefix.

questions.q: Enable masquerading (source NAT) in the current zone permanently.
questions.explain: Then `firewall-cmd --reload`.

questions.q: Forward incoming TCP port 80 to port 8080 on this host.
questions.explain: Requires masquerade for forwarding to another host.

questions.q: Put the source 192.168.10.0/24 into the trusted zone permanently.
questions.explain: `--get-active-zones` shows which sources/interfaces map to which zone.

labs.title: Zone-based access control (exam-plus)
labs.scenario: Put your management subnet in the "internal" zone with ssh allowed, keep "public" for everything else with only http, and verify.

labs.scenario: Reject SSH from one subnet with a logged rich rule, test from that subnet, and read the log.
steps: firewall-cmd --permanent --add-rich-rule='rule family="ipv4" source address="192.168.50.0/24" service name="ssh" log prefix="SSH-REJ " level="info" reject'
# from a host in 192.168.50.0/24:  ssh <this-host>   -> refused

blocks.x: firewalld organises rules into **zones**, each a trust level bound to interfaces or source addresses. `public` is the cautious default; `trusted` allows everything; `drop` silently discards. `firewall-cmd --get-active-zones` shows which interfaces/sources map to which zone, and `--set-default-zone=` changes the default.
When a host **routes** traffic for a private network out to the internet, it must translate the private source addresses to its own — this is **masquerading** (source NAT):
`firewall-cmd --permanent --add-masquerade` enables it. It is required whenever the host acts as a gateway/router for other machines.
firewalld can redirect traffic arriving on one port to another port (or host):
`firewall-cmd --permanent --add-forward-port=port=80:proto=tcp:toport=8080` sends incoming port 80 to a service on 8080. Forwarding to another **host** also needs masquerade.
For precise control — matching a specific source, logging, rate-limiting — use a **rich rule**:
`firewall-cmd --permanent --add-rich-rule='rule family="ipv4" source address="10.0.0.66" log prefix="DROP66 " level="info" drop'` logs and drops traffic from one host.
Remember **reject** replies "refused" while **drop** stays silent (the host appears offline). Always follow permanent changes with `firewall-cmd --reload`.

steps: nft add chain inet filter input '{ type filter hook input priority 0; policy drop; }'

labs.scenario: Add a rule, list with handles, then delete that specific rule by its handle.

nft -a list table inet filter        # shows # handle N
nft delete rule inet filter input handle <N>
verify: the 8080 rule is gone; the rest remain

blocks.x: **nftables** is the modern Linux packet-filtering framework that replaced the old iptables. Importantly, **firewalld uses nftables as its backend** — so on a normal RHEL system you manage the firewall through firewalld, and nftables is what actually enforces the rules underneath. You would write raw nftables rules only on a host **not** using firewalld; mixing the two on one host causes conflicts.
nftables is organised in three levels:
A **table** (with a **family** such as `inet` for both IPv4+IPv6) holds chains.
A **chain** holds rules. A **base chain** must declare a **type**, a **hook** (input/forward/output) and a **priority**, plus a default **policy** (accept or drop).
**Rules** match traffic and take an action.
Example base chain: `type filter hook input priority 0; policy drop;`.
`nft list ruleset` shows the entire active ruleset (with firewalld running, you see firewalld's generated tables here).

Build one by hand: `nft add table inet filter`, then `nft add chain inet filter input '{ type filter hook input priority 0; policy drop; }'`, then rules like `nft add rule inet filter input tcp dport 22 accept` and `nft add rule inet filter input ct state established,related accept`.
`nft -a list table inet filter` shows rule **handles**; delete one with `nft delete rule inet filter input handle N`.
To load a ruleset at boot, save it to `/etc/nftables.conf` (starting with `#!/usr/sbin/nft -f` and `flush ruleset`) and enable the `nftables` service: `systemctl enable --now nftables`.

questions.q: A software bridge (br0) is commonly used to:

questions.explain: VMs attach to the bridge and appear on the LAN directly.

questions.q: A VLAN interface (eth0.10) lets one physical NIC:
options: Carry multiple isolated networks tagged with 802.1Q VLAN IDs
questions.explain: The switch port must be a trunk allowing that VLAN.

nmcli con add type ethernet vlan 10

questions.q: To let a Linux host forward packets between networks you must:
questions.explain: Set it in /etc/sysctl.d/ and apply with `sysctl --system`.

questions.q: Create a bridge br0 with nmcli.
accept: nmcli con add type bridge con-name br0 ifname br0
questions.explain: Then attach a NIC: `nmcli con add type ethernet con-name br0-port ifname eth1 master br0`.

questions.q: Create VLAN 20 on eth0 with a static IP.

questions.explain: Bring it up with `nmcli con up vlan20`.

steps: nmcli con add type bridge con-name br0 ifname br0 ipv4.addresses 192.168.1.30/24 ipv4.gateway 192.168.1.1 ipv4.method manual
nmcli con add type ethernet con-name br0-port ifname eth1 master br0

ip -d link show eth0.30 | grep -i vlan

blocks.x: A **bridge** (`br0`) acts like a virtual switch in software, most commonly used to connect **virtual machines** to the physical network so they appear on the LAN directly. Build one with nmcli:

`nmcli con add type bridge con-name br0 ifname br0` (add an IP as needed), then attach a NIC as a port: `nmcli con add type ethernet con-name br0-port ifname eth1 master br0`. The bridge, not the NIC, then holds the IP.
A **VLAN** (Virtual LAN) lets one physical NIC carry several isolated networks, each tagged with an 802.1Q **VLAN ID**. The switch port must be a **trunk** that allows those VLANs:
`nmcli con add type vlan con-name vlan20 ifname eth0.20 dev eth0 id 20 ipv4.addresses 192.168.20.5/24 ipv4.method manual` creates VLAN 20 on eth0 (the interface name convention is `device.vlanid`).
Persist a route in a profile: `nmcli con mod eth0 +ipv4.routes "10.10.0.0/16 192.168.1.254"`. A bare `ip route add` is lost on reboot.

To let a host **forward** packets between networks (act as a router), enable IP forwarding persistently: put `net.ipv4.ip_forward=1` in `/etc/sysctl.d/99-forward.conf` and apply with `sysctl --system`. Combine with masquerade when routing to the internet.
**Policy routing** with `ip rule` can choose different routing tables based on the source address, for advanced multi-uplink setups.

days.title: Networking: troubleshooting and diagnostics
days.objective: Diagnose connectivity, ports, DNS and performance methodically.

questions.q: What is a sound order for troubleshooting "I can't reach a server"?
options: Link -> IP/route -> gateway -> DNS -> the remote port/service
questions.explain: Work up the stack: is the link up, do I have an IP and route, can I reach the gateway, does the name resolve, is the port open?

questions.q: Which command shows listening TCP/UDP ports with the owning process?
questions.explain: t=TCP, u=UDP, l=listening, p=process, n=numeric.

questions.q: `ping` succeeds to an IP but a website fails by name. The likely problem is:
questions.explain: Test with `dig <name>` or `getent hosts <name>`.

questions.q: Which tool combines traceroute and ping to show per-hop loss over time?
questions.explain: mtr is excellent for spotting a flaky hop.

questions.q: `ethtool eth0` is used to check:
options: Link speed, duplex and whether the link is detected on a NIC
questions.explain: A half-duplex or down link explains many "slow/no network" issues.

questions.q: Where do you look for NetworkManager errors during troubleshooting?
questions.explain: Add `-b` for this boot, `-f` to follow live while you reactivate a connection.

questions.q: `getent hosts server1` is useful because it:
options: Resolves a name using the system's full nsswitch order (files + DNS), like real apps do
questions.explain: It reflects what applications actually see, unlike a raw DNS query.

questions.q: Show all interfaces, their state and IPs in one short line each.
questions.explain: `ip -br link` shows just link state; great for a quick health check.

questions.q: Show the routing table including the default gateway.
questions.explain: The default route line (`default via ...`) is the gateway.

questions.q: Test whether TCP port 443 is open on a remote host without extra tools.
questions.explain: `nc -z` scans without sending data; authorized targets only.

questions.q: Follow NetworkManager's log live while you reactivate a connection.
questions.explain: In another terminal run `nmcli con up <name>` and watch the messages.

labs.title: Methodical connectivity triage (exam-plus)
labs.scenario: A host cannot reach an internal server by name. Work the stack: check link, IP/route, gateway, DNS, then the remote port, and identify the failing layer.
steps: ip -br a; ip -br link            # link + IP
getent hosts server1              # does the name resolve?
nc -zv server1 22                 # is the service port open?
verify: you can state which layer is broken and the fix

labs.title: DNS troubleshooting
labs.scenario: Diagnose a name that will not resolve: check the resolver, query directly, and confirm the search domain.
verify: you can tell whether it is a resolver, record, or search-domain problem

labs.title: Port and service check
labs.scenario: Find what is listening locally, then verify a remote host's port is reachable from here.
verify: you know which local ports listen and whether the remote port is open

labs.title: Capture and read traffic for a stubborn issue
labs.scenario: On an authorized host, capture a few packets of a failing connection to see where it stops.
steps: sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -n host 192.168.1.50 and port 443 -c 20
# look for SYN with no SYN-ACK (blocked/no service) vs RST (refused)
verify: you can interpret the handshake to locate the failure

labs.title: Link-layer check
labs.scenario: Confirm a NIC's link, speed and duplex, and review recent driver/link messages.
verify: you can confirm the physical link is healthy or spot a flapping NIC

blocks.x: When "I can't reach a server", resist guessing and work **up the stack** in order — each step tells you the next: 1. **Link** — is the interface up with an IP? `ip -br a`, `ip -br link`. 2. **Route** — is there a default gateway? `ip route`. 3. **Gateway** — can you reach it? `ping -c2 <gateway>`. 4. **DNS** — does the name resolve? `getent hosts <name>` or `dig <name>`. 5. **Service/port** — is the remote port open? `nc -zv host 443`. Whichever step fails tells you which layer to fix.
`ss -tulpn` lists listening TCP/UDP ports with the owning process (t=TCP, u=UDP, l=listening, p=process, n=numeric) — the modern replacement for `netstat`.
`ip -br a` / `ip route` give a quick health check of addresses and routing.
`getent hosts name` resolves a name using the system's full order (files then DNS), reflecting exactly what applications see — better than a raw DNS query when `/etc/hosts` is involved.
`mtr` combines ping and traceroute to show per-hop loss over time; `ethtool eth0` shows link speed, duplex and whether the link is detected.
`ping` reaches an IP but a name fails → a **DNS** problem, not connectivity.
A local `curl localhost` works but another host cannot connect → the **firewall**.
A service refuses to **bind** to a new port with "Permission denied" → **SELinux** (label the port).

Watch NetworkManager's own logs during changes with `journalctl -u NetworkManager -f`, and capture a stubborn connection with `tcpdump` — a SYN with no reply means blocked, a RST means refused. Methodical layering beats random rebooting every time.

days.title: The CIA triad and security goals
days.objective: Compare and contrast the core security concepts that every other topic builds on.

questions.q: What does the "C" in the CIA triad stand for?
options: Confidentiality — data is seen only by those authorized
questions.explain: CIA = Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability. It is the foundation of every security decision.

questions.q: Encrypting a hard drive primarily protects which part of the CIA triad?
questions.explain: Encryption stops unauthorized reading. Hashing protects integrity; backups and redundancy protect availability.

questions.q: A hash value is used to verify that a file has not changed. Which goal is this?
questions.explain: If the hash still matches, the data is intact. A changed byte changes the hash.

questions.q: Which concept ensures a sender cannot later deny sending a message?
questions.explain: Digital signatures provide non-repudiation because only the sender holds the private key.

questions.q: A DDoS attack most directly threatens which security goal?
questions.explain: Flooding a service so real users cannot reach it is an availability attack.

questions.q: What is the difference between authentication and authorization?
options: Authorization proves identity; authentication grants access
Authentication proves who you are; authorization decides what you may do
questions.explain: You authenticate (log in), then the system authorizes (checks permissions).

questions.q: Which term describes the assurance that a system or data is available when needed?
questions.explain: Achieved with redundancy, backups, failover and DDoS protection.

questions.q: In AAA, what does the third A (Accounting) provide?
options: A record of what a user did, for auditing
questions.explain: Authentication, Authorization, Accounting — logs and audit trails are the accounting piece.

questions.q: On Linux, generate a SHA-256 hash of the file report.pdf to check its integrity.
questions.explain: Compare the value later; a single changed bit produces a completely different hash.

labs.scenario: For each control, write down which CIA goal it mainly serves: full-disk encryption, RAID, a load balancer, a digital signature, a firewall rule blocking a port, a daily backup.
hints: One control can serve more than one goal, but pick the primary.

verify: you can justify each mapping in one sentence

labs.title: Spot the goal being attacked
labs.scenario: For each scenario name the CIA goal harmed: (a) ransomware encrypts your files, (b) an attacker reads your email, (c) a hacker alters a bank balance.
steps: # (a) Availability (you can't reach your data) -- and Confidentiality if copied

blocks.x: Almost every security idea traces back to three goals, remembered as the **CIA triad**:
**Confidentiality** — information is seen only by those authorised. Achieved mainly with **encryption** and access controls.
**Integrity** — information is accurate and unaltered. Verified with **hashing** and digital signatures; if a file's hash still matches, it hasn't changed.
**Availability** — systems and data are usable when needed. Protected with **redundancy, backups, and DDoS defences**.
Every control you learn supports one or more of these. A denial-of-service attack harms availability; eavesdropping harms confidentiality; tampering harms integrity.
Three related ideas that are easy to confuse:
**Authentication** proves *who you are* (you log in).
**Authorization** decides *what you may do* once identified (your permissions).
**Accounting** records *what you did* (logs and audit trails).
Together they are called **AAA**. A fourth idea, **non-repudiation**, means someone cannot later deny an action — digital signatures provide it because only the signer holds the private key.

When you evaluate any control, ask which goal it serves. Full-disk encryption → confidentiality. A RAID array or load balancer → availability. A file hash or digital signature → integrity. This framing keeps security decisions grounded rather than reacting to fear — you spend effort where a real goal is at risk.

days.title: Security control types
days.objective: Categorise controls by type (technical, managerial, operational, physical) and function (preventive, detective, corrective, etc.).

questions.q: A firewall is which control TYPE?
questions.explain: Technical controls are enforced by technology. A security policy is managerial; a guard is physical.

questions.q: A written security policy is which control type?
questions.explain: Managerial controls are the policies and procedures that direct the security program.

questions.q: Security guards, fences and locks are which control type?
questions.explain: Physical controls protect the tangible world — buildings, hardware, people.

questions.q: A backup is which control FUNCTION?
options: Corrective — it restores after an incident
questions.explain: Corrective controls fix or recover. Backups let you recover from ransomware or hardware failure.

questions.q: Motion-sensor lights and warning signs are which control function?
options: Deterrent — they discourage an attacker from trying
questions.explain: A deterrent influences behaviour; a preventive control actually blocks the action.

questions.q: Which control function is an intrusion DETECTION system (IDS)?
questions.explain: An IDS alerts you that something happened. An IPS that blocks it is preventive.

questions.q: What is a compensating control?
options: A control that replaces all others permanently
A control that pays for damages
An alternative control used when the primary control is not feasible
questions.explain: Example: if you cannot patch a legacy server, you isolate it on its own VLAN as a compensating control.

questions.q: A door lock is which control function?
questions.explain: It prevents unauthorized entry. A camera that records entry would be detective.

labs.scenario: For each item give both its TYPE and its FUNCTION: antivirus software, a CCTV camera, an incident-response plan, a bollard, encryption, a re-imaging procedure.

# put it behind a reverse proxy that terminates modern TLS
