labs.scenario: On a suspect Linux host, collect volatile data in the right order (most volatile first) without rebooting.
steps: # then image memory/disk with proper tools before shutdown
verify: you captured connections and processes before touching the disk

labs.title: Order of volatility
labs.scenario: List the order you would collect evidence from most to least volatile.
steps: # 4 running processes  5 disk  6 remote logs / backups  7 archival media

blocks.x: When something goes wrong, a structured process keeps the response effective. The NIST phases in order: 1. **Preparation** — plans, playbooks, tools and training ready *before* an incident. 2. **Detection & Analysis** — recognise and confirm the incident. 3. **Containment** — stop it spreading while **preserving evidence**. 4. **Eradication & Recovery** — remove the threat (malware, backdoors, compromised accounts), then restore clean systems. 5. **Lessons Learned** — improve controls and playbooks so it doesn't recur; this closes the loop back to preparation.
A **playbook/runbook** is a step-by-step procedure for a specific incident type, making response fast and consistent.
A **tabletop exercise** is a discussion-based drill through a hypothetical incident — testing the plan without touching production.
An **incident commander** declares the incident and coordinates, so roles are clear.
Don't immediately power off a compromised machine — you may lose **volatile evidence** in RAM; consider isolating it from the network first, then capturing memory.

Containment must not destroy evidence. Isolate hosts, block command-and-control, and disable accounts, but keep logs and captures intact. This overlaps with forensics: the same care that makes evidence useful in court also helps you understand and fully eradicate the intrusion.

days.title: Digital forensics
days.objective: Apply forensic concepts: chain of custody, acquisition, integrity.

questions.q: "Chain of custody" documents:
options: Who handled evidence, when, and what they did — to keep it admissible
The network path of an attack
questions.explain: A broken chain of custody can make evidence unusable in court.

questions.q: Why hash evidence before and after acquisition?
options: To prove the copy is identical to the original and was not altered
questions.explain: Matching hashes demonstrate integrity of the forensic image.

questions.q: What is a "write blocker"?
options: A device/tool that lets you read a drive without changing it
questions.explain: It preserves the original evidence during acquisition.

questions.q: "Legal hold" means:
options: Preserving relevant data because litigation or investigation is anticipated
questions.explain: Normal deletion/retention is suspended for the relevant data.

questions.q: Which is the best practice for forensic analysis?
options: Work on a verified copy (image), never the original evidence
questions.explain: You keep the original pristine and analyze the image.

questions.q: "Order of volatility" tells you to collect first:
options: The most volatile data (RAM, network state) before it disappears
questions.explain: Data in memory vanishes on power loss.

questions.q: e-Discovery refers to:
options: Identifying and producing electronic evidence for legal proceedings
questions.explain: It ties into legal hold and data retention.

questions.q: Metadata in a file can reveal:
options: Author, timestamps, GPS, device info useful in an investigation
questions.explain: Timestamps and authorship often matter in forensics.

questions.q: Create a verified image of a file/partition and record its hash for the evidence log.
questions.explain: Record the hash immediately after imaging; re-verify before analysis.

labs.title: Practice evidence integrity
labs.scenario: Image a small file, hash the original and the copy, and show they match; then log it as a chain-of-custody entry.
steps: # add: date, collector name, source, method to custody.log
verify: both hashes match and the log has who/when/what

labs.title: Extract file metadata
labs.scenario: Pull timestamps and metadata from a file as an investigator would.
steps: # if available: exiftool suspicious.jpg  (author, GPS, camera, timestamps)
verify: you can report at least three metadata fields

labs.title: Write a chain-of-custody form
labs.scenario: Draft the fields a chain-of-custody form must contain.
steps: # case ID, item description, collected by, date/time, location
# hash value, transferred to (name/sig), reason, storage location
verify: the form would survive a courtroom challenge

blocks.x: Digital forensics is about handling evidence so it is trustworthy and admissible:
**Chain of custody** documents *who* handled evidence, *when*, and *what* they did. A break in the chain can make evidence unusable.
Before and after acquiring evidence, you **hash** it (e.g. SHA-256) and compare — matching hashes prove the copy is identical to the original and unaltered.
A **write blocker** lets you read a drive without changing it, preserving the original.
Work on a **verified copy (image)**, never the original — the original stays pristine.

Follow the **order of volatility**: collect the most fleeting data first — CPU registers/cache, then RAM, then network state and running processes, then disk, then remote logs and archives. Data in memory vanishes on power loss.
**Metadata** (timestamps, author, GPS, device info) is often central to an investigation.
**Legal hold** means preserving relevant data because litigation or investigation is anticipated — normal deletion/retention is suspended for that data.
**e-Discovery** is identifying and producing electronic evidence for legal proceedings. These tie forensics to data-retention policy and the law.

days.title: Resilience, backups and recovery
days.objective: Apply resilience and recovery concepts (RTO, RPO, backup types).

questions.q: What does RTO (Recovery Time Objective) define?
options: The maximum acceptable time to restore a service after an outage
How much data you can lose
questions.explain: RTO = "how fast must we be back?"

questions.q: What does RPO (Recovery Point Objective) define?
options: The maximum acceptable amount of data loss, measured in time
questions.explain: RPO = "how much data can we afford to lose?" It drives backup frequency.

questions.q: A full backup:
options: Copies all selected data every time
Copies only changes since the last full
questions.explain: Simple to restore but large and slow.

questions.q: An incremental backup copies:
options: Changes since the last full only
Only data changed since the last backup of any type
questions.explain: Fast backups, but restore needs the full plus every increment in order.

questions.q: A differential backup copies:
options: Only changes since the last backup
All changes since the last FULL backup
questions.explain: Restore needs just the full plus the latest differential.

questions.q: The "3-2-1" backup rule means:
options: 3 copies, on 2 different media, with 1 copy off-site
questions.explain: A modern variant adds "1 offline/immutable" to survive ransomware.

questions.q: High availability (HA) is achieved with:
options: Redundancy and failover so service continues if a component fails
questions.explain: Clusters, load balancers, and redundant power/network provide HA.

questions.q: Why test backups regularly?
options: An untested backup may be corrupt or incomplete when you need it
questions.explain: "You don't have a backup until you've restored it."

questions.q: On Linux, create a compressed, dated backup of /etc for safekeeping.
questions.explain: Store a copy off-site and test the restore.

labs.title: Choose RTO/RPO
labs.scenario: For an online store's order database, propose an RTO and RPO and the backup strategy that meets them.
steps: # RPO 15 min -> transaction log backups every 15 min (or replication)
# RTO 1 hr -> warm standby + tested restore runbook
verify: the backup frequency matches the RPO

labs.title: Backup and verify restore
labs.scenario: Back up a directory, delete a file, and restore just that file to prove the backup works.
verify: the file is restored from backup

labs.title: Plan for ransomware resilience
labs.scenario: List the backup properties that let you recover from ransomware without paying.
steps: # off-site + offline/immutable copy attackers can't reach or encrypt
# versioned backups (restore to a point before infection)
verify: the plan survives an attacker with domain admin

blocks.x: Resilience planning uses two key numbers:
**RTO (Recovery Time Objective)** — the maximum acceptable *time* to restore a service after an outage ("how fast must we be back?").

**RPO (Recovery Point Objective)** — the maximum acceptable *data loss*, measured in time ("how much data can we lose?"). RPO drives backup frequency: a 15-minute RPO means backing up (or replicating) at least every 15 minutes.
**Full** — copies everything each time; simple to restore, but large and slow.
**Incremental** — copies only what changed since the *last backup of any type*; fast backups, but restore needs the full plus every increment in order.
**Differential** — copies everything changed since the last *full*; restore needs only the full plus the latest differential.
The **3-2-1 rule**: keep **3** copies, on **2** different media, with **1** off-site — modern practice adds **1 offline/immutable** copy to survive ransomware.
**High availability (HA)** uses redundancy and failover (clusters, load balancers, redundant power/network) so service continues if a component fails.

**Test your backups regularly** — an untested backup may be corrupt or incomplete: "you don't have a backup until you've restored it." For ransomware, the recovery essentials are off-site, offline/immutable, versioned backups plus a tested, documented restore.

days.title: Secure protocols and services
days.objective: Select secure protocols and replace insecure ones.

questions.q: Which protocol securely replaces Telnet for remote administration?
questions.explain: Telnet sends everything in plaintext; SSH is encrypted.

questions.q: HTTPS uses which protocol to encrypt web traffic?
questions.explain: Modern HTTPS uses TLS 1.2/1.3; SSL is deprecated.

questions.q: Which is the secure way to transfer files?
options: SFTP or FTPS (encrypted), not plain FTP
questions.explain: SFTP runs over SSH; FTPS adds TLS to FTP.

questions.q: Which protocol secures email transport between servers?
questions.explain: Also use IMAPS/POP3S for clients, and SPF/DKIM/DMARC for authenticity.

questions.q: SNMPv3 improves on earlier versions by adding:
questions.explain: SNMPv1/v2c send community strings in plaintext.

questions.q: DNSSEC provides:
options: Integrity/authenticity of DNS records via digital signatures
questions.explain: It stops forged records; DoH/DoT add confidentiality.

questions.q: Which port does HTTPS use by default?
questions.explain: 80 = HTTP, 22 = SSH, 25 = SMTP, 443 = HTTPS.

questions.q: LDAPS secures directory queries by:
questions.explain: Plain LDAP (389) exposes directory traffic; LDAPS uses 636.

questions.q: Test whether a mail server offers STARTTLS encryption.
questions.explain: If TLS negotiates, the server supports encrypted mail transport.

labs.title: Replace insecure services
labs.scenario: For a legacy setup using Telnet, FTP, and HTTP, name the secure replacement and the port for each.
verify: each insecure service has a secure, encrypted replacement

labs.title: Verify TLS version and ciphers
labs.scenario: Check which TLS versions and ciphers a web server accepts and flag any weak ones.
verify: you can state whether TLS 1.0/1.1 are (insecurely) enabled

theory.h: Replacing insecure protocols with secure ones

blocks.x: A core Security+ skill is knowing which protocols are safe and what to replace the unsafe ones with. Insecure protocols send data (and passwords) in **plaintext**, so anyone on the path can read them:
**Telnet (23) → SSH (22)** for encrypted remote administration.
**FTP (21) → SFTP (over SSH) or FTPS (FTP+TLS)** for file transfer.
**HTTP (80) → HTTPS (443)**, which uses **TLS** (SSL is deprecated).
Plain **SMTP → SMTP with STARTTLS**; **IMAP/POP3 → IMAPS/POP3S** for mail.
**SNMPv3** adds authentication and encryption (v1/v2c send community strings in plaintext).
**LDAPS** wraps directory queries in TLS (plain LDAP on 389 is exposed; LDAPS uses 636).
**DNSSEC** adds integrity/authenticity to DNS records via signatures; **DoH/DoT** add confidentiality by encrypting queries.

Recognising ports helps you reason about traffic: 22 SSH, 25 SMTP, 53 DNS, 80 HTTP, 443 HTTPS, 389 LDAP, 636 LDAPS. Email authenticity is further protected by **SPF, DKIM and DMARC** — records that verify a sender's domain and reduce spoofing.

days.title: Wireless and mobile security
days.objective: Secure wireless networks and mobile/endpoint devices.

questions.q: Which is the strongest common Wi-Fi security standard?
questions.explain: WEP is broken; WPA2 is okay; WPA3 is current best (SAE handshake).

questions.q: Why is WEP considered insecure?
options: Its weak RC4/IV design lets attackers recover the key quickly
questions.explain: WEP should never be used; it can be cracked in minutes.

questions.q: WPA2-Enterprise differs from WPA2-Personal by using:
options: 802.1X/RADIUS for per-user authentication instead of a shared passphrase
questions.explain: Enterprise gives each user unique credentials and easy revocation.

questions.q: Hiding the SSID (network name) provides:
options: Very little real security (it is easily discovered)
questions.explain: It is "security by obscurity," not a real control.

questions.q: What is MDM (Mobile Device Management) used for?
options: Enforcing security policy on mobile devices (encryption, PIN, remote wipe)
questions.explain: MDM/UEM manages and secures fleets of devices.

questions.q: "BYOD" introduces risk because:
options: Personal devices are outside full corporate control yet access company data
questions.explain: Containerization separates work and personal data on BYOD.

questions.q: A captive portal is:
options: A web page that forces authentication/acceptance before granting network access
questions.explain: Common on guest Wi-Fi; not a strong security control by itself.

questions.q: Remote wipe is important because:
options: A lost/stolen device's data can be erased to prevent exposure
questions.explain: Paired with full-device encryption and a screen lock.

questions.q: Scan for nearby Wi-Fi networks and their security type (your own area, lawful use).
questions.explain: Note which networks still use WEP/WPA vs WPA2/WPA3.

labs.title: Secure a home/office AP (checklist)
labs.scenario: Write the settings you would apply to a wireless router to secure it.
steps: # WPA3 (or WPA2-AES) with a long passphrase
# change default admin password; disable WPS

labs.title: Enterprise Wi-Fi design (concept)
labs.scenario: Explain how WPA2/WPA3-Enterprise authenticates a user and why it beats a shared key for a company.
steps: # client -> AP -> RADIUS (802.1X/EAP) validates the user's own credentials/cert
# unique creds: revoke one user without changing everyone's password
verify: you can describe the 802.1X flow at a high level

blocks.x: Wi-Fi encryption has improved over generations, and using the strongest available matters:
**WEP** — badly broken (weak cipher/IV); can be cracked in minutes — never use it.
**WPA2** — acceptable, using AES.
**WPA3** — the current best, using the SAE handshake.

Two deployment modes: **WPA2/3-Personal** uses a shared passphrase, while **Enterprise** uses **802.1X/RADIUS** for per-user authentication — so credentials can be revoked individually without changing everyone's key. Hiding the SSID and MAC filtering are "security by obscurity," not real controls; disable **WPS**, which can be brute-forced.
Organisations manage fleets of devices with **MDM/UEM**, enforcing policy: encryption, screen-lock PINs, and **remote wipe** so a lost or stolen device's data can be erased.
**BYOD (Bring Your Own Device)** raises risk because personal devices are outside full corporate control yet access company data; **containerization** separates work and personal data on them.

A solid wireless posture: **WPA3 (or WPA2-AES)** with a long passphrase, WPS disabled, firmware updated, remote admin off, and a **separate guest/IoT VLAN**. In enterprises, 802.1X gives each user unique, revocable credentials and lets clients validate the network — defending against rogue and evil-twin access points.

days.title: Data protection and DLP
days.objective: Classify data and apply protection controls.

questions.q: Data classification (public, internal, confidential, restricted) exists to:
options: Apply the right level of protection based on sensitivity
questions.explain: You spend the strongest controls on the most sensitive data.

questions.q: "Data at rest" refers to:
options: Data stored on disk/media (protected mainly by encryption)
questions.explain: At rest = storage; in transit = network; in use = memory/processing.

questions.q: "Data in transit" is best protected by:
questions.explain: TLS/IPsec protect data as it crosses the network.

questions.q: What does a DLP system do?
options: Detects and blocks sensitive data from leaving the organization
questions.explain: Data Loss Prevention inspects email, uploads, and endpoints for regulated data.

questions.q: "Tokenization" protects data by:
options: Replacing sensitive values with non-sensitive tokens mapped in a secure vault
questions.explain: Common for payment card data; the real value never leaves the vault.

questions.q: "Data masking" is used to:
options: Hide parts of data (e.g., show only last 4 digits) for non-privileged views
questions.explain: Useful in test environments and customer-service screens.

questions.q: A data "owner" is responsible for:
options: Classifying the data and deciding who may access it
questions.explain: The custodian implements the controls the owner defines.

questions.q: "Right to be forgotten" comes from which kind of regulation?
questions.explain: Data-subject rights require you to locate and delete personal data on request.

questions.q: Find files that may contain card numbers before they leak (simple DLP-style scan).
questions.explain: A real DLP tool adds validation (Luhn check) and context.

labs.title: Classify and label data
labs.scenario: For a folder with an HR salary sheet, a public brochure, and a customer list, assign a classification and one control each.
steps: # salary sheet -> Confidential -> encrypt + restrict to HR group
# brochure -> Public -> integrity check, no confidentiality needed
# customer list -> Restricted (PII) -> encrypt, DLP, access logging
verify: each item's controls match its sensitivity

labs.title: Protect data three ways
labs.scenario: Demonstrate protection for data at rest, in transit, and in use (conceptually) on one file.
steps: # in transit: send over scp/TLS, never plain FTP
# in use: restrict process privileges + memory, limit who can open it

blocks.x: You cannot protect everything equally, so you **classify** data by sensitivity (public, internal, confidential, restricted) and apply controls to match. Roles matter: the **data owner** classifies data and decides who may access it; the **data custodian** implements the controls.
Data needs protection in each state:
**At rest** (stored on disk/media) — protected mainly by **encryption** (LUKS, BitLocker).
**In transit** (crossing a network) — protected by **TLS/IPsec**.
**In use** (being processed in memory) — protected by restricting privileges and access.
**DLP (Data Loss Prevention)** detects and blocks sensitive data from leaving the organisation (via email, uploads, endpoints).
**Tokenization** replaces a sensitive value with a non-sensitive token mapped in a secure vault (common for payment cards) — the real value never leaves the vault.
**Data masking** hides parts of data (showing only the last four digits) for non-privileged views and test environments.

Privacy regulations (like **GDPR**) grant rights such as the "right to be forgotten," requiring you to find and delete personal data on request — which is only possible if you know where your data is (classification again).

days.title: Physical security
days.objective: Apply physical security controls.

questions.q: A mantrap (access control vestibule) prevents:
options: Tailgating, by allowing one person through at a time
questions.explain: Two interlocking doors stop a second person slipping in.

questions.q: Why place security cameras (CCTV) at entrances?
options: To deter and to detect/record who enters
questions.explain: Visible cameras deter; recordings provide detective evidence.

questions.q: A bollard is used to:
options: Physically block vehicles from ramming a building
questions.explain: Physical, preventive control against vehicle attacks.

questions.q: "Faraday cage" protects against:
questions.explain: Used for shielding sensitive equipment and preventing signal leakage.

questions.q: Biometric access control is which authentication factor?
questions.explain: Fingerprints, iris, face. Watch for false accept/reject rates.

questions.q: A "proximity badge" is which factor?
questions.explain: Combine with a PIN (know) for MFA at the door.

questions.q: Why use security lighting and clear sightlines?
options: They deter intruders and improve camera/guard effectiveness
questions.explain: Environmental design (CPTED) reduces hiding spots.

questions.q: A "honeyfile" or honeytoken is:
options: A decoy file/credential that alerts defenders when touched
questions.explain: Any access to it strongly implies an intruder.

labs.title: Design layered physical security
labs.scenario: For a small server room, list controls from the perimeter inward (defense in depth).
steps: # building: badge + PIN door, reception, visitor logs
# server room: mantrap, separate badge, camera, locked racks
verify: each layer backs up the others

labs.title: FAR vs FRR (concept)
labs.scenario: Explain false acceptance rate and false rejection rate and which is worse for a high-security door.
steps: # FAR: wrongly admits an impostor (security risk)
# FRR: wrongly rejects a valid user (annoyance)
# high security: tune to lower FAR even if FRR rises

blocks.x: Security starts in the physical world; if someone can touch the hardware, most logical controls can be bypassed. Common physical controls and what they do:
**Locks, fences, bollards** — prevent entry or vehicle attacks (preventive/deterrent).
**Access control vestibule (mantrap)** — two interlocking doors that let one person through at a time, defeating **tailgating**.
**CCTV cameras** — deter (when visible) and detect/record who enters.
**Security lighting and clear sightlines** (CPTED) reduce hiding spots.
A **Faraday cage** blocks electromagnetic signals to prevent eavesdropping or interference.
A **proximity badge** is "something you have"; a **biometric** (fingerprint, iris, face) is "something you are." Combine a badge with a PIN for MFA at the door.

Biometrics are tuned by two error rates: the **False Acceptance Rate (FAR)** — wrongly admitting an impostor (a security risk) — and the **False Rejection Rate (FRR)** — wrongly rejecting a valid user (an annoyance). High-security doors tune toward a low FAR.

Apply defence in depth physically — perimeter (fence, lighting, cameras), building (badge doors, reception, visitor logs), server room (mantrap, locked racks). A **honeyfile/honeytoken** is a decoy file or credential that alerts defenders the moment anyone touches it, strongly implying an intruder.

days.title: Governance, policies and standards
days.objective: Summarize governance, policies, standards and frameworks.

questions.q: What is the difference between a policy and a procedure?
options: A policy states what/why (high level); a procedure states step-by-step how
questions.explain: Standards and guidelines sit between them.

questions.q: An Acceptable Use Policy (AUP) defines:
options: How employees may use company systems and data
questions.explain: Users typically sign it during onboarding.

questions.q: A "standard" (vs a policy) is:
options: A mandatory specific rule that supports a policy (e.g., "AES-256 for encryption")
questions.explain: Guidelines are recommended, not mandatory; standards are mandatory.

questions.q: What is a security framework used for?
options: A structured set of best practices to build and measure a security program
questions.explain: Examples: NIST CSF, ISO 27001, CIS Controls.

questions.q: "Separation of duties" prevents fraud by:
options: Requiring more than one person to complete a sensitive task
questions.explain: No single person can both request and approve a payment, for example.

questions.q: "Mandatory vacation" and "job rotation" are controls that:
options: Help detect fraud and reduce dependence on one person
questions.explain: Fraud often surfaces when the usual person is away.

questions.q: Onboarding and offboarding processes matter because:
options: They ensure access is granted correctly and fully removed when someone leaves
questions.explain: Orphaned accounts of ex-employees are a major risk.

questions.q: What is "due care" vs "due diligence"?
options: Due diligence is investigating/planning; due care is acting on it responsibly
questions.explain: Diligence = doing your homework; care = the ongoing responsible action.

labs.title: Write an access-control policy snippet
labs.scenario: Draft three policy statements for user account management (creation, review, removal).
steps: # Accounts are created only via approved onboarding tickets with manager sign-off.
# Access is reviewed quarterly; unused/excess access is revoked.
# Accounts are disabled within 1 hour of termination.
verify: each statement is enforceable and auditable

labs.title: Map to a framework
labs.scenario: Pick three CIS Controls (or NIST CSF functions) and give one action your org would take for each.
steps: # e.g. NIST CSF: Identify -> asset inventory
verify: each function has a concrete action

blocks.x: Security needs direction from the top, expressed as documents at different levels:
A **policy** states *what and why* at a high level (an **Acceptable Use Policy** defines how staff may use company systems).
A **standard** is a *mandatory* specific rule supporting a policy (e.g. "use AES-256 for encryption").
A **procedure** is the step-by-step *how*.
A **guideline** is *recommended*, not mandatory.

A **security framework** is a structured set of best practices to build and measure a program — examples include **NIST CSF**, **ISO 27001**, and the **CIS Controls**. They give you a checklist and a common language, and help demonstrate **compliance** with regulations.
Governance also shapes how people work:
**Separation of duties** requires more than one person to complete a sensitive task, so no single person can both request and approve a payment.
**Job rotation** and **mandatory vacation** help detect fraud (it often surfaces when the usual person is away).
Solid **onboarding/offboarding** ensures access is granted correctly and **fully removed** when someone leaves — orphaned ex-employee accounts are a major risk.
**Due diligence** is investigating/planning; **due care** is acting responsibly on it.

days.title: Risk management
days.objective: Apply risk-management concepts and calculations.

questions.q: What is "risk" in security terms?
options: The likelihood of a threat exploiting a vulnerability and the resulting impact
questions.explain: Risk = likelihood x impact, roughly.

questions.q: The four risk-response strategies are:
questions.explain: Transfer often means buying insurance; mitigate means adding controls.

questions.q: Buying cyber-insurance is an example of risk:
questions.explain: You shift the financial impact to a third party.

questions.q: "Residual risk" is:
options: The risk that remains after controls are applied
questions.explain: You cannot usually reach zero; leadership accepts the residual.

questions.q: SLE x ARO equals:
questions.explain: Single Loss Expectancy x Annual Rate of Occurrence = expected yearly loss.

questions.q: If an asset is worth $10,000 and an incident destroys 50% of it, the SLE is:
questions.explain: SLE = Asset Value x Exposure Factor = 10,000 x 0.5.

questions.q: A "risk register" is:
options: A living document listing risks, owners, and treatment status
questions.explain: It tracks each risk from identification to closure.

questions.q: Qualitative risk analysis uses:
options: Ratings like high/medium/low rather than exact numbers
questions.explain: Quantitative analysis uses numbers (SLE/ALE); qualitative uses judgment scales.

labs.title: Calculate ALE
labs.scenario: A server worth $20,000 faces a flood that would destroy 25% of it, expected once every 4 years. Compute SLE, ARO, and ALE.
steps: # ALE = SLE x ARO = 5000 x 0.25 = $1,250 per year
verify: a control costing < $1,250/yr that removes this risk is justified

labs.title: Build a mini risk register
labs.scenario: Add three risks for a web app, each with likelihood, impact, response strategy, and owner.
steps: # SQLi -> High/High -> Mitigate (WAF+prepared stmts) -> Dev lead
verify: each row is complete and actionable

blocks.x: **Risk** is the chance that a threat exploits a vulnerability, and the impact if it does — roughly **likelihood × impact**. Security is really risk management: you cannot remove all risk, so you decide which risks to reduce and which to accept.
For each risk you choose one of:
**Mitigate** — add controls to reduce likelihood or impact.
**Transfer** — shift the impact to someone else (buying cyber-insurance).
**Avoid** — stop doing the risky activity.
**Accept** — knowingly live with the residual risk.
**Residual risk** is what remains after controls are applied; leadership formally accepts it. A **risk register** is a living document listing each risk, its owner, and its treatment status.
**Qualitative** analysis rates risk high/medium/low by judgement.
**Quantitative** analysis uses numbers:

- **SLE (Single Loss Expectancy)** = asset value × exposure factor. - **ARO (Annualized Rate of Occurrence)** = how many times per year it's expected. - **ALE (Annualized Loss Expectancy)** = SLE × ARO. Example: a $20,000 asset, 25% destroyed, once every 4 years → SLE = $5,000, ARO = 0.25, ALE = $1,250/year. A control costing less than $1,250/year that removes this risk is justified.

days.title: Third-party and vendor risk
days.objective: Manage supply-chain and third-party risk.

questions.q: Why assess third-party vendors' security?
options: Their weaknesses can become your breach (supply-chain risk)
questions.explain: A vendor with access to your data extends your attack surface.

questions.q: An SLA (Service Level Agreement) defines:
options: The measurable service levels a vendor must meet (e.g., uptime)
questions.explain: Include security requirements and penalties in the SLA.

questions.q: An MOU/MOA is:
options: A (often non-binding) agreement outlining intentions between parties
questions.explain: It sets expectations before a formal contract.

questions.q: A BPA (Business Partners Agreement) governs:
options: The relationship and responsibilities between business partners
questions.explain: It clarifies liability, data handling, and responsibilities.

questions.q: "Right to audit" clauses let you:
options: Verify a vendor's security controls yourself or via a third party
questions.explain: Without it, you rely only on the vendor's word.

questions.q: A SOC 2 report tells you:
options: How well a vendor's controls meet security/availability criteria
questions.explain: It is independent assurance about a service provider's controls.

questions.q: "Vendor lock-in" is a risk because:
options: It makes leaving a provider costly/difficult, reducing your options
questions.explain: Consider exit strategy and data portability up front.

questions.q: End-of-life (EOL) hardware/software from a vendor means:
options: No more security updates, so risk rises over time
questions.explain: Plan replacement before EOL; isolate if you cannot.

labs.title: Vendor security questionnaire
labs.scenario: Write five questions you would ask a SaaS vendor before storing customer data with them.
steps: # Where is data stored, and is it encrypted at rest/in transit?
# Do you have SOC 2 / ISO 27001? Can we see it?
# How do you handle breach notification and in what timeframe?
# What is your access control and MFA posture for staff?
# What is our data export/deletion process on exit?
verify: the answers would materially change your decision

labs.title: Assess supply-chain risk
labs.scenario: For a software dependency your app pulls from the internet, list three controls to reduce supply-chain risk.
steps: # use a private/proxy registry and scan dependencies for CVEs
# review before upgrading; monitor for compromised packages
verify: a poisoned update would be caught before deployment

blocks.x: Your security is only as strong as the vendors who touch your data — a weakness in one of them can become **your** breach (supply-chain risk). So you assess vendors before and during the relationship.
**SLA (Service Level Agreement)** — the measurable service levels a vendor must meet (uptime, response times); include security requirements and penalties.
**MOU/MOA** — a (often non-binding) statement of intentions between parties.
**BPA (Business Partners Agreement)** — governs responsibilities and liability between business partners.
A **right-to-audit** clause lets you verify a vendor's controls yourself or via a third party — without it you rely only on their word.
A **SOC 2** report gives independent assurance about a service provider's security/availability controls.
**Vendor lock-in** is a risk because leaving becomes costly — plan an exit strategy and data portability up front.
**End-of-life (EOL)** vendor products stop getting security updates, so plan replacement before EOL.
For a software dependency, reduce supply-chain risk by pinning versions, verifying checksums/signatures, using a private/proxy registry, and scanning for CVEs before upgrading.

days.title: Audits, assessments and testing
days.objective: Compare security assessments, audits and testing types.

questions.q: A vulnerability scan differs from a penetration test because it:
options: Identifies weaknesses but does not exploit them
questions.explain: A pen test goes further and proves impact by exploiting.

questions.q: "Black box" penetration testing means the tester:
options: Has no prior internal knowledge of the target
questions.explain: White box = full knowledge; gray box = partial.

questions.q: The "rules of engagement" in a pen test define:
options: Scope, timing, allowed techniques, and contacts — the authorized boundaries
questions.explain: Testing outside the authorized scope can be illegal.

questions.q: An internal audit's main purpose is to:
options: Independently verify that controls exist and work as intended
questions.explain: Audits check compliance with policy/standards.

questions.q: "Attestation" in an audit is:
options: A formal statement that controls were reviewed and meet criteria
questions.explain: Often provided to customers as assurance.

questions.q: A "red team" exercise:
options: Simulates a real adversary to test detection and response, not just find bugs
questions.explain: The "blue team" defends; "purple" is the two collaborating.

questions.q: Why do a "bug bounty" program?
options: To pay external researchers to responsibly report vulnerabilities
questions.explain: It widens your testing pool under defined rules.

questions.q: A compliance scan checks systems against:
options: A required standard/benchmark (e.g., PCI DSS, CIS)
questions.explain: It reports gaps you must remediate for compliance.

questions.q: Run an authorized vulnerability-style scan of your lab host with nmap scripts.
questions.explain: Authorized targets only; interpret results and prioritize by severity + exposure.

labs.title: Plan a penetration test
labs.scenario: Draft the rules of engagement for testing a single web app: scope, window, allowed/forbidden actions, and emergency contact.
steps: # scope: app.example.com only, no DoS, no social engineering
# forbidden: data destruction, pivoting to other systems
# contact: on-call number to stop the test immediately
verify: the ROE keeps the test legal and safe

labs.title: Compare assessment types
labs.scenario: In one line each, distinguish vulnerability scan, penetration test, audit, and red-team exercise.
steps: # vuln scan: automated find weaknesses (no exploit)
# pen test: exploit to prove impact within scope
# red team: adversary simulation to test detection/response
verify: you can pick the right one for a given goal

blocks.x: Different activities verify security in different ways:
A **vulnerability scan** identifies weaknesses automatically but does **not** exploit them.
A **penetration test** goes further, **exploiting** flaws to prove real impact within an authorised scope.
An **audit** independently verifies that controls exist and work against a standard or policy; **attestation** is a formal statement that they were reviewed and meet criteria.
A **compliance scan** checks systems against a required benchmark (PCI DSS, CIS).
**Black box** = the tester has no internal knowledge; **white box** = full knowledge and credentials; **gray box** = partial.
**Rules of engagement** define the authorised scope, timing, allowed techniques and contacts — testing outside them can be illegal.
A **red team** simulates a real adversary to test detection and response; the **blue team** defends; **purple** is the two collaborating.
A **bug bounty** program pays external researchers to responsibly report vulnerabilities under defined rules, widening your testing pool.
Retesting after remediation confirms fixes actually worked. The point of all of this is to find and fix weaknesses *before* an attacker does — and prioritise by real risk, not raw counts.

days.title: Automation, orchestration and secure ops
days.objective: Apply automation to security operations securely.

questions.q: A key benefit of automation in security operations is:
options: Consistent, fast, repeatable responses that reduce human error
questions.explain: Playbooks in SOAR auto-triage and contain common incidents.

questions.q: A risk of over-automation is:
options: A flawed script can cause damage at scale, quickly
questions.explain: Guardrails, approvals, and testing keep automation safe.

questions.q: Storing secrets (API keys, passwords) in code is bad because:
options: Anyone with the code gets the secret; use a secrets manager instead
questions.explain: Use a vault and inject secrets at runtime.

questions.q: "Idempotent" automation means:
options: Running it repeatedly yields the same safe end state
questions.explain: Configuration tools like Ansible aim for idempotency.

questions.q: CI/CD security ("shift left") means:
options: Adding security testing early in the development pipeline
questions.explain: Catch flaws before production with SAST/DAST and dependency scans.

questions.q: A "least-privilege" service account for automation should:
options: Have only the permissions the task needs, and be monitored
questions.explain: Over-privileged automation accounts are prime targets.

questions.q: Why sign your scripts/artifacts in a pipeline?
options: To ensure integrity and that only trusted code runs (supply-chain defense)
questions.explain: Signature verification stops tampered artifacts from deploying.

questions.q: Store a secret in an environment variable for a script instead of hard-coding it (lab).
questions.explain: Better: use a real secrets manager; never commit secrets to Git.

labs.title: Automate a safe check
labs.scenario: Write a short script that checks disk usage and alerts (logs) if over 80%, and make it idempotent.
verify: running it twice does not cause harm

labs.title: Find hard-coded secrets
labs.scenario: Scan a code directory for likely secrets before committing.
verify: you can spot secrets that should move to a vault

blocks.x: Automation runs security tasks consistently, quickly and repeatably, reducing human error — for example **SOAR** playbooks that auto-triage and contain common incidents. But automation cuts both ways: a flawed script can cause damage at scale, so it needs guardrails, approvals and testing. **Idempotent** automation (running it repeatedly yields the same safe end state) is the goal, as with configuration tools like Ansible.

**Shift left** means adding security testing early in the development pipeline (CI/CD) — catching flaws with SAST/DAST and dependency scans *before* production, which is far cheaper than fixing them later.
**Sign your scripts and artifacts** so only trusted, untampered code runs — a supply-chain defence; verification stops a tampered artifact from deploying.
Never store secrets (API keys, passwords) in code — anyone with the code gets them. Use a **secrets manager** and inject them at runtime.

Automation **service accounts** must follow least privilege and be monitored; an over-privileged automation account is a prime target. Scanning code for hard-coded secrets before committing is a simple, high-value habit.

days.title: Endpoint and email security
days.objective: Protect endpoints and email against modern threats.

questions.q: EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response) provides:
options: Continuous monitoring, detection, and response on endpoints
questions.explain: EDR sees behavior and enables remote investigation/containment.

questions.q: How does EDR differ from traditional antivirus?
options: It focuses on behavior/telemetry and response, not just known-signature files
questions.explain: AV catches known malware; EDR catches suspicious behavior and enables hunting.

questions.q: SPF, DKIM and DMARC together help:
options: Verify email sender authenticity and reduce spoofing/phishing
questions.explain: SPF authorizes senders, DKIM signs messages, DMARC sets policy + reporting.

questions.q: Application allow-listing on endpoints:
questions.explain: Strong against unknown malware, but needs upkeep.

questions.q: "Sandboxing" a suspicious attachment means:
options: Detonating it in an isolated environment to observe behavior safely
questions.explain: Email gateways and EDR use sandboxes to catch unknown malware.

questions.q: A key control against ransomware on endpoints is:
options: EDR + least privilege + tested offline backups + patching
questions.explain: Layered defenses reduce both the chance and the impact.

questions.q: "Host-based intrusion prevention" (HIPS) does what?
options: Blocks malicious behavior on the endpoint itself
questions.explain: Complements EDR and host firewall.

questions.q: Email attachment "content disarm and reconstruction" (CDR):
options: Strips active content and rebuilds a safe version of the file
questions.explain: It removes macros/scripts while keeping the document usable.

questions.q: On Linux, check a downloaded file's type before opening it, to avoid disguised executables.
questions.explain: If "PDF" is actually an executable or script, do not run it.

labs.title: Configure email authentication (concept)
labs.scenario: Write the DNS records (conceptually) for SPF, DKIM and DMARC for example.com and say what each does.
verify: you can explain how the three work together

labs.title: Endpoint hardening quick win
labs.scenario: On a Linux endpoint, ensure automatic security updates are considered and the firewall is on, and verify.
steps: dnf install -y dnf-automatic 2>/dev/null; systemctl enable --now dnf-automatic.timer 2>/dev/null || true
verify: firewall is active and update automation is considered

blocks.x: Endpoints (laptops, servers, phones) are where users work and where attacks often land, so they get layered protection:
**Antivirus** catches known-signature malware.

**EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response)** goes further — continuous monitoring of behaviour and telemetry, with the ability to investigate and contain remotely. It catches suspicious *behaviour*, not just known files.
**Application allow-listing** blocks unknown executables from running.
**HIPS** (host intrusion prevention) blocks malicious behaviour on the host itself.
The strong anti-ransomware combination is EDR + least privilege + patching + tested offline backups.
Email is the top delivery route for attacks, so it gets dedicated defences:
**SPF, DKIM and DMARC** together verify a sender's authenticity and reduce spoofing/phishing — SPF authorises sending servers, DKIM signs messages, DMARC sets policy and reporting.
**Sandboxing** detonates a suspicious attachment in an isolated environment to observe its behaviour safely.
**Content Disarm and Reconstruction (CDR)** strips active content (macros/scripts) and rebuilds a safe version of a file.
Combined with user awareness training and MFA, these blunt both the delivery and the payoff of email attacks.

blocks.x: The Security+ exam is up to **90 questions in 90 minutes**, mixing multiple-choice with **performance-based questions (PBQs)** — small hands-on scenarios like configuring a firewall rule, reading logs, or matching controls. The passing score is **750 on a 100–900 scale** (so not a simple percentage).
PBQs take longer, so a common tactic is to **flag** them, answer the quick multiple-choice questions first to bank those points, then return.
Watch for keywords: **"BEST"** and **"MOST likely"** signal that more than one answer looks correct — rank them and pick the strongest, most secure, most directly relevant option.
There's **no penalty for guessing**, so never leave a blank — eliminate wrong options and make your best choice.

Security+ rewards understanding *concepts* and choosing the *best* control for a situation, not memorising trivia. The PBQs reward hands-on familiarity — reading a log, picking firewall rules, hardening a config — which is exactly why practising the labs and command drills alongside the theory pays off. Think like a defender: which option most reduces real risk?

courses.exam: CompTIA PenTest+ · PT0-003 · authorized testing only

days.title: Authorization and rules of engagement
days.objective: Understand why written authorization defines a legal, ethical engagement.

questions.q: What single document makes a penetration test legal?
options: Written authorization (a signed contract / statement of work) from the asset owner
A verbal "go ahead" from a manager
questions.explain: Without signed authorization scoping the work, testing systems is illegal, no matter your intent.

questions.q: The Rules of Engagement (ROE) primarily define:
options: Scope, timing, permitted techniques, and points of contact
questions.explain: ROE keep the engagement inside legal and safe boundaries.

questions.q: "Scope" in an engagement specifies:
options: Exactly which systems, networks, and applications may be tested
questions.explain: Anything outside scope is off-limits, even if you find a way in.

questions.q: Why include an emergency contact and a "stop" procedure in the ROE?
options: So the client can halt testing immediately if something breaks or an incident occurs
questions.explain: A live production issue must be stoppable within minutes.

questions.q: "Get out of jail free" letter refers to:
options: Written authorization the tester carries proving the work is sanctioned
A real legal immunity from all laws
questions.explain: It documents permission; it does not excuse illegal acts outside scope.

questions.q: Which is usually explicitly FORBIDDEN unless specifically authorized?
options: Using an approved scanner in scope
Denial-of-service, social engineering, and physical intrusion
questions.explain: High-impact techniques require explicit written permission.

questions.q: A "target of evaluation" list exists so that:
options: Testers can scan the whole internet
Testers only touch approved hosts and avoid third-party/shared systems
questions.explain: Cloud/shared hosting often requires the provider's permission too.

questions.q: Testing a cloud-hosted app usually also requires:
options: Awareness of the provider's testing policy and possibly their authorization
questions.explain: Some providers require notification; DoS is typically banned.

# exclude any shared/third-party ranges; get written OK for cloud

# 2 document what you found and how
# 4 continue only if scope is formally amended in writing

theory.h: What makes a penetration test legal

blocks.x: A penetration test is authorised, ethical hacking done to find weaknesses **before** a real attacker does. The single thing that separates it from a crime is **written authorization** — a signed contract or statement of work from the owner of the systems being tested. No matter how good your intent, testing systems without that permission is illegal. On the job and on the exam, the first instinct for any scenario is always: *are we scoped and authorised for this?*
The **Rules of Engagement** define the boundaries of the test:
**Scope** — exactly which systems, networks and applications may be tested. Anything outside scope is off-limits, even if you find a way in.
**Timing** — when testing may happen (often a maintenance window).
**Permitted and forbidden techniques** — high-impact actions like **denial-of-service, social engineering and physical intrusion** are usually forbidden unless explicitly authorised.
**Points of contact and a stop procedure** — so the client can halt testing immediately if something breaks.
A "get out of jail free" letter is the written authorisation you carry proving the work is sanctioned — it documents permission, it does not excuse acting outside scope.
Testing cloud-hosted or shared systems may also require the **provider's** permission.

If you discover a path into an **out-of-scope** system, you stop, document it, and notify the client — you continue only if scope is formally amended in writing. Scope applies at **every** phase, from recon to reporting.

days.title: Methodologies and frameworks
days.objective: Compare penetration-testing methodologies and standards.

questions.q: The typical penetration-test phases are:
options: Planning, Reconnaissance, Scanning/Enumeration, Exploitation, Post-exploitation, Reporting
questions.explain: A structured methodology keeps the test thorough and repeatable.

questions.q: MITRE ATT&CK is used by testers to:
options: Map real adversary tactics and techniques to plan and describe attacks
questions.explain: ATT&CK gives a shared language of TTPs for both red and blue teams.

questions.q: The Cyber Kill Chain describes:
options: The stages of an attack from reconnaissance to actions on objectives
questions.explain: Understanding the chain helps you emulate and disrupt attacks.

questions.q: OSSTMM, PTES and NIST 800-115 are:
questions.explain: They guide consistent, defensible testing.

questions.q: "OWASP Testing Guide / Top 10" is most relevant to:
questions.explain: The OWASP Top 10 lists the most critical web app risks.

questions.q: What is the difference between a red team and a standard pen test?
options: Red teaming emulates a real adversary to test detection/response, often stealthy and goal-based
questions.explain: A standard pen test aims for coverage; red teaming aims for realism and objectives.

questions.q: "Assumed breach" testing starts from:
options: The premise that an attacker already has some foothold (e.g., a workstation)
questions.explain: It focuses on lateral movement and detection rather than initial access.

questions.q: Why document your methodology in the report?
options: So findings are reproducible and the client understands coverage and limits
questions.explain: Reproducibility and transparency build trust and let the client re-test fixes.

labs.title: Map an attack to ATT&CK
labs.scenario: For a phishing-to-foothold scenario, list one technique per kill-chain stage and its ATT&CK-style label.
verify: each stage has a plausible technique

labs.title: Choose a methodology
labs.scenario: For (a) a web app assessment and (b) a full-scope red team, name the most fitting methodology/framework and why.
steps: # (a) OWASP Testing Guide + PTES -> thorough web coverage
# (b) MITRE ATT&CK + assumed breach -> realistic adversary emulation

blocks.x: A structured methodology keeps a test thorough and repeatable. The typical phases: 1. **Planning** — scoping, ROE, legal. 2. **Reconnaissance** — gather information about the target. 3. **Scanning / Enumeration** — find live hosts, ports, services and detail. 4. **Exploitation** — prove a vulnerability is real within scope. 5. **Post-exploitation** — situational awareness, escalation, lateral movement. 6. **Reporting** — the deliverable that creates value. Knowing the order matters on the exam: you *enumerate before you exploit*, and you *report at the end*.
Testers use shared frameworks so results are consistent and defensible:
**MITRE ATT&CK** — a catalogue of real adversary tactics and techniques (TTPs), used to plan and describe attacks.
**The Cyber Kill Chain** — the stages of an attack from reconnaissance to actions on objectives.
**PTES, OSSTMM, NIST 800-115** — penetration-testing/assessment methodologies.
**OWASP Testing Guide / Top 10** — the reference for web application testing.
A standard pen test aims for broad **coverage** of vulnerabilities.
**Red teaming** emulates a real adversary to test the defenders' detection and response, often stealthy and goal-based.
**Assumed breach** testing starts from the premise that an attacker already has a foothold, focusing on lateral movement and detection rather than initial access.
Documenting your methodology in the report makes findings reproducible and shows what was and wasn't covered.

days.title: Passive reconnaissance and OSINT
days.objective: Gather information without touching the target directly.

questions.q: Passive reconnaissance means:
options: Collecting information without directly interacting with the target's systems
questions.explain: OSINT (open-source intelligence) uses public data, so it is low-risk and stealthy.

questions.q: WHOIS lookups can reveal:
options: Domain registration details, registrar, and sometimes contacts/name servers
questions.explain: Much contact data is now privacy-protected, but registrar and NS often show.

questions.q: DNS enumeration can reveal:
options: Subdomains, mail servers, and name servers of a domain
questions.explain: Records like A, MX, NS, TXT, CNAME are useful map-building data.

questions.q: "Google dorking" refers to:
options: Using advanced search operators to find exposed files, logins, or info
questions.explain: e.g. site:, filetype:, intitle: reveal unintentionally public content.

questions.q: Why is OSINT valuable early in an engagement?
options: It builds the attack surface picture without alerting the target
questions.explain: You learn domains, emails, tech stack, and employees quietly.

questions.q: Certificate transparency logs are useful because they:
options: List issued certificates, often revealing subdomains
questions.explain: crt.sh and similar reveal hostnames from public CT logs.

questions.q: Social media OSINT helps a tester by:
options: Revealing employees, roles, tech used, and phishing pretext material
questions.explain: Job posts often leak the exact technologies in use.

questions.q: Look up the DNS name servers and mail servers for a domain you are authorized to assess.
questions.explain: Passive query of public DNS; no direct contact with the target's servers.

labs.title: Build a passive footprint
labs.scenario: For an authorized domain, gather: registrar, name servers, MX records, and any subdomains from public sources — without scanning the target.
steps: dig example.com NS +short; dig example.com MX +short
# subdomains from CT logs (crt.sh) reviewed in a browser
verify: you have a passive map with zero packets sent to the target hosts

labs.title: OSINT email/user harvest (authorized)
labs.scenario: Describe how you would ethically collect likely employee email formats for an authorized social-engineering test.
steps: # find the email pattern (first.last@domain) from public sources
# list roles from public job posts / company site
# only use within the authorized social-engineering scope
verify: you have a pretext list without contacting the target infra

labs.title: Reduce your own footprint
labs.scenario: Explain two ways an organization can limit what OSINT reveals about it.
steps: # privacy-protect WHOIS; minimize info in job posts
# review CT logs/subdomains for unintended exposure; remove metadata from public files
verify: each measure shrinks the public attack surface

blocks.x: Reconnaissance is gathering information about the target, and **passive** recon does it **without directly touching** the target's systems — so it is low-risk and stealthy. It relies on **OSINT (Open-Source Intelligence)**: public data anyone can access. Early passive recon builds a picture of the attack surface without alerting anyone.
**WHOIS** — domain registration details, registrar, and name servers.
**DNS records** — subdomains, mail servers (MX), name servers (NS), text records (TXT).
**Certificate Transparency logs** (e.g. crt.sh) — publicly list issued certificates, often revealing subdomains.
**Google dorking** — advanced search operators (`site:`, `filetype:`, `intitle:`) that surface exposed files or logins.
**Social media and job posts** — employees, roles, and the exact technologies in use (job ads often leak the tech stack).

The key distinction for the exam: passive recon uses only public data and sends nothing to the target; **active** recon (scanning) directly interacts with target systems and can be detected. You gather all you can passively first, then move to active techniques on authorised, in-scope hosts. Organisations reduce their own exposure by privacy-protecting WHOIS, minimising info in job posts, and reviewing what CT logs reveal.

days.title: Active scanning with Nmap
days.objective: Discover hosts, ports and services on authorized targets.

questions.q: Active reconnaissance differs from passive because it:
options: Directly interacts with target systems (and can be detected)
questions.explain: Scanning is active; run it only on authorized, in-scope targets.

questions.q: A TCP SYN scan (-sS) is often preferred because it:
options: Is fast and does not complete the full handshake ("half-open")
questions.explain: It is stealthier and quick; needs raw-socket privileges.

questions.q: Nmap's -sV flag does what?
options: Detects service and version information on open ports
questions.explain: Version detection helps match services to known vulnerabilities.

questions.q: Nmap's -O flag attempts to:
questions.explain: OS detection uses TCP/IP stack behavior.

questions.q: Which Nmap option runs the default script set for extra discovery?
questions.explain: NSE scripts add banner grabbing, vuln checks, and enumeration.

questions.q: Nmap's -Pn tells Nmap to:
options: Skip host discovery and treat the host as online
questions.explain: Useful when ICMP is blocked but you know the host is up (and in scope).

questions.q: A UDP scan (-sU) is slower because:
options: UDP is connectionless, so open/filtered states are ambiguous and need timeouts
questions.explain: Still important: DNS, SNMP, and DHCP live on UDP.

questions.q: Nmap timing template -T4 vs -T1: -T4 is:
questions.explain: Slower timing reduces detection and load on fragile targets.

questions.q: Do a service/version scan of a single authorized lab host, top ports only.
questions.explain: Authorized, in-scope targets only. -F scans the 100 most common ports.

labs.title: Full discovery workflow (authorized lab)
labs.scenario: On your own lab network, discover live hosts, then scan one host for open ports, services, versions and OS.
verify: you have a list of services and likely OS for one host

labs.title: Save and compare scans
labs.scenario: Run a scan, save it, change something on the lab host, rescan, and diff to detect changes.
steps: # (open/close a service on the lab host)
verify: you can see exactly which ports/services changed

labs.title: Targeted UDP check
labs.scenario: Check a few important UDP services on an authorized host and explain why UDP results are less certain.
steps: # open|filtered means no reply -- could be open or dropped

blocks.x: Once passive recon is done, **active** scanning directly probes authorised, in-scope hosts to discover what's there. **Nmap** (Network Mapper) is the standard tool — it finds live hosts, open ports and the services behind them. Run it only on systems you own or are authorised to test.
`-sS` — a **SYN (half-open)** scan: fast and relatively stealthy because it doesn't complete the full handshake (needs privileges).
`-sV` — **version detection**, identifying the software and version on each open port so you can match it to known vulnerabilities.
`-O` — **OS fingerprinting**, guessing the operating system from network-stack behaviour.
`-sC` — run the **default NSE scripts** for extra discovery (banner grabbing, common checks).
`-sU` — a **UDP** scan (slower and more ambiguous because UDP is connectionless; still needed for DNS, SNMP, DHCP).
`-Pn` — skip host discovery and treat the host as online (useful when ICMP is blocked).
**Timing templates** `-T0`–`-T5` trade speed for stealth/load: `-T4` is fast, `-T1` is slow and quiet (gentler on fragile targets).
`-p-` scans **all** 65,535 TCP ports; `-F` scans a fast common set.
`-oA basename` saves output in all formats for later parsing and comparison. A UDP result of "open|filtered" means no reply — it could be open or dropped, which is why UDP scanning is less certain.

days.title: Enumeration of services
days.objective: Enumerate specific services to gather actionable detail.

questions.q: "Enumeration" goes beyond scanning by:
options: Actively extracting detailed info (users, shares, versions, config) from services
questions.explain: It turns "port 445 open" into "these shares and users exist."

questions.q: SMB enumeration on port 445 can reveal:
options: Shares, users, and OS details (when misconfigured)
questions.explain: Tools query shares and null sessions where allowed.

questions.q: Enumerating a web server's directories/files is called:
questions.explain: Wordlist tools find hidden endpoints like /admin or /backup.

questions.q: Banner grabbing retrieves:
options: Service identification strings that hint at software and version
questions.explain: Versions map to known CVEs.

questions.q: SNMP with a default community string ("public") can leak:
options: System info, interfaces, running processes, and sometimes config
questions.explain: Default/read community strings are a common misconfiguration.

questions.q: Enumerating DNS with a zone transfer (AXFR) succeeds when:
options: A misconfigured name server allows anyone to pull all records
questions.explain: A successful AXFR dumps the whole zone — a finding in itself.

questions.q: LDAP enumeration can reveal:
options: Directory users, groups, and organizational structure
questions.explain: Anonymous binds sometimes expose the directory.

questions.q: Why enumerate thoroughly before exploiting?
options: Precise detail makes exploitation reliable and reduces noise/damage
questions.explain: Good enumeration is what separates a pro from a script kiddie.

questions.q: Enumerate hidden web directories on an authorized target with a wordlist.
questions.explain: Authorized targets only. Review responses (200/301/403) for interesting paths.

labs.scenario: On a lab web host, identify the server software, discover directories, and note any interesting endpoints.
