labs.scenario: On a lab host with SMB, list shares and (if allowed) users, and note misconfigurations.
verify: you can list shares and identify anonymous access if present

labs.title: Try a DNS zone transfer
labs.scenario: Against an authorized name server, attempt an AXFR and record whether it (insecurely) succeeds.
steps: # success = misconfiguration finding; failure = properly restricted
verify: you can state whether the zone transfer was allowed

blocks.x: **Enumeration** goes deeper than scanning: it actively extracts detailed information — users, shares, versions, configuration — from the services a scan found. It turns "port 445 is open" into "these shares and these users exist." Thorough enumeration is what separates a professional from a script kiddie, because precise detail makes later exploitation reliable and reduces the risk of causing damage.
**SMB (445)** — shares, users and OS details when misconfigured (tools query shares and null sessions where allowed).
**Web servers** — **content discovery** (directory brute-forcing) with wordlist tools finds hidden endpoints like `/admin` or `/backup`.
**SNMP** — a default community string ("public") can leak system info, interfaces and running processes.
**DNS** — a misconfigured server may allow a **zone transfer (AXFR)** that dumps every record — a finding in itself.
**LDAP** — anonymous binds can expose directory users, groups and structure.

theory.h: Banner grabbing and why detail matters

blocks.x: **Banner grabbing** retrieves the identification string a service returns, revealing its software and version — which map directly to known CVEs. The reason to enumerate thoroughly *before* exploiting is control: you exploit precisely, quietly, and without breaking things, because you understand exactly what you're dealing with.

days.title: Vulnerability scanning
days.objective: Run and interpret automated vulnerability scans.

questions.q: A vulnerability scanner works by:
options: Checking targets against a database of known weaknesses and misconfigurations
questions.explain: It reports likely issues; a tester then validates them.

questions.q: "Authenticated" (credentialed) scanning gives:
options: Deeper, more accurate results by logging in to check patch levels/config
questions.explain: Credentialed scans find missing patches unauthenticated scans cannot see.

questions.q: A "false positive" from a scanner is:
options: A reported vulnerability that is not actually exploitable/present
questions.explain: Validation (manual testing) separates real issues from noise.

questions.q: CVSS base score ranges roughly as:
questions.explain: 9.0-10.0 is Critical; context (exposure) still matters for real risk.

questions.q: A CVE identifier is:
options: A unique ID for a publicly known vulnerability (e.g., CVE-2024-1234)
questions.explain: CVEs let everyone reference the same flaw.

questions.q: Why avoid running an aggressive scanner against fragile production systems?
options: It can crash unstable services or cause outages
questions.explain: Coordinate timing and intensity in the ROE; some hosts need gentle scans.

questions.q: Scanner output should be:
options: Validated and prioritized before it goes in the report
Pasted raw as the final report
questions.explain: Raw scan dumps are not a professional deliverable.

questions.q: "Compliance scanning" checks systems against:
questions.explain: It reports configuration gaps for a specific requirement set.

questions.q: Run an authorized Nmap NSE vulnerability check against a lab host.
questions.explain: NSE vuln scripts are a lightweight starting point; validate anything flagged.

labs.title: Scan, then validate (authorized lab)
labs.scenario: Run a vuln scan on a lab host, pick one finding, and manually confirm whether it is real.
steps: # pick e.g. an outdated service; check its real version banner
nc 192.168.56.10 <port>            # grab banner to confirm version
verify: you classified the finding as confirmed or false positive

labs.title: Prioritize findings
labs.scenario: Given four findings with CVSS 9.8 (internet-facing), 7.5 (internal), 5.0 (needs local access), 3.1 (info), put them in remediation order and justify.

labs.title: Reduce false positives
labs.scenario: Describe two ways to make scan results more accurate and trustworthy.
steps: # manually validate high-impact findings before reporting
verify: your report would contain confirmed, prioritized issues

blocks.x: A **vulnerability scanner** checks targets against a database of known weaknesses and misconfigurations, then reports likely issues. It **reports**, it doesn't exploit — a tester validates the findings afterward. Scanners save huge time but must be used carefully: an aggressive scan can crash fragile production services, so intensity and timing are agreed in the ROE.
**Authenticated (credentialed) scanning** logs in to check patch levels and configuration, giving far deeper and more accurate results than an unauthenticated scan.
A **false positive** is a reported vulnerability that isn't actually exploitable; validation separates real issues from noise.
Raw scanner output is **not** a professional report — findings must be validated and prioritised first.
**CVSS** scores severity from 0.0 to 10.0 (9.0+ is Critical); real risk also depends on **exposure** and business impact.
A **CVE** is the unique public identifier for a known vulnerability.
**Compliance scanning** checks systems against a benchmark (CIS, PCI DSS) and reports configuration gaps.
The workflow is: scan, **validate** the important findings by hand (e.g. grab the real version banner), then prioritise.

days.title: Analyzing and prioritizing findings
days.objective: Turn raw findings into risk-ranked, actionable results.

questions.q: Real-world risk of a vulnerability depends on:
options: Severity AND exposure/exploitability AND business impact
questions.explain: A critical CVE on an isolated box may rank below a medium on an internet-facing app.

questions.q: "Chaining" vulnerabilities means:
options: Combining several lower-severity issues to achieve a high-impact result
questions.explain: e.g., info leak + weak password + misconfig = full compromise.

questions.q: Why map findings to business impact?
options: It helps leadership prioritize fixes by what actually matters to the business
questions.explain: "This exposes customer PII" motivates action more than a raw CVSS number.

questions.q: An "attack path" in a report shows:
options: The steps from initial access to the objective, so defenders can break the chain
questions.explain: Visualizing the path highlights the cheapest place to add a control.

questions.q: A finding's "remediation" section should be:
options: Specific, actionable guidance to fix or mitigate the issue
questions.explain: Tell the client exactly what to change.

questions.q: Which finding likely deserves the highest priority?
options: A verbose error message on an internal test box
A missing security header on an internal page
An unauthenticated remote code execution on an internet-facing server
questions.explain: Unauthenticated + RCE + exposed = maximum urgency.

questions.q: Why avoid only listing "critical" findings?
options: Chained lows/mediums and quick wins also matter to the client's risk
questions.explain: A good report covers the full picture with clear priorities.

questions.q: "Risk acceptance" by the client means:
options: The finding was a false positive
They knowingly choose to live with a residual risk rather than fix it now
questions.explain: Document accepted risks and who accepted them.

labs.title: Rank a findings list
labs.scenario: Given five mixed findings, assign each a priority (P1-P4) using severity, exposure, and impact, and write a one-line justification each.
steps: # P1: internet-facing auth-bypass leading to data access
# P2: internal service with known RCE (needs foothold)
verify: priorities reflect real risk, not raw CVSS alone

labs.title: Write an attack-path narrative
labs.scenario: Chain three findings into one attack path from external to sensitive data, and identify the single control that best breaks it.
steps: # exposed admin panel -> default creds -> file upload -> data access
# best break point: remove/authenticate the admin panel + MFA
verify: one well-placed control stops the whole chain

labs.title: Write a remediation
labs.scenario: For "SQL injection in the login form," write a clear, specific remediation the developers can act on.
steps: # use parameterized queries/prepared statements for all DB access
# validate/allow-list input; least-privilege DB account; WAF as defense-in-depth
verify: a developer could fix it from your text alone

blocks.x: A pile of scanner output isn't useful until you turn it into risk-ranked, actionable results. Real-world risk depends on **severity AND exposure/exploitability AND business impact** — a critical CVE on an isolated box may rank *below* a medium flaw on an internet-facing app. Mapping findings to **business impact** ("this exposes customer PII") is what motivates leadership to fix them.
**Chaining** combines several lower-severity issues into one high-impact result — e.g. an information leak + a weak password + a misconfiguration = full compromise.

An **attack path** in the report shows the steps from initial access to the objective, so defenders can see the cheapest place to break the chain — often a single well-placed control stops the whole thing.

Each finding needs a clear **remediation** — specific, actionable guidance, not "be more secure." Prioritise findings (P1–P4) by severity, exposure and impact so the client fixes the most dangerous issues first. Don't list only "critical" items — chained lows and quick wins matter too. When a client knowingly chooses to live with a risk, that's a documented **risk acceptance**, recorded with who accepted it. The report, not the number of shells, is what delivers value.

days.title: Exploitation fundamentals and Metasploit
days.objective: Safely validate vulnerabilities on authorized targets.

questions.q: In a pen test, the point of exploitation is to:
options: Demonstrate real impact of a vulnerability within the authorized scope
questions.explain: You prove risk, then document and clean up.

questions.q: What is a "proof of concept" (PoC)?
options: A demonstration that a vulnerability is genuinely exploitable
questions.explain: A PoC turns a theoretical finding into a confirmed one.

questions.q: In Metasploit, a "payload" is:
options: The code that runs on the target after a successful exploit (e.g., a shell)
questions.explain: Payloads can be a simple shell or a fuller agent, per authorization.

questions.q: A "reverse shell" connects:
options: From the tester to the target only
From the target back to the tester's listener
questions.explain: Useful when the target cannot accept inbound connections (bind shell does the opposite).

questions.q: Why prefer a low-impact PoC over a destructive exploit?
options: You prove the risk without harming the client's systems or data
questions.explain: "Do no harm" is core to professional testing.

questions.q: Before running an exploit, a professional tester:
options: Confirms the target is in scope and understands the exploit's impact
questions.explain: Know what the exploit does so you do not cause an outage.

questions.q: A "staged" vs "stageless" payload differs in:
options: Whether the payload is delivered in stages or all at once
questions.explain: Staged payloads are smaller initially; stageless are self-contained.

questions.q: After a successful PoC, the tester should:
options: Document evidence, timestamps, and clean up any artifacts left behind
questions.explain: Remove test accounts, files, and implants; record everything.

questions.q: In Metasploit, search for a module matching a service you are authorized to test.
questions.explain: Read the module's description and impact before use; authorized lab targets only.

labs.title: Validate a known-vuln lab box (authorized)
labs.scenario: On a deliberately vulnerable lab VM (e.g., Metasploitable), confirm one vulnerability with a low-impact PoC and capture evidence.
steps: # search <service> ; use <module> ; set RHOSTS <lab-ip> ; check (if supported)
# run a benign PoC; screenshot proof; then clean up
verify: you have evidence a real vulnerability is exploitable, with no lasting damage

labs.title: Set up a listener safely
labs.scenario: Explain and set up a reverse-shell listener on your attacker VM for an authorized test, and how you would tear it down afterward.
steps: # after PoC: close the listener, remove any dropped files on target
verify: the listener works and you can cleanly stop it

labs.title: Document a PoC
labs.scenario: Write the fields your PoC evidence must include for the report.
steps: # target host/IP, timestamp, vulnerability + CVE, steps taken
# screenshot/output proof, impact demonstrated, cleanup performed
verify: another tester could reproduce it from your notes

blocks.x: In a pen test, exploitation exists to **demonstrate the real impact** of a vulnerability within the authorised scope — not to cause maximum damage. You produce a **proof of concept (PoC)** that turns a theoretical finding into a confirmed one, then document it and clean up. The professional mindset is "do no harm": prove the risk with the lowest-impact method, and always confirm the target is in scope before firing an exploit.
**Metasploit** is a framework that organises exploits and payloads:
An **exploit** module abuses a specific vulnerability; a **payload** is the code that runs on the target afterward (for example a shell).
A **reverse shell** connects *from* the target back to the tester's listener (useful when the target can't accept inbound connections); a **bind shell** does the opposite.
Payloads can be **staged** (delivered in stages, smaller initially) or **stageless** (self-contained).
`search`, `use`, `set RHOSTS`, and `run` are the typical flow; always read a module's description and impact first.

Before running any exploit, understand what it does so you don't cause an outage — untrusted PoC code can be destructive or backdoored, so test in a lab first. After a successful PoC, **document** the evidence (host, timestamp, steps, screenshot, impact) and **clean up** anything you left behind — test accounts, files, implants. Prove it, record it, restore the system.

days.title: Password attacks
days.objective: Test authentication strength on authorized systems.

questions.q: "Offline" password cracking means:
options: Cracking captured password hashes without contacting the live system
questions.explain: Offline attacks avoid lockouts and are limited only by compute and hash strength.

questions.q: A dictionary attack uses:
options: The password hash as input to nothing
questions.explain: Wordlists (e.g., rockyou) plus rules cover most weak passwords.

questions.q: Why does a strong, slow hash (bcrypt/argon2) with salt resist cracking?
options: Salting stops precomputation and slow hashing limits guesses per second
questions.explain: Fast unsalted hashes (MD5) crack far quicker.

questions.q: "Password spraying" avoids lockouts by:
options: Trying many passwords on one account
Trying one common password across many accounts
questions.explain: It stays under per-account lockout thresholds.

questions.q: Hashcat vs John the Ripper: hashcat is known for:
options: GPU-accelerated cracking of many hash types
questions.explain: Both crack hashes; hashcat leverages GPUs heavily.

questions.q: "Pass-the-hash" lets an attacker:
options: Authenticate using a captured hash without knowing the plaintext
questions.explain: It abuses protocols that accept the hash as proof.

questions.q: A good defense a tester recommends against these attacks is:
options: MFA, strong salted hashing, lockout/rate limiting, and long passphrases
questions.explain: Report the fix, not just the finding.

questions.q: Why must password testing stay within scope and ROE?
options: Lockouts and account access can disrupt real users and cross legal lines
questions.explain: Coordinate spraying/lockout thresholds with the client.

questions.q: Crack a provided lab hash file with a wordlist using John (authorized lab).
questions.explain: Only crack hashes you are authorized to test; -m 0 is raw MD5 in hashcat.

labs.title: Crack lab hashes and report impact
labs.scenario: Given a lab hash file, identify the hash type, crack the weak ones, and write the remediation.
steps: # identify: hashid <hash>   or  john will guess the format
# remediation: enforce passphrases + MFA, use bcrypt/argon2 with salt
verify: you cracked the weak passwords and gave a real fix

labs.title: Demonstrate spraying safely (lab)
labs.scenario: On an authorized lab directory, describe a low-and-slow spray that respects lockout policy, and the detection a defender would use.
steps: # one common password across accounts, spaced to avoid lockout
# defender detects: many failed logins for different users from one source
verify: your approach avoids locking real accounts and is detectable

labs.title: Recommend authentication hardening
labs.scenario: List five controls that would have stopped the password attacks you demonstrated.
steps: # MFA everywhere; long passphrases; account lockout + rate limiting
# salted slow hashing (bcrypt/argon2); ban breached passwords
verify: each control maps to an attack you performed

blocks.x: Password attacks in a test show how weak credentials really are, always within scope and ROE (lockouts and account access can disrupt real users). Two broad approaches:
**Offline cracking** works on captured **hashes** without touching the live system — no lockouts, limited only by compute and hash strength.
**Online attacks** try credentials against the live service and must respect lockout policy.
A **dictionary attack** tries passwords from a wordlist (like rockyou.txt); **brute force** tries every combination.
**Password spraying** tries one common password across many accounts to stay under per-account lockout thresholds.
**Pass-the-hash** authenticates using a captured hash without cracking it.
Tools: **hashcat** (GPU-accelerated, many hash types) and **John the Ripper** (CPU-based) crack hashes offline.

A strong, **salted, slow** hash (bcrypt/argon2) resists cracking: the salt defeats precomputation (rainbow tables) and the slowness limits guesses per second. Fast, unsalted hashes (MD5) fall quickly. The remediations a tester recommends are the same defences: **MFA**, long passphrases, account lockout/rate limiting, banning breached passwords, and slow salted hashing server-side.

days.title: Web application attacks
days.objective: Test common web vulnerabilities on authorized apps.

questions.q: SQL injection is possible when:
options: User input is concatenated into a database query without parameterization
questions.explain: Prepared statements are the primary fix.

questions.q: Cross-site scripting (XSS) lets an attacker:
options: Run script in a victim's browser via unsanitized output
questions.explain: Output encoding and CSP mitigate it.

questions.q: The difference between stored and reflected XSS is:
options: Stored is saved on the server and served to many; reflected bounces off a single request
questions.explain: Stored XSS can hit every viewer of a page.

questions.q: "IDOR" (Insecure Direct Object Reference) occurs when:
options: Changing an ID in a request exposes another user's data due to missing authorization checks
questions.explain: Enforce object-level authorization on every request.

questions.q: CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery) tricks a browser into:
options: Sending an authenticated request the user did not intend
questions.explain: Anti-CSRF tokens and SameSite cookies defend against it.

questions.q: "SSRF" (Server-Side Request Forgery) abuses a server to:
options: Make requests to internal systems the attacker cannot reach directly
questions.explain: Often used to reach cloud metadata endpoints; validate/allow-list outbound URLs.

questions.q: A proxy tool like Burp Suite / OWASP ZAP is used to:
options: Intercept, inspect and modify HTTP requests between browser and app
questions.explain: It is the core tool for manual web testing.

questions.q: "Command injection" happens when:
options: User input is passed to a system shell without sanitization
questions.explain: Avoid shelling out with user input; use safe APIs and allow-lists.

questions.q: Fuzz a web parameter for hidden values on an authorized target with ffuf.
questions.explain: Authorized targets only; watch response codes/sizes for anomalies.

labs.title: Test a login form (authorized lab)
labs.scenario: On a deliberately vulnerable lab app (e.g., DVWA/Juice Shop), test the login for SQL injection and document the result and fix.
steps: # try   ' OR '1'='1' --    in the username (lab only)
# if it bypasses auth: confirm, screenshot, then write the fix
# fix: parameterized queries + input validation + least-privilege DB user
verify: you demonstrated (or ruled out) SQLi and gave remediation

labs.title: Find IDOR (authorized lab)
labs.scenario: On a lab app, change a resource ID in a request and check whether you can view another user's data.
steps: # log in as user A, note a URL like /account?id=1001
# change to id=1002 -- if you see user B's data, that's IDOR

labs.title: Map to OWASP Top 10
labs.scenario: For three vulnerabilities you tested, name the OWASP Top 10 category and one defense each.
steps: # broken access (IDOR) -> A01 Broken Access Control -> server-side authz
# XSS -> A03 Injection (XSS) -> output encoding + CSP
verify: each maps to a category and a concrete defense

blocks.x: Web apps are a huge attack surface, tested against the **OWASP Top 10**. The classics:
**SQL injection** — user input concatenated into a database query, letting the attacker run their own SQL. Fixed with **parameterized queries**.

**Cross-site scripting (XSS)** — injecting script that runs in a victim's browser; **stored** XSS is saved on the server and served to many, **reflected** bounces off a single request. Fixed with output encoding and a CSP.
**IDOR / broken access control** — changing an ID in a request exposes another user's data because authorization isn't enforced per object.
**CSRF** — tricking a browser into sending an authenticated request the user didn't intend; defended with anti-CSRF tokens and SameSite cookies.
**SSRF** — abusing a server to make requests to internal systems the attacker can't reach directly (often to steal cloud metadata credentials).
**Command injection** — passing user input to a system shell without sanitisation.

A **proxy tool** like **Burp Suite** or **OWASP ZAP** intercepts, inspects and modifies HTTP requests between the browser and the app — the core of manual web testing. You can also test purely from the command line with `curl` and fuzz parameters with `ffuf`. For each finding, name the OWASP category and give a concrete defence — the common thread is again "never trust user input; treat it as data, not code."

days.objective: Test network protocols and services on authorized targets.

questions.q: An on-path (MITM) position lets a tester:
options: Observe and potentially modify traffic between two hosts (authorized lab only)

questions.q: "LLMNR/NBT-NS poisoning" works because:

questions.q: A key defense a tester recommends against sniffing is:

questions.explain: Recommend SNMPv3 with auth+privacy and no default strings.

questions.q: Why coordinate any DoS-style test carefully?
options: It is required in every test
It can take down production; usually it is out of scope unless explicitly authorized
questions.explain: Most engagements forbid DoS.

questions.q: Network segmentation limits a tester (and attacker) by:
options: Preventing easy movement between zones after a foothold
questions.explain: You then report where segmentation is missing.

questions.explain: Lab/authorized networks only. Shows why encrypted protocols matter.

labs.title: Demonstrate a plaintext-credential finding (lab)
labs.scenario: On your isolated lab, capture a Telnet or FTP login and show the credentials in the clear, then write the remediation.

# remediation: replace FTP with SFTP/FTPS; disable plaintext services

labs.title: Identify name-resolution exposure (concept)
labs.scenario: Explain how LLMNR/NBT-NS poisoning captures hashes on a Windows LAN and the two settings that stop it.

labs.scenario: List four network-layer recommendations from a test that captured plaintext and saw flat networking.
steps: # segment with VLANs + firewall between zones
# SNMPv3 only, no default community strings
verify: each recommendation ties to an observed weakness

blocks.x: On the authorised network, testers demonstrate the risk of weak protocols and configurations:

An **on-path (MITM)** position lets you observe and possibly modify traffic between two hosts — proving why unencrypted protocols (Telnet, FTP, HTTP) are dangerous, since credentials and data can be captured.
**SMB relay** abuses authentication being relayed to a host that trusts it; **SMB signing** and disabling legacy auth mitigate it.
**LLMNR/NBT-NS poisoning** works because Windows falls back to these name-resolution protocols that an attacker can answer, capturing hashes; disabling LLMNR/NBT-NS removes the path.
A service using **plaintext** is a finding on its own — recommend encrypted replacements (SSH, SFTP, HTTPS, LDAPS).
**SNMP** with a default/writable community string can leak or even change device configuration; recommend SNMPv3 with auth+privacy.
**DoS-style tests** can take down production and are usually out of scope unless explicitly authorised.

The recommendations that come out of network testing are consistent: **encrypt everything in transit**, **segment** the network so a foothold can't reach every zone, disable legacy name-resolution and enable SMB signing, and use SNMPv3. Encryption makes captured traffic useless; segmentation limits lateral movement.

questions.explain: Not all adapters support it; an external adapter is often required.

It is encrypted end to end

questions.explain: Per-user credentials are revocable without changing everyone's key.

options: WPA3 (or WPA2-AES), a strong passphrase, disable WPS, and separate guest/IoT VLANs
questions.explain: Layer real controls, not obscurity.

labs.title: Assess your own lab Wi-Fi
labs.scenario: On a Wi-Fi network you OWN, document the security type, whether WPS is on, and recommend improvements.
steps: # check the router admin page: encryption type, WPS state, firmware version
# recommend: WPA3/WPA2-AES, disable WPS, strong passphrase, guest VLAN

labs.title: Explain handshake cracking resistance
labs.scenario: Explain why a 20-character random passphrase makes WPA2 handshake cracking impractical.
steps: # offline cracking speed x keyspace = infeasible time for long random keys
# weak/dictionary passphrases fall quickly; length + randomness win

labs.scenario: List how an enterprise detects and prevents rogue/evil-twin APs.
steps: # wireless IDS/WIPS monitoring for unknown BSSIDs/SSIDs
# 802.1X so clients validate the network (mutual auth)

theory.h: Testing Wi-Fi (only what you own or are authorised for)

blocks.x: Wireless testing is legal only on networks you own or have explicit written authorisation for — deauth and injection against others' Wi-Fi is illegal. The goal is to show weak wireless security and recommend fixes.
**WEP** is a finding because its broken cipher/IV scheme can be cracked in minutes — recommend WPA2-AES at minimum, ideally **WPA3**.
Capturing a **WPA2 handshake** allows *offline* passphrase cracking — but a long, random passphrase makes this impractical.
An **evil twin** (a rogue AP impersonating a trusted SSID) shows the risk of users connecting to fake networks.
**WPS** is a finding because its PIN can be brute-forced to recover the passphrase — recommend disabling it.
**Monitor mode** on a wireless adapter is needed to capture raw 802.11 frames; not all adapters support it, so an external USB adapter is often required.
**WPA2/3-Enterprise (802.1X)** authenticates each user via RADIUS instead of a shared key, so credentials are individually revocable.

The remediation after a wireless assessment is real controls, not obscurity: **WPA3 (or WPA2-AES)** with a strong passphrase, WPS disabled, separate guest/IoT VLANs, and a wireless IDS to detect rogue/evil-twin APs.

days.title: Cloud and container attacks
days.objective: Test cloud and container weaknesses (authorized accounts).

questions.q: A common cloud misconfiguration finding is:
options: Publicly readable/writable storage buckets exposing data
questions.explain: Check bucket ACLs/policies first; public data is a frequent breach source.

questions.q: Over-privileged IAM roles are dangerous because:
options: A compromised credential inherits far more access than needed
questions.explain: Least privilege limits blast radius.

questions.q: The cloud "metadata service" (e.g., 169.254.169.254) can be abused via SSRF to:

questions.explain: IMDSv2 and blocking SSRF mitigate this.

Some layers belong to the provider and are out of scope

questions.explain: Report concrete, provider-specific fixes.

blocks.x: Cloud testing focuses on the customer-owned layers, since the provider owns the rest (shared responsibility). The most common findings:
**Public storage buckets** exposing data — check bucket ACLs/policies first.
**Over-privileged IAM roles** — a compromised credential inherits far more access than needed; least privilege limits the blast radius.
The **metadata service** (e.g. 169.254.169.254) can be abused via **SSRF** to retrieve temporary role credentials; IMDSv2 and blocking SSRF mitigate this.
A **container escape** breaks out of a container to the host, defeating isolation; non-root containers, seccomp/AppArmor and avoiding `--privileged` reduce it.
**Hard-coded secrets** in an image or repo are a finding — anyone with the image gets the credentials; use a secrets manager and scan images.
Enumerating cloud **IAM** during a test finds excessive permissions and privilege-escalation paths (role/trust chaining).

The fixes after a cloud test are consistent: **least-privilege IAM**, **block public storage**, **enable logging/monitoring**, use **IMDSv2**, and harden containers (non-root, minimal image, no baked-in secrets, scanned for CVEs). Stay within the authorised, customer-owned scope unless the provider authorises more.

days.title: Social engineering and physical
days.objective: Test the human and physical layers under authorization.

questions.q: Social-engineering tests are only ethical when:
options: Explicitly authorized in the ROE with agreed limits and care for staff wellbeing
questions.explain: Scope who, how, and what is off-limits (no real HR harm).

questions.q: A phishing simulation measures:
options: How many users click/report, to improve training and controls
questions.explain: The goal is improvement, not punishment.

questions.q: A "pretext" is:

questions.explain: e.g., posing as IT support during an authorized test.

questions.q: Tailgating (piggybacking) during a physical test demonstrates:
options: Weak physical access control (following staff through secure doors)
questions.explain: Recommend mantraps, badge discipline, and awareness.

questions.q: "Baiting" with a dropped USB tests whether:
options: Staff plug in unknown devices, enabling code execution
questions.explain: Recommend disabling autorun and USB controls + training.

questions.q: Why capture metrics (click rate, report rate) in a phishing test?
options: To baseline and measure improvement over time
questions.explain: Report rate rising is a good sign of a security-aware culture.

questions.q: The strongest defense a tester recommends against social engineering is:
options: Ongoing awareness training plus verification procedures and MFA
questions.explain: People are the target, so empower and train them.

questions.q: Vishing (voice phishing) in an authorized test might attempt to:
options: Convince staff to reveal info or reset credentials over the phone
questions.explain: Recommend callback verification and identity checks.

labs.title: Design a phishing simulation
labs.scenario: Plan an authorized phishing test: pretext, target group, success metric, and the safeguards to avoid harm.
steps: # metric: click rate + report rate; landing page = training, not real capture
# safeguards: no real credential capture, opt-out for sensitive roles, debrief
verify: the test improves security without harming staff

labs.title: Physical access walkthrough (concept)
labs.scenario: List the physical weaknesses you would check on an authorized on-site test and one fix each.
steps: # unlocked server room -> access control + camera
verify: each observation has a matching control

labs.title: Write the awareness recommendation
labs.scenario: After a phishing test with a 30% click rate, write the improvement plan.
steps: # targeted training for repeat clickers; simulated phishing quarterly
# easy "report phishing" button; MFA to blunt credential theft
# measure report rate as the key success metric
verify: the plan raises reporting and lowers clicks over time

theory.h: Testing the human and physical layers

blocks.x: People and buildings are part of the attack surface, and testing them is ethical **only** when explicitly authorised in the ROE with agreed limits and care for staff wellbeing. The goal is improvement, not punishment.
A **phishing simulation** measures how many users click versus report, to improve training and controls — the landing page teaches, it doesn't harvest real credentials.
A **pretext** is a believable cover story used to gain trust (posing as IT support).
**Vishing** (phone) might try to get staff to reveal info or reset credentials; recommend callback verification.
Capturing metrics (click rate and, importantly, **report rate**) baselines behaviour; a rising report rate shows a healthier security culture.
**Tailgating** (following staff through a secure door) demonstrates weak access control — recommend mantraps and badge discipline.
**Baiting** with a dropped USB tests whether staff plug in unknown devices — recommend disabling autorun plus training.

The strongest defence a tester can recommend against social engineering is ongoing **awareness training** plus **verification procedures** and **MFA** — because people are the target, so empowering and training them is what actually works.

days.title: Establishing a foothold and situational awareness
days.objective: Understand what to do immediately after gaining authorized access.

questions.q: The first goal after gaining a foothold (authorized) is usually:
options: Situational awareness: who am I, where am I, what can I reach
questions.explain: Enumerate the local host and network before acting.

questions.q: "whoami" and checking privileges tells you:
options: The account context and whether you have elevated rights
questions.explain: It guides whether you need privilege escalation next.

questions.q: Local enumeration after foothold includes checking:
options: Users, groups, running services, scheduled tasks, and network connections
questions.explain: You look for escalation and pivot opportunities.

questions.q: Why enumerate network reachability from the foothold?
options: To find internal hosts/services you can now reach for lateral movement
questions.explain: The foothold changes what is reachable versus from outside.

questions.q: "Living off the land" means:
options: Using built-in system tools to avoid dropping detectable malware
questions.explain: It reduces footprint and evades signature detection.

questions.q: Why document every command run during post-exploitation?
options: For the report, reproducibility, and to enable full cleanup
questions.explain: A clear log lets the client verify and remediate.

questions.q: Checking scheduled tasks/cron after foothold helps find:
options: Privilege-escalation and persistence opportunities (and existing malware)
questions.explain: Writable scripts run by root/SYSTEM are classic escalation paths.

questions.q: A professional limits post-exploitation activity to:
options: What is necessary to demonstrate impact within scope
questions.explain: Prove risk, then stop and document.

questions.q: On a Linux foothold, quickly gather who you are and your privileges (authorized lab).
questions.explain: Follow with sudo -l to see what you may run as root.

labs.title: Local enumeration script (lab)
labs.scenario: On an authorized Linux foothold, gather user, privileges, sudo rights, listening services, and cron jobs, saving output for the report.
verify: you have a situational-awareness snapshot for the report

labs.title: Find internal reachability
labs.scenario: From the foothold, identify other reachable internal hosts/services (authorized scope only).
steps: for h in 10.0.0.{1..20}; do (ping -c1 -W1 $h >/dev/null && echo "$h up") & done; wait
verify: you have a short list of reachable internal hosts in scope

labs.title: Plan the next step
labs.scenario: Based on enumeration showing you are a low-priv user with a writable root cron script, write your intended next action and why.
steps: # target: the writable script executed by root -> privilege escalation
# action: demonstrate PoC escalation, capture proof, then clean up
verify: your plan is scoped, justified, and reversible

blocks.x: Once you gain authorised access to a host, the first job is **situational awareness**, not immediate further attack. You answer: *who am I, where am I, what can I reach?* On Linux, `id` and `whoami` reveal your account context and whether you have elevated rights; `sudo -l` shows what you may run as root. Enumerate the local host — users, groups, running services, scheduled tasks (`cron`), network connections — before acting.

The foothold changes what's reachable: internal hosts and services that were invisible from outside may now be accessible, opening the way to lateral movement. Checking scheduled tasks and writable files owned by root reveals privilege-escalation opportunities (and sometimes existing malware).
**Living off the land** means using built-in system tools rather than dropping detectable malware — smaller footprint, harder to detect.
**Document every command** you run: for the report, for reproducibility, and to enable full cleanup afterward.
Limit activity to what's necessary to demonstrate impact within scope — prove the risk, then stop. A scoped, justified, reversible next step is the professional standard.

days.title: Privilege escalation (Linux)
days.objective: Escalate privileges on authorized Linux systems and report fixes.

questions.q: A classic Linux privilege-escalation check is:
options: Finding SUID binaries that can be abused (GTFOBins)
questions.explain: find / -perm -4000 lists SUID binaries to review.

questions.q: "sudo -l" is useful because it shows:
options: Which commands the current user may run as root, some abusable
questions.explain: A misconfigured NOPASSWD entry can be an instant escalation.

questions.q: A writable script executed by root (e.g., via cron) allows:
options: Escalation by inserting commands that run with root privileges
questions.explain: Recommend correct ownership/permissions on scheduled scripts.

questions.q: An outdated kernel can allow escalation via:
questions.explain: Patching and least privilege are the fixes.

questions.q: "Path hijacking" escalation abuses:
options: A privileged program calling a binary by name with an attacker-controlled PATH
questions.explain: Use absolute paths and a clean environment in privileged scripts.

questions.q: Weak file permissions on /etc/shadow or a config could allow:
options: Reading hashes or altering privileged settings
questions.explain: Recommend correct permissions and auditing.

questions.q: Capabilities (getcap) matter because:
options: A binary with cap_setuid or similar can escalate without the SUID bit
questions.explain: Review file capabilities during enumeration.

questions.q: After demonstrating escalation, the tester must:
options: Document it, capture proof, and remediate/clean up any changes
questions.explain: Prove impact responsibly, then restore state.

questions.q: List SUID binaries on an authorized Linux host to look for escalation paths.
questions.explain: Cross-reference results with GTFOBins; report and fix risky ones.

labs.title: Escalate via a misconfiguration (lab)
labs.scenario: On a lab box, find one escalation path (SUID, sudo NOPASSWD, or writable root cron), demonstrate it, and write the fix.
steps: # exploit the one misconfig (PoC), capture id showing uid=0, then:
# fix: correct permissions/ownership, remove NOPASSWD, patch
verify: you gained root in the lab and documented the fix

labs.title: Enumerate with a helper (concept)
labs.scenario: Explain what an enumeration script (e.g., linpeas-style) checks for and why you still verify manually.
steps: # checks SUID, sudo, cron, kernel, writable files, creds in configs
# manual verification avoids false positives and confirms exploitability
verify: you can list the main categories it checks

labs.title: Report escalation findings
labs.scenario: Write the finding + remediation for a writable root cron script you exploited.
steps: # Finding: /etc/cron.d/backup runs a world-writable script as root -> local root
# Impact: any local user gains root
# Remediation: chown root:root, chmod 700 the script; audit cron dir perms
verify: a sysadmin could fix it from your write-up

blocks.x: After landing as a low-privilege user, the goal is to become **root**, then document the path and its fix. Classic checks:
**SUID binaries** — `find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null` lists programs that run with their owner's (often root's) privileges; some can be abused (cross-reference **GTFOBins**).
**`sudo -l`** — shows what you may run as root; a misconfigured `NOPASSWD` entry can be an instant escalation.
**Writable root cron scripts** — a script run by root that you can edit lets you run commands as root.
**Outdated kernel** — a known local kernel exploit.
**Path hijacking** — a privileged program calling a binary by name with an attacker-controlled PATH; fix with absolute paths.
**File capabilities** (`getcap`) — a binary with `cap_setuid` can escalate without the SUID bit.

Enumeration scripts (linpeas-style) automate these checks — SUID, sudo, cron, kernel, writable files, credentials in configs — but you still verify manually to avoid false positives. After demonstrating escalation, capture proof (`id` showing `uid=0`), then **remediate and clean up** any changes. A typical finding + fix reads: "world-writable script run by root as cron → local root; fix: `chown root:root`, `chmod 700`, audit the cron directory."

days.title: Privilege escalation (Windows)
days.objective: Escalate privileges on authorized Windows systems and report fixes.

questions.q: A common Windows privilege-escalation check is:
options: Misconfigured service permissions (unquoted paths, weak ACLs, writable service binaries)
questions.explain: Services running as SYSTEM with weak config are prime targets.

questions.q: "Unquoted service path" escalation abuses:
options: A service path with spaces and no quotes, letting a planted binary run as SYSTEM
questions.explain: Fix by quoting the ImagePath.

questions.q: "AlwaysInstallElevated" being enabled allows:
options: Any user to install an MSI as SYSTEM
questions.explain: A dangerous policy; disable it.

questions.q: Windows access tokens matter because:
options: Token impersonation/theft can let a process act as a higher-privilege account
questions.explain: Certain privileges (SeImpersonate) enable known escalation techniques.

questions.q: Stored credentials in the registry or files can allow:
options: Reuse to access higher-privilege accounts or other systems
questions.explain: Recommend credential hygiene and not storing secrets in plaintext.

questions.q: "DLL hijacking/search-order" escalation abuses:
options: A privileged process loading a DLL from a writable/attacker-controlled location
questions.explain: Fix with correct search paths and folder ACLs.

questions.q: A tool commonly used to enumerate Windows priv-esc paths is:
questions.explain: They automate the checks; still validate manually.

questions.q: After demonstrating Windows escalation, you should:
options: Capture proof (whoami /priv, SYSTEM shell), then remediate and clean up
questions.explain: Prove it, document it, restore state.

questions.q: On an authorized Windows host, show your privileges to look for escalation opportunities.
questions.explain: Look for SeImpersonatePrivilege and similar; enumerate services next.

labs.title: Enumerate Windows escalation (lab)
labs.scenario: On an authorized Windows lab VM, list your privileges and check for unquoted service paths and weak service ACLs.
steps: # note any unquoted path with spaces or writable service binary
verify: you identified at least one potential escalation vector

labs.title: Report a service-path finding
labs.scenario: Write the finding + fix for an unquoted service path you found.
steps: # Finding: service "App Backup" ImagePath is unquoted (C:\Program Files\App Backup\svc.exe)
# Impact: a planted C:\Program.exe could run as SYSTEM
# Fix: quote the ImagePath; restrict folder write permissions
verify: an admin could fix it directly

labs.title: Credential-hygiene recommendations
labs.scenario: List four Windows recommendations that reduce credential-based escalation.
steps: # LAPS for local admin passwords; no plaintext creds in scripts/registry
# least privilege + separate admin accounts; enable Credential Guard

blocks.x: On Windows the escalation paths differ but the mindset is the same — find a misconfiguration that grants SYSTEM. Common checks:

**Service misconfigurations** — services running as SYSTEM with weak permissions: an **unquoted service path** with spaces lets a planted binary run as SYSTEM; a **writable service binary** or weak service ACLs do the same.
**AlwaysInstallElevated** — if enabled, any user can install an MSI as SYSTEM.
**Access tokens** — certain privileges (like `SeImpersonate`) enable token-impersonation escalation.
**Stored credentials** in the registry or files can be reused for higher-privilege accounts.
**DLL hijacking** — a privileged process loading a DLL from a writable location.
`whoami /priv` shows your privileges (look for `SeImpersonatePrivilege`); tools like **WinPEAS** or **PowerUp** automate the checks.
After demonstrating escalation, capture proof and then remediate/clean up.

The remediations you recommend improve credential hygiene: **LAPS** for unique local admin passwords, no plaintext credentials in scripts/registry, least privilege with separate admin accounts, and enabling protections like Credential Guard.

days.title: Lateral movement and pivoting
days.objective: Move through an authorized network to demonstrate impact.

questions.q: Lateral movement means:
options: Using a compromised host to reach and compromise other in-scope systems
questions.explain: It shows how far an attacker could get from one foothold.

questions.q: "Pivoting" is:
options: Routing your traffic through a compromised host to reach otherwise unreachable networks
questions.explain: e.g., a foothold in the DMZ used to reach the internal LAN (in scope).

questions.q: Pass-the-hash enables lateral movement by:
options: Authenticating to other hosts with a captured hash, no plaintext needed
questions.explain: Recommend unique local admin passwords (LAPS) and SMB signing.

questions.q: Why is network segmentation the key defense against lateral movement?
options: It stops a single foothold from freely reaching other zones
questions.explain: Microsegmentation + least privilege contain a breach.

questions.q: "Credential dumping" during a test demonstrates:
options: That reusable credentials can be harvested to move laterally
questions.explain: Recommend Credential Guard, LAPS, and monitoring.

questions.q: A "jump/pivot host" reachable to many segments is high value because:
options: Compromising it grants broad reach across the network
questions.explain: Harden and closely monitor administrative jump hosts.

questions.q: Why keep lateral movement strictly in scope?
options: Reaching out-of-scope or third-party systems is illegal and harmful
questions.explain: Scope applies at every phase, always.

questions.q: A tester demonstrates lateral movement, then:
options: Documents the path and recommends segmentation and credential controls
questions.explain: The value is the reported attack path and its fixes.

questions.q: Set up a pivot (SSH dynamic port forward) through an authorized foothold host.
questions.explain: Then route in-scope tools through the SOCKS proxy (e.g., proxychains) to reach internal hosts.

labs.title: Demonstrate a pivot (authorized lab)
labs.scenario: Using an authorized foothold, reach an internal-only lab host through it and prove connectivity.
steps: ssh -D 1080 -N user@foothost &          # SOCKS proxy through the foothold
proxychains nmap -sT -Pn 10.0.50.5      # reach internal host via pivot
verify: you reached an internal host only accessible through the foothold

labs.title: Map an attack path
labs.scenario: Document a three-hop path (external -> DMZ -> app server -> DB) and the one control that best breaks it.
steps: # external phish -> DMZ web host -> reused creds -> app server -> DB
# best break: segment DMZ from internal + unique creds (LAPS) + MFA

labs.title: Recommend anti-lateral-movement controls
labs.scenario: List four controls that limit lateral movement and credential reuse.
steps: # LAPS (unique local admin passwords) + SMB signing
# least privilege + tiered admin; MFA on admin access
# EDR + monitoring for credential dumping/anomalous logons
verify: each control maps to a technique you used

blocks.x: A single foothold is rarely the objective — you show how far an attacker could get.
**Lateral movement** is using a compromised host to reach and compromise **other** in-scope systems.

**Pivoting** is routing your traffic *through* a compromised host to reach networks you otherwise couldn't — for example a DMZ foothold used to reach the internal LAN (in scope). An SSH dynamic port-forward (`ssh -D`) plus a SOCKS proxy is a common technique.
**Pass-the-hash** and **pass-the-ticket** reuse captured credentials/tickets to authenticate to other hosts without cracking passwords.
**Credential dumping** harvests reusable credentials to move on.
A **jump/pivot host** reachable to many segments is high value — compromising it grants broad reach.

The key defence against lateral movement is **network segmentation/microsegmentation**, so one foothold can't freely reach other zones. Add **unique local admin passwords (LAPS)** and **SMB signing** to stop credential reuse, least privilege and tiered admin, MFA on admin access, and EDR/monitoring for credential dumping and anomalous logons. Everything stays strictly in scope — reaching out-of-scope or third-party systems is illegal.

Keep secret access after the engagement

questions.q: Common Linux persistence mechanisms include:
options: Cron jobs, systemd services, SSH authorized_keys, and modified startup scripts

questions.q: Common Windows persistence mechanisms include:

questions.explain: EDR and autoruns tools detect these.

questions.q: Why must every persistence artifact be documented?
options: So it can be fully removed and the client can verify a clean environment
questions.explain: Leaving hidden access would be unethical and dangerous.

questions.q: "Cleanup" at the end of an engagement means:
options: Removing tools, accounts, implants, and changes you introduced
questions.explain: Restore systems to their prior state and confirm with the client.

questions.q: Why should you NOT delete the client's logs after testing?
options: Logs are the client's evidence and needed for detection review; deleting them is harmful
questions.explain: Attackers clear logs; ethical testers preserve them and note their own activity.

questions.q: Testing whether your actions were detected helps the client by:
questions.explain: Note which actions triggered (or should have triggered) alerts.

questions.q: A persistence finding in the report should include:
options: How it was established, where, and how to detect/remove similar techniques
questions.explain: Give defenders detection and removal guidance.

questions.q: List cron-based persistence locations to review on an authorized Linux host.
questions.explain: Also check ~/.ssh/authorized_keys and systemd user services for unexpected entries.

labs.title: Establish and remove persistence (lab)
labs.scenario: On an authorized lab host, add a benign persistence mechanism, confirm it, then fully remove it and verify.
steps: # add (lab): a marked cron entry, e.g. '# PENTEST-TEST' comment + harmless job
# remove it and confirm nothing remains
crontab -l | grep -c PENTEST-TEST     # should be 0 after cleanup
verify: the system is returned to its original state

labs.title: Detection review (purple)
labs.scenario: For two persistence techniques, describe how a defender would detect each.
steps: # cron/systemd changes -> file integrity monitoring + config audits
# SSH authorized_keys change -> alert on key additions + EDR
verify: each technique has a detection method

labs.title: Engagement cleanup checklist
labs.scenario: Write the end-of-engagement cleanup checklist.
steps: # remove test accounts, tools, implants, persistence
# restore any changed configs; confirm services normal
# deliver artifacts list to client; verify clean state together
verify: nothing you introduced remains on client systems

blocks.x: **Persistence** is how an attacker keeps access. In an authorised test you demonstrate it only if it's in scope, and — crucially — **everything you add must be documented and removed at the end**. Testing persistence also measures the client's detection (a purple-team benefit).
**Linux** persistence: cron jobs, systemd services, SSH `authorized_keys`, modified startup scripts.
**Windows** persistence: scheduled tasks, services, registry Run keys, startup folders.
Defenders monitor exactly these locations for unexpected changes.
**Cleanup** at the end of an engagement means removing every tool, account, implant and change you introduced, restoring systems to their prior state and confirming with the client.
**Never delete the client's logs** — those are the client's evidence needed for detection review. Attackers clear logs; ethical testers preserve them and note their own activity.
Leaving hidden access would be unethical and dangerous, so a persistence finding in the report includes how it was established and how to detect and remove similar techniques.

For each technique, note how a defender would catch it — cron/systemd changes via file-integrity monitoring and config audits; an `authorized_keys` change via key-addition alerts and EDR; beaconing via flow analysis. Testing whether your actions were detected is the purple-team value: undetected TTPs are exactly what the client needs to know about.
